name: Myocardial infarction (acute coronary syndrome)
epi: Common cardiovascular emergency in adults, rising with age and atherosclerotic risk factors; NSTEMI and unstable angina are more frequent than STEMI.
eti: Usually atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with platelet activation and coronary thrombosis; vasospasm and spontaneous coronary artery dissection are nonatherosclerotic causes.
cli: Substernal chest pressure radiating to arm, jaw or neck with dyspnea, diaphoresis or nausea; women, older adults and diabetics more often present atypically.
inv: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes distinguishes STEMI from NSTE-ACS; serial high-sensitivity troponin confirms infarction, with risk scores and coronary angiography guiding management.
tre: Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, parenteral anticoagulation, anti-ischemic therapy and high-intensity statin; primary PCI is preferred reperfusion for STEMI, with fibrinolysis if timely PCI is unavailable.

name: Essential hypertension
epi: Very common, affecting nearly half of adults worldwide; prevalence rises with age, and family history, obesity, high salt intake and inactivity increase risk.
eti: Multifactorial primary hypertension without an identifiable secondary cause, involving salt sensitivity and volume expansion, RAAS dysregulation and sympathetic overactivity on a genetic background.
cli: Usually asymptomatic and found on screening; symptoms arise mainly from target-organ damage such as stroke, coronary disease, heart failure or kidney disease.
inv: Confirm with repeated standardized office readings on separate occasions, ideally with home or ambulatory monitoring; check ECG, creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, lipids, glucose and urine albumin to assess risk and target organs.
tre: Lifestyle change (weight loss, salt restriction, exercise, limited alcohol) plus first-line drugs such as thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or calcium-channel blockers chosen by comorbidity.

name: Asthma
epi: Common chronic airway disease affecting about 260 million people worldwide; often begins in childhood but can start at any age.
eti: Chronic airway inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness from gene-environment interaction; allergens, viral infections, exercise, irritants and occupational exposures trigger reversible airflow obstruction.
cli: Episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal), dyspnea and chest tightness; severe attacks cause inability to speak in sentences, and a silent chest or exhaustion signals impending respiratory failure.
inv: Spirometry showing obstruction with bronchodilator reversibility (FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 mL) supports diagnosis; peak-flow variability, FeNO or bronchoprovocation help when spirometry is normal.
tre: Stepwise inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, with GINA favoring as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol over SABA-only relief; acute attacks need repeated bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids and oxygen, with magnesium for severe cases.

name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
epi: Common, underdiagnosed chronic respiratory disease and a leading cause of death worldwide; strongly linked to smoking, though a substantial minority never smoked.
eti: Abnormal inflammatory response to tobacco smoke, biomass fuel or occupational dusts causing small-airway disease and emphysema; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic cause.
cli: Chronic cough, sputum and progressive exertional dyspnea; exacerbations, often infective, bring increased dyspnea and sputum volume or purulence.
inv: Post-bronchodilator spirometry with FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent obstruction; symptom scores, blood eosinophils, imaging and alpha-1 antitrypsin testing guide assessment.
tre: Smoking cessation, vaccination and pulmonary rehabilitation; long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA/LABA) are maintenance mainstays, with ICS added by exacerbations and eosinophils, and oxygen for chronic severe hypoxemia.

name: Community-acquired pneumonia
epi: Common lower respiratory infection acquired outside hospital and a leading infectious cause of death; risk rises with age, smoking, chronic disease and immune compromise.
eti: Most often Streptococcus pneumoniae; also Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) and respiratory viruses, usually via microaspiration.
cli: Fever, chills, productive cough, dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with tachypnea and focal crackles; older or immunocompromised patients may present with confusion or weakness.
inv: Chest radiograph shows a new infiltrate; CBC, chemistry and oximetry, CURB-65 or PSI to guide site of care, and blood and sputum cultures before antibiotics in hospitalized patients.
tre: Empiric antibiotics by severity: amoxicillin, doxycycline or a macrolide for healthy outpatients, beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone for inpatients, usually 5-7 days, plus oxygen and supportive care.

name: Obstructive sleep apnea
epi: Very common, affecting nearly a billion people worldwide; more frequent in men, with obesity and increasing age.
eti: Recurrent upper-airway collapse during sleep due to anatomic narrowing (obesity, tonsillar hypertrophy, retrognathia) and reduced dilator muscle tone, causing intermittent hypoxemia and arousals.
cli: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping, unrefreshing sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness and morning headache; associated with hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
inv: In-laboratory polysomnography is the gold standard, giving the apnea-hypopnea index; home sleep apnea testing suits high-probability adults without major comorbidity; STOP-BANG and Epworth help screen.
tre: CPAP is the most effective treatment; weight loss, positional therapy, oral appliances and surgery for selected patients or anatomic causes.

name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
epi: Very common, affecting about one in five adults in Western populations; risk rises with obesity, pregnancy, smoking, hiatal hernia and certain medications.
eti: Reflux of gastric contents due to transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, low LES pressure, hiatal hernia, impaired esophageal clearance or delayed gastric emptying.
cli: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical; chest pain, chronic cough, laryngitis, asthma and dental erosion are extraesophageal features, and dysphagia or weight loss are alarm signs.
inv: Presumptive diagnosis from typical symptoms with PPI trial; upper endoscopy for alarm features or refractory symptoms, and ambulatory pH monitoring to confirm uncertain cases.
tre: Lifestyle measures (weight loss, head-of-bed elevation, avoiding late meals) plus a once-daily proton-pump inhibitor; antireflux surgery or endoscopic therapy for selected refractory cases.

name: Acute appendicitis
epi: Common surgical emergency, most frequent between ages 5 and 45 with a slight male predominance.
eti: Luminal obstruction by appendicolith, lymphoid hyperplasia (especially in children) or tumor raises pressure, causing ischemia, bacterial overgrowth and potential perforation.
cli: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with anorexia, nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever; McBurney point tenderness and rebound, with atypical presentations in young, old and pregnant patients.
inv: Clinical assessment with leukocytosis and raised CRP; ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, CT (over 95% accurate) in adults.
tre: Laparoscopic appendectomy with antibiotics is standard; antibiotics alone are an option for selected uncomplicated cases, and perforation with abscess may need drainage.

name: Acute pancreatitis
epi: Leading cause of gastrointestinal hospitalization in the US, peaking in middle age; gallstones and alcohol cause most cases.
eti: Premature intra-acinar trypsin activation causes autodigestion and inflammation; triggers include gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia, drugs, post-ERCP injury and genetic variants, with some cases idiopathic.
cli: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting; severe disease causes SIRS, organ failure and occasionally Cullen or Grey Turner signs.
inv: Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, lipase or amylase at least 3 times normal, or compatible imaging; ultrasound for gallstones, CT reserved for unclear diagnosis or complications.
tre: Moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer fluids, analgesia and early oral or enteral feeding; no prophylactic antibiotics, urgent ERCP for cholangitis or obstruction and same-admission cholecystectomy for gallstone disease.

name: Peptic ulcer disease
epi: Common, with a lifetime risk of about 5-10%; duodenal ulcers outnumber gastric ulcers, and incidence is falling with H. pylori treatment.
eti: Imbalance between acid-pepsin injury and mucosal defense, mainly from Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID-induced prostaglandin inhibition; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare cause.
cli: Epigastric pain, classically worse after meals in gastric and relieved by food in duodenal ulcer; complications include bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation and gastric outlet obstruction.
inv: Upper endoscopy is the gold standard, with biopsy of gastric ulcers; test for H. pylori by urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy; urgent endoscopy after resuscitation for bleeding.
tre: Proton-pump inhibitor, stop NSAIDs and eradicate H. pylori with a regimen chosen by local resistance (often bismuth quadruple therapy); endoscopic hemostasis for bleeding, with embolization or surgery if it fails.

name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
epi: Accounts for about 5-10% of diabetes; usually begins in childhood or adolescence but can occur at any age, with marked geographic variation (highest in Finland).
eti: T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells in genetically susceptible (HLA-linked) people, possibly triggered by viral or other environmental factors, causing absolute insulin deficiency.
cli: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and fatigue, often developing over weeks; diabetic ketoacidosis is a common presentation in children, while adult onset may be slower and mistaken for type 2.
inv: Diabetes confirmed by fasting glucose, random glucose with symptoms or HbA1c criteria; islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) and low C-peptide confirm type 1.
tre: Lifelong insulin by multiple daily injections or pump with glucose monitoring (often CGM), carbohydrate counting, education, hypoglycemia management and complication screening; DKA needs emergency protocol.

name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
epi: Accounts for about 90% of diabetes; very common and rising, associated with older age, obesity, inactivity, family history and certain ethnic groups.
eti: Insulin resistance, promoted by central obesity, combined with progressive beta-cell failure leads to chronic hyperglycemia; strong polygenic inheritance.
cli: Often asymptomatic for years; may cause polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision, infections and poor wound healing, with acanthosis nigricans and micro- and macrovascular complications.
inv: Diagnosed by HbA1c at least 6.5%, fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour OGTT glucose at least 200 mg/dL, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with symptoms; screen for complications.
tre: Diet, exercise and weight loss, with metformin usually first-line; SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists are added for cardiorenal benefit or weight, plus blood pressure, lipid and complication management.

name: Diabetes mellitus (overview)
epi: Affects about 1 in 11 adults worldwide; type 2 makes up about 90% of cases, while type 1 usually begins in childhood.
eti: Type 1 results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction causing absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 from insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; other types include gestational and monogenic diabetes.
cli: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue and blurred vision; chronic hyperglycemia causes retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy and cardiovascular disease, and acute crises include DKA and HHS.
inv: HbA1c at least 6.5%, fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour OGTT at least 200 mg/dL or symptomatic random glucose at least 200 mg/dL; classify type and screen urine albumin, lipids, eyes and feet.
tre: Education, diet and exercise for all; type 1 requires insulin, while type 2 starts with metformin and adds agents such as SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists or insulin as needed.

name: Ischemic stroke
epi: About 87% of strokes are ischemic; a leading cause of death and disability, with risk rising with age, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes and smoking.
eti: Thrombotic or embolic arterial occlusion causing focal brain ischemia; TOAST subtypes are large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel (lacunar) occlusion, other and undetermined causes.
cli: Sudden focal deficit by territory: MCA strokes cause contralateral face/arm weakness and sensory loss with aphasia or neglect; posterior strokes cause visual loss, ataxia and vertigo; NIHSS grades severity.
inv: Urgent noncontrast CT excludes hemorrhage, with CT angiography or perfusion for large-vessel occlusion and MRI DWI to confirm infarction; glucose, ECG, labs and later cardiac and vascular workup.
tre: IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours for eligible patients and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients; then antiplatelets or anticoagulation and risk-factor control.

name: Alzheimer disease
epi: Most common cause of dementia; incidence doubles about every 5 years after 65, affecting roughly 10% over 65 and far more over 85.
eti: Neurodegeneration with extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau tangles and cholinergic loss; age and APOE e4 are major risk factors, and APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 mutations cause early-onset familial disease.
cli: Insidious progressive loss of recent memory, then language, visuospatial and executive decline with neuropsychiatric symptoms, ending in complete dependence.
inv: Cognitive testing (MMSE, MoCA), labs to exclude reversible causes (B12, TSH), MRI showing hippocampal atrophy; CSF amyloid/tau or amyloid PET biomarkers in selected patients.
tre: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and memantine for symptoms; anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) for selected early disease; caregiver support and behavioral management.

name: Bell palsy
epi: Most common cause of acute unilateral facial palsy, with a lifetime risk of about 1 in 60; peaks at 20-30 and 60-70 years, more common in pregnancy and diabetes.
eti: Idiopathic inflammation and edema of the facial nerve in the narrow labyrinthine segment of the facial canal, probably from herpes simplex virus 1 reactivation.
cli: Unilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness, including the forehead, peaking within 72 hours, with incomplete eye closure, ear pain, hyperacusis and altered taste.
inv: Clinical diagnosis after excluding stroke, Lyme disease, Ramsay Hunt syndrome and tumor; imaging and electrodiagnostic testing only for atypical, recurrent or complete palsy.
tre: Oral corticosteroids started within 72 hours, optionally with an antiviral in severe cases, plus eye protection with lubricants and taping; most patients recover fully.

name: Acute cystitis (lower urinary tract infection)
epi: Very common in women, with about half having at least one UTI; risk rises with sexual activity, pregnancy, menopause, catheters and, in men, prostatic obstruction.
eti: Ascending infection by bowel flora, mostly uropathogenic Escherichia coli (about 80%), also Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella and Proteus.
cli: Sudden dysuria, frequency, urgency, nocturia and suprapubic pain with cloudy urine or hematuria; fever or flank pain suggests pyelonephritis.
inv: Typical uncomplicated cystitis in women can be diagnosed clinically or with dipstick (leukocyte esterase, nitrite); culture for men, pregnancy, complicated, recurrent or failed cases.
tre: Short-course nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (where resistance is low) or single-dose fosfomycin for uncomplicated cystitis, adjusted for local resistance.

name: Superficial candidiasis (oral thrush / vulvovaginal candidiasis)
epi: Common; about 75% of women have at least one vulvovaginal episode, and oral thrush occurs in infants, older denture wearers, inhaled-steroid users and immunocompromised people, especially HIV.
eti: Overgrowth of commensal Candida, mostly C. albicans, when local or systemic defenses are disturbed by antibiotics, corticosteroids, diabetes, pregnancy or immunosuppression; VVC is not usually sexually acquired.
cli: Oral thrush shows creamy white plaques that wipe off leaving red mucosa, with soreness or altered taste; VVC causes vulval itch, soreness, dysuria and thick white discharge.
inv: Usually clinical; KOH or saline microscopy shows budding yeast and hyphae with normal vaginal pH (under 4.5), and culture is reserved for recurrent or treatment-failing cases.
tre: Topical antifungals (nystatin, clotrimazole, miconazole) for oral thrush and topical azole or single-dose oral fluconazole for uncomplicated VVC; address predisposing factors, partners not treated.

name: Acute gastroenteritis
epi: Extremely common worldwide and a major cause of child deaths in low-income countries; dehydration risk is highest in infants and older adults.
eti: Mostly viral (norovirus, rotavirus), also bacterial (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, C. difficile) or parasitic (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), spread by fecal-oral, food or water routes.
cli: Sudden nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhea, sometimes fever; bloody diarrhea suggests invasive bacteria, and severe dehydration can cause shock.
inv: Usually clinical; stool testing for bloody, severe, persistent, outbreak or high-risk cases, with electrolytes and renal function when dehydration is significant.
tre: Oral rehydration solution is the cornerstone, with IV fluids for severe dehydration; antibiotics only for specific pathogens, and antimotility agents avoided in bloody diarrhea, C. difficile or E. coli O157:H7.

name: Impetigo
epi: Very common superficial skin infection, about 10% of pediatric skin complaints, peaking at ages 2-5 in warm months; bullous form mainly affects infants.
eti: Staphylococcus aureus causes most cases, with Streptococcus pyogenes alone or combined; bullous impetigo is due to staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, and spread is by direct contact.
cli: Nonbullous form shows vesicles or pustules rupturing into honey-colored crusts on the face and limbs; bullous form shows flaccid bullae, often intertriginous.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; culture for extensive, recurrent or nonresponding disease or suspected MRSA.
tre: Topical mupirocin, retapamulin or fusidic acid for localized disease; oral antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin or dicloxacillin) for extensive or bullous disease, with hygiene to limit spread.

name: Psoriasis
epi: Chronic immune-mediated skin disease affecting about 2% of people, with onset peaks at 15-20 and 55-60 years.
eti: T-cell-driven (IL-23/IL-17) inflammation causes keratinocyte hyperproliferation in genetically predisposed people; triggers include skin trauma (Koebner), streptococcal infection, stress and drugs such as lithium and beta-blockers.
cli: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp and lower back; variants include guttate, pustular, inverse and erythrodermic, with nail pitting and psoriatic arthritis in about 30%.
inv: Clinical diagnosis (Auspitz sign); biopsy showing parakeratosis and Munro microabscesses if uncertain; screen for psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic comorbidity.
tre: Emollients, topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues for limited disease; narrowband UVB, methotrexate or other systemics, and biologics (TNF, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors) for extensive or severe disease.

name: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
epi: Affects 10-30% of children and 2-10% of adults in developed countries; about 60% begin in the first year of life, often with asthma or allergic rhinitis.
eti: Epidermal barrier dysfunction (e.g., filaggrin mutations) with type 2 immune inflammation and Staphylococcus aureus colonization; irritants, allergens, sweat and stress trigger flares.
cli: Intensely itchy dry eczema: facial and extensor in infants, flexural in children, lichenified hand and flexural lesions in adults; complications include secondary bacterial infection and eczema herpeticum.
inv: Clinical diagnosis based on age-typical pattern, itch and chronic relapsing course; patch testing, swabs or biopsy only for suspected contact allergy, infection or atypical cases.
tre: Regular emollients and trigger avoidance with topical corticosteroids for flares; topical calcineurin inhibitors as steroid-sparing agents, and phototherapy, dupilumab or JAK inhibitors for severe disease.

name: Tinea cruris
epi: Common superficial fungal infection, mostly in adolescent and adult males, favored by sweating, obesity, occlusive clothing and hot humid climates.
eti: Dermatophyte infection of groin skin, mainly Trichophyton rubrum, often spread from the patient's own tinea pedis.
cli: Itchy erythematous scaly annular plaque with raised advancing border and central clearing on the inner thighs and groin, typically sparing the scrotum.
inv: Usually clinical; KOH microscopy of scrapings shows septate hyphae, with culture for uncertain or resistant cases.
tre: Topical allylamine (terbinafine) or azole for 2-4 weeks, keeping the area dry and treating coexisting tinea pedis; oral antifungals for extensive or refractory disease.

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
epi: Affects about 0.5% of people worldwide; two to three times more common in women, with onset usually in middle age.
eti: Systemic autoimmune disease in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DRB1 shared epitope), with smoking the strongest environmental trigger; RF and anti-CCP precede chronic synovitis that erodes cartilage and bone.
cli: Symmetric polyarthritis of small hand and foot joints (MCP, PIP, MTP) with morning stiffness over an hour; deformities, rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease and secondary Sjogren can occur.
inv: RF and highly specific anti-CCP antibodies, ESR/CRP and imaging for erosions; 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria score joints, serology, acute-phase reactants and duration of at least 6 weeks.
tre: Early methotrexate-based DMARD therapy with treat-to-target strategy, short-term glucocorticoids or NSAIDs for flares, and biologic or JAK inhibitor therapy if response is inadequate.

name: Gout
epi: Most common inflammatory arthritis in men, affecting about 4% of US adults; risk rises with age, obesity, alcohol, kidney disease and diuretic use.
eti: Persistent hyperuricemia (urate above about 6.8 mg/dL), usually from reduced renal excretion, leads to monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints and tissues.
cli: Sudden severe red, hot, swollen monoarthritis, classically the first MTP joint (podagra), peaking within 24 hours; recurrent attacks can lead to tophi and chronic polyarticular disease.
inv: Synovial fluid polarized microscopy showing needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals is diagnostic and excludes septic arthritis; serum urate may be normal during a flare.
tre: Flares: NSAIDs, colchicine or corticosteroids started early; urate-lowering therapy, first-line allopurinol titrated to urate below 6 mg/dL, for recurrent flares or tophi, with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis at initiation.

name: Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones)
epi: Affects about 1 in 11 people over a lifetime, twice as often in men; recurrence approaches 50% within 10 years without prevention.
eti: Urinary supersaturation from low fluid intake, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria or hypocitraturia; calcium oxalate causes most stones, with uric acid, struvite and cystine less common.
cli: Sudden colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria, nausea and restlessness; fever with obstruction indicates infected obstruction, a urologic emergency.
inv: Noncontrast CT is the gold standard, with ultrasound in pregnancy and children; urinalysis, renal function, stone analysis and 24-hour urine metabolic testing for recurrent formers.
tre: Analgesia (NSAIDs first-line) and hydration, with tamsulosin expulsive therapy for selected distal ureteral stones; urgent stent or nephrostomy for infected obstruction, and lithotripsy or ureteroscopy for large or persistent stones.

name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
epi: Very common in aging men, with histologic BPH in about half of men in their 60s and most men over 80.
eti: Androgen (DHT)-dependent hyperplasia of the prostatic transition zone causes static obstruction, while smooth-muscle tone adds a dynamic component to bladder outlet obstruction.
cli: Lower urinary tract symptoms: weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, incomplete emptying, frequency, urgency and nocturia; complications include retention, UTI, stones and hematuria.
inv: History with IPSS score, digital rectal exam and urinalysis; PSA, post-void residual and uroflowmetry selectively, with cystoscopy and imaging before surgery.
tre: Watchful waiting and lifestyle measures for mild symptoms; alpha-blockers for rapid relief, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors for large glands, combination therapy, and TURP or other procedures for refractory symptoms or complications.

name: Iron deficiency anemia
epi: Most common cause of anemia worldwide, especially in menstruating or pregnant women, infants and toddlers; in men and postmenopausal women it usually signals GI blood loss.
eti: Iron loss or deficit from chronic bleeding (menstrual, gastrointestinal), increased requirements, poor intake or malabsorption (celiac disease, gastric surgery) limits hemoglobin synthesis.
cli: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea, headache and pica; glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia and, rarely, Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
inv: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin (most specific test) and low transferrin saturation; investigate cause, including endoscopy for GI loss in men and postmenopausal women.
tre: Oral iron (e.g., ferrous sulfate) is first-line, with IV iron for intolerance, malabsorption or ongoing loss; treat the underlying cause and confirm hemoglobin and ferritin response.

name: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)
epi: Common in children aged 6 months to 3 years, slightly more in boys, peaking in autumn and early winter.
eti: Viral infection, mainly parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, causing subglottic laryngeal and tracheal inflammation and edema.
cli: After 1-2 days of coryza and low fever, barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor, worse at night; stridor at rest, retractions, agitation or lethargy indicate severe obstruction.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with severity graded by the Westley score; neck radiograph (steeple sign) only if diagnosis is uncertain, and it should not delay treatment.
tre: Single-dose oral dexamethasone for all severities, plus nebulized epinephrine for moderate-severe stridor; oxygen and airway expertise if respiratory failure threatens.

name: RSV bronchiolitis
epi: Leading cause of infant hospitalization, affecting children under 2 in autumn-winter epidemics; prematurity, age under 3 months and heart or lung disease raise risk.
eti: Viral lower respiratory infection, most often respiratory syncytial virus, causing small-airway inflammation, edema, necrosis and mucus plugging.
cli: Coryza followed after 2-3 days by cough, tachypnea, retractions, wheeze and fine crackles with feeding difficulty; young infants may have apnea.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with pulse oximetry; chest radiograph, blood tests and viral testing are not routinely needed.
tre: Supportive care with nasal suctioning, hydration and oxygen or high-flow support as needed; bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not recommended, and nirsevimab or maternal RSV vaccination prevents disease.

name: Febrile seizure
epi: Most common childhood seizure, affecting 2-5% of children aged 6 months to 5 years with a peak at 12-18 months; about 30% recur.
eti: Seizure provoked by fever (at least 38 C) without CNS infection in a developmentally susceptible brain, often with viral illness such as HHV-6 and a family history.
cli: Simple: single generalized seizure under 15 minutes with rapid return to baseline; complex: focal, 15 minutes or longer, or recurring within 24 hours.
inv: Simple febrile seizures need no routine EEG, imaging or blood tests beyond finding the fever source; lumbar puncture if meningeal signs, incomplete immunization or pretreatment with antibiotics.
tre: Treat the fever source and reassure; benzodiazepine for seizures over 5 minutes; antipyretics do not prevent recurrence and long-term antiseizure drugs are not indicated, with epilepsy risk only slightly raised.

name: Acute cholecystitis
epi: Common complication of gallstones, more frequent in women, obesity and pregnancy; about 95% of cases are calculous.
eti: Persistent cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone causes gallbladder distension and inflammation with secondary infection; acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients or with TPN.
cli: Constant right upper quadrant pain lasting over several hours, radiating to the right shoulder, with fever, nausea, vomiting and positive Murphy sign; jaundice suggests duct stones or Mirizzi syndrome.
inv: Leukocytosis and raised CRP; ultrasound is first-line, showing stones, wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid and sonographic Murphy sign, with HIDA scan if equivocal.
tre: IV fluids, analgesia, bowel rest and antibiotics, then early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ideally within 72 hours); percutaneous cholecystostomy for patients too ill for surgery.

name: Anaphylaxis
epi: Lifetime prevalence of about 1-3% and rising; occurs at any age, with foods common in children and drugs and venom in adults.
eti: Acute systemic mast-cell and basophil degranulation, usually IgE-mediated, triggered by foods (peanut, tree nuts, shellfish), insect venom, drugs or latex; some cases are non-IgE or idiopathic.
cli: Rapid onset of urticaria or flushing, angioedema, stridor, wheeze, hypotension, collapse and GI symptoms; most deaths occur within the first hour, and biphasic reactions can follow.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; treatment must not wait for tests. Serum tryptase drawn within hours can support the diagnosis, and allergy testing later identifies the trigger.
tre: Immediate IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5-10 minutes as needed, with airway support, oxygen and IV fluids; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only, followed by observation and an epinephrine autoinjector.

name: Enterobiasis (pinworm infection)
epi: Most common worm infection in the US, mainly in preschool and school-aged children, institutions and their household contacts.
eti: Enterobius vermicularis; females lay eggs perianally at night, which become infective within hours and spread by fingernails, bedding and surfaces (fecal-oral autoinfection).
cli: Nocturnal perianal itching with disturbed sleep and excoriation; may cause vulvovaginitis in girls, and many infections are asymptomatic.
inv: Adhesive tape test of perianal skin on waking, before bathing, on several mornings; stool ova testing is insensitive.
tre: Mebendazole, albendazole or pyrantel pamoate, with a second dose 2 weeks later; treat household members together and reinforce hand washing, nail trimming and laundering.

name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
epi: Common, especially in children, with winter-spring peaks; most cases are self-limiting.
eti: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae in adults, and H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae and Moraxella in children; Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute disease and Chlamydia chronic follicular conjunctivitis.
cli: Red eye with mucopurulent discharge and morning lid matting, usually without pain or visual loss; copious rapidly progressive pus suggests gonococcal infection.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; Gram stain and culture or NAAT for hyperacute, neonatal, severe, contact-lens-related or nonresponding cases.
tre: Hygiene with optional topical antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, trimethoprim-polymyxin) for mild cases; fluoroquinolones for contact lens wearers, and systemic therapy for gonococcal or chlamydial disease.

name: Acute otitis media
epi: Very common, affecting most children at least once, with peak incidence at 6-12 months; daycare, smoke exposure and bottle feeding raise risk.
eti: Eustachian tube dysfunction after viral URI allows middle-ear infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis, or viruses.
cli: Ear pain or tugging, fever, irritability and reduced hearing, sometimes otorrhea; otoscopy shows a bulging, opaque, poorly mobile tympanic membrane.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by (pneumatic) otoscopy requiring moderate-severe bulging, new otorrhea, or mild bulging with recent pain or erythema; imaging and cultures are not routine.
tre: Analgesia for all; observation for selected older children with mild unilateral disease, and high-dose amoxicillin first-line when antibiotics are needed (amoxicillin-clavulanate if recent amoxicillin); tympanostomy tubes for recurrent AOM.

name: Acute pyelonephritis
epi: Common upper UTI, most frequent in young sexually active women; pregnancy, obstruction, diabetes and catheters increase risk.
eti: Usually ascending infection from the bladder, mostly Escherichia coli, with Klebsiella, Proteus and other gram-negatives; rarely hematogenous (e.g., S. aureus).
cli: Fever, chills, flank pain, nausea and vomiting with costovertebral angle tenderness, often with dysuria and frequency; can progress to urosepsis.
inv: Urinalysis plus urine culture before antibiotics, with blood tests and cultures if unwell; contrast CT or ultrasound for severe, complicated or nonresponding cases.
tre: Oral fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX (per susceptibility) for mild outpatient cases; IV ceftriaxone or broader agents for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy or failure, with urgent drainage of obstruction.

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
epi: Most common entrapment neuropathy, affecting 1-5% of people, three times more often women, typically aged 40-60.
eti: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, associated with repetitive or vibrating hand use, pregnancy, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis.
cli: Pain, numbness and paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger, worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand; thenar wasting and weakness in advanced disease.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by Tinel and Phalen tests; nerve conduction studies and EMG confirm and grade severity before surgery.
tre: Night splinting in neutral position and activity modification for mild cases, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief, and surgical carpal tunnel release for severe, persistent or motor disease.

name: Tinea corporis (ringworm)
epi: Very common worldwide, especially in children, athletes, hot humid climates and immunocompromised people.
eti: Dermatophyte infection of keratinized skin by Trichophyton (mainly T. rubrum), Microsporum or Epidermophyton, spread from people, animals, soil or fomites.
cli: Itchy annular plaque with a sharply marginated raised scaly red edge and central clearing on the trunk or limbs; steroid misuse causes atypical tinea incognito.
inv: Usually clinical; KOH microscopy of edge scrapings shows septate branching hyphae, with culture for confirmation in atypical cases.
tre: Topical azole or terbinafine for 2-3 weeks for localized disease; oral terbinafine or itraconazole for extensive, scalp, nail or resistant infection, avoiding steroid-only creams.

name: Acute pharyngitis
epi: Extremely common; most cases are viral, while group A streptococcus causes up to about a third of cases in children aged 5-15 and fewer in adults.
eti: Respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza, EBV) cause most cases; Streptococcus pyogenes is the main bacterial cause.
cli: Sore throat, odynophagia and fever; tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and absent cough favor strep, while cough, coryza and conjunctivitis suggest viral infection.
inv: Centor/McIsaac criteria guide testing; rapid antigen test or throat culture confirms GAS, and heterophile testing if mononucleosis is suspected.
tre: Analgesia and supportive care for viral disease; confirmed GAS is treated with penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever, with alternatives for penicillin allergy.

name: Hordeolum (stye)
epi: Common at all ages; more frequent with blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, rosacea, diabetes and poor lid hygiene.
eti: Acute bacterial infection of an eyelid gland, caused by Staphylococcus aureus in about 90-95% of cases; external involves Zeis or Moll glands, internal the meibomian glands.
cli: Acute painful red eyelid swelling: external forms point at the lash line as a pustule, internal forms cause diffuse swelling seen on lid eversion; a painless lump suggests chalazion.
inv: Clinical diagnosis on eyelid examination; culture or biopsy only for recurrent or atypical lesions, and assess for preseptal cellulitis.
tre: Warm compresses and lid hygiene, with most resolving in 1-2 weeks; topical antibiotic ointment is often used though evidence is limited, and incision and drainage or oral antibiotics for persistent lesions or cellulitis.

name: Contact dermatitis
epi: Very common, especially occupational dermatitis, of which about 80% is irritant; allergic forms are frequent with jewelry, cosmetics and plant exposure.
eti: Irritant type is direct nonimmune skin damage (detergents, wet work); allergic type is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity to nickel, fragrances, preservatives, topical neomycin or poison ivy.
cli: Itchy or burning erythema, vesicles and scaling confined to the contact site, becoming lichenified when chronic; allergic reactions appear 24-72 hours after exposure.
inv: Clinical diagnosis from distribution and exposure history; patch testing is the gold standard for identifying allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis.
tre: Identify and avoid the irritant or allergen, use protective gloves and emollients, and treat inflammation with topical corticosteroids; systemic steroids for severe widespread allergic reactions.

name: Plantar fasciitis
epi: Most common cause of plantar heel pain, affecting about 10% of people over a lifetime, peaking at ages 40-60 and with obesity, running or prolonged standing.
eti: Repetitive overload causing microtears and degeneration (fasciosis) of the plantar fascia at its medial calcaneal origin; flat or high-arched feet and tight calf muscles contribute, and heel spurs are incidental.
cli: Sharp heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with walking then worsening with prolonged standing; tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle and positive windlass test.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; imaging is unnecessary in typical cases, with radiograph or ultrasound to exclude stress fracture or other causes in refractory disease.
tre: Stretching of calf and plantar fascia, activity modification, supportive footwear or orthotics, NSAIDs and night splints; shock-wave therapy or injections for persistent cases, with surgery rarely after 6-12 months.

name: Acute rhinosinusitis
epi: Very common, affecting about 15% of US adults yearly and a leading reason for antibiotic prescription; most cases follow a viral cold.
eti: Mostly viral (rhinovirus, influenza, others); about 0.5-2% become bacterial, due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis.
cli: Purulent nasal discharge with nasal obstruction or facial pain or pressure, plus reduced smell; bacterial disease suggested by symptoms over 10 days, severe onset with high fever or double worsening.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; imaging is not routine, with CT reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications or chronic disease.
tre: Supportive care with saline irrigation, analgesics and intranasal corticosteroids; watchful waiting or amoxicillin (with or without clavulanate) for suspected bacterial cases, and urgent care for complications.

name: Otitis externa (swimmer's ear)
epi: Affects about 10% of people over a lifetime, peaking in childhood and summer, with swimming, humidity and ear-canal trauma as risk factors.
eti: Usually bacterial infection of the external canal, mainly Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, promoted by moisture and skin barrier loss; fungal (Aspergillus, Candida) cases are less common.
cli: Ear pain disproportionate to findings, tragal or pinna tenderness, itch, canal edema and discharge; malignant otitis externa in diabetic or immunocompromised patients causes severe pain and cranial nerve palsies.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by otoscopy; culture for recurrent, resistant or immunocompromised cases, and CT or MRI if malignant otitis externa is suspected.
tre: Topical antibiotic drops (fluoroquinolone or neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone) with analgesia, aural toilet and a wick if swollen; keep ear dry, and systemic antipseudomonal therapy for malignant disease.

name: Urticaria (hives)
epi: Acute urticaria affects about 20% of people in their lifetime; chronic urticaria (over 6 weeks) affects about 1%, mostly women aged 30-50.
eti: Mast-cell degranulation releases histamine causing dermal edema; acute cases are often triggered by infections, drugs, foods or stings, while chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune or idiopathic.
cli: Itchy, migratory, well-circumscribed raised wheals, each resolving within 24 hours without marks; angioedema may accompany them, and systemic features suggest anaphylaxis.
inv: Clinical diagnosis from history and examination; limited tests (CBC, CRP or ESR, TSH) in chronic urticaria, and lesional biopsy if wheals last over 24 hours to look for urticarial vasculitis.
tre: Avoid triggers; second-generation H1 antihistamines first-line, up-dosed to 4 times standard dose if needed, then omalizumab for refractory chronic disease; short steroid courses only for severe acute flares.

name: Scabies
epi: Affects about 200-300 million people yearly worldwide, especially in crowded, low-resource settings, nursing homes, children and older adults.
eti: Infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis mites burrowing in the epidermis, spread by prolonged skin-to-skin contact; itching reflects a delayed hypersensitivity to mites and their products.
cli: Intense nocturnal itch with papules and burrows in finger webs, wrists, axillae, umbilicus, genitals and buttocks; infants can have scalp, palm and sole lesions, and crusted scabies occurs in immunocompromised people.
inv: Usually clinical; dermoscopy (delta-wing or jetliner sign) or skin scraping microscopy showing mites, eggs or feces confirms.
tre: Topical permethrin 5% repeated after 7-14 days or oral ivermectin, treating all close contacts at once and washing bedding and clothing; crusted scabies needs combined permethrin, ivermectin and keratolytics.

name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
epi: Common in older adults; found in many patients with macrocytosis, with risk from vegan diet, pernicious anemia, gastric or ileal surgery, metformin and long-term acid suppression.
eti: Inadequate intake, loss of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), ileal malabsorption or drugs (metformin, nitrous oxide) impair DNA synthesis and myelination via methylmalonyl-CoA and homocysteine pathways.
cli: Megaloblastic anemia with fatigue, pallor and glossitis; neurologic disease, which may occur without anemia, includes neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration with vibration and proprioceptive loss, ataxia and cognitive change.
inv: CBC with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, low serum B12, raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine in borderline cases; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies and MRI dorsal-column changes when relevant.
tre: IM hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin for malabsorption or neurologic disease, with high-dose oral B12 an alternative for dietary or mild deficiency; treat the cause, and do not give folate alone.

name: Pernicious anemia
epi: Most common cause of severe B12 deficiency in developed countries, mainly affecting adults over 60, often with other autoimmune diseases.
eti: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis destroys parietal cells and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies block B12 binding, so B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
cli: Macrocytic anemia with fatigue, pallor, glossitis and weight loss, plus neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration, cognitive and psychiatric changes; raised risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and carcinoid.
inv: Macrocytic anemia with low B12 and raised methylmalonic acid; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (highly specific) and parietal cell antibodies, high gastrin, and endoscopy to confirm atrophic gastritis.
tre: Lifelong B12 replacement, usually IM injections loading then maintenance, with high-dose oral B12 as an alternative maintenance option; monitor response and consider endoscopic surveillance.

name: Cholelithiasis (gallstones / biliary colic)
epi: Common, affecting about 6% of men and 9% of women in the US; risk rises with female sex, age, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss and Native American ancestry, and most stones stay asymptomatic.
eti: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile (most stones), excess bilirubin from hemolysis (black pigment stones) or biliary infection (brown stones), with gallbladder hypomotility.
cli: Often asymptomatic; biliary colic causes constant RUQ or epigastric pain lasting hours, often after fatty meals, with nausea; complications include cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis and pancreatitis.
inv: RUQ ultrasound is first-line, showing echogenic stones with acoustic shadowing; liver tests, and MRCP or EUS if bile duct stones are suspected.
tre: No treatment for asymptomatic stones in most patients; laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic stones, ERCP for duct stones, and ursodeoxycholic acid rarely for nonsurgical candidates.

name: Common wart (verruca vulgaris)
epi: Very common, affecting about 10% of people and up to 20% of school-aged children, peaking in adolescence.
eti: Human papillomavirus infection of keratinocytes, mainly HPV types 2 and 4 for common warts, spread by direct or indirect contact and autoinoculation through broken skin.
cli: Rough, firm hyperkeratotic papules, usually on hands and fingers, with black dots of thrombosed capillaries seen on paring; plantar warts are painful on pressure.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; paring reveals pinpoint capillaries, with biopsy only for atypical or nonresponding lesions.
tre: Observation is reasonable since about two-thirds resolve within 2 years; topical salicylic acid and cryotherapy are first-line, with other destructive or immunotherapies for persistent warts.

name: Acute bronchitis
epi: Very common self-limited lower respiratory infection, diagnosed in about 5% of adults yearly with a winter peak.
eti: Mostly viral (influenza, rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronavirus, RSV); bacteria such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae and Bordetella pertussis cause under 10%.
cli: Acute cough with or without sputum lasting 1-3 weeks, sometimes with wheeze, chest discomfort and low-grade fever; purulent sputum does not imply bacterial infection.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; chest radiograph only if pneumonia is suspected (heart rate over 100, respiratory rate over 24, temperature over 38 C or focal signs), with pertussis or influenza testing when indicated.
tre: Supportive care with fluids, analgesics and antipyretics, and bronchodilators for wheeze; antibiotics are not recommended for uncomplicated cases, except for pertussis, and antivirals for confirmed influenza.

name: Herpes simplex
epi: Extremely common; about two-thirds of people under 50 worldwide carry HSV-1, and HSV-2 infects a substantial minority of adults, most undiagnosed.
eti: HSV-1 and HSV-2 spread by close contact, including asymptomatic shedding, and establish lifelong latency in sensory ganglia with reactivation by stress, UV light, fever or immunosuppression.
cli: Grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base progressing to ulcers: gingivostomatitis or cold sores, genital herpes, keratitis, whitlow; serious forms include encephalitis and neonatal herpes.
inv: Often clinical; lesion swab PCR is the test of choice, CSF PCR for encephalitis, and type-specific serology in selected cases.
tre: Oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for episodes, with suppressive therapy for frequent recurrences; IV acyclovir for encephalitis, neonatal or severe disseminated disease.

name: Infective endocarditis
epi: About 3-10 cases per 100,000 per year, now mostly in people over 65; risk factors include prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, congenital or valvular heart disease, injection drug use and intravascular devices.
eti: Infection of endocardium, usually valves, by Staphylococcus aureus (most common), viridans streptococci, enterococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci, HACEK organisms or rarely fungi; injection drug users often have tricuspid S. aureus disease.
cli: Fever in over 95% with malaise and weight loss, a new or changed murmur, heart failure and emboli; Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages and Roth spots are uncommon.
inv: At least three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography (TTE first, TEE if negative or prosthetic valve); modified Duke criteria combine microbiologic, imaging and minor findings.
tre: Prolonged (often 4-6 weeks) IV bactericidal antibiotics guided by organism; early surgery for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or abscess, large vegetations with emboli and many prosthetic-valve or fungal infections.

name: Acute pericarditis
epi: Most common pericardial disease, causing about 5% of nonischemic chest pain ED visits, mostly in young and middle-aged men; recurrence occurs in 15-30%.
eti: Most cases in developed countries are idiopathic or viral (coxsackievirus, echovirus); others include tuberculosis (endemic regions), autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, post-MI or post-cardiotomy syndromes.
cli: Sharp pleuritic central chest pain relieved by sitting forward and worse lying flat, pericardial friction rub, and sometimes effusion; tamponade causes hypotension, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus.
inv: Diagnosis needs 2 of: typical pain, friction rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, new effusion; check CRP, troponin (myopericarditis) and echocardiography.
tre: NSAID or high-dose aspirin plus colchicine (about 3 months) to reduce recurrence and exercise restriction; corticosteroids only if NSAIDs are contraindicated or specific causes, and admit high-risk features.

name: Pulmonary embolism
epi: Third most common cardiovascular disease after MI and stroke; risk rises with surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, estrogen therapy, prior VTE and thrombophilia.
eti: Usually thrombus from deep leg or pelvic veins embolizing to the pulmonary arteries, arising through Virchow triad of stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.
cli: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea and hypoxemia, sometimes hemoptysis or syncope; massive PE causes hypotension and right heart failure.
inv: Wells or Geneva score and PERC; D-dimer to exclude in low or intermediate probability; CT pulmonary angiography is the main test, V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated, and echo or troponin for RV strain.
tre: Anticoagulation (DOAC preferred for most, or LMWH) for at least 3 months; systemic thrombolysis for hemodynamically unstable PE, with catheter-directed therapy or embolectomy if contraindicated.

name: Tension pneumothorax
epi: Uncommon but immediately life-threatening; occurs mainly after chest trauma, in mechanically ventilated patients and after procedures such as central line insertion.
eti: A one-way valve air leak into the pleural space progressively raises intrapleural pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum, which impairs venous return and causes obstructive shock.
cli: Severe respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side, distended neck veins and late tracheal deviation away from the affected side.
inv: Clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment without waiting for imaging; bedside ultrasound (absent lung sliding) can help, and chest radiograph after decompression.
tre: Immediate needle decompression (4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line in adults, or 2nd space midclavicular) or finger thoracostomy, followed by chest tube insertion.

name: Pneumothorax
epi: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax mainly affects tall thin young men who smoke; secondary pneumothorax occurs in older patients with lung disease, and recurrence is common.
eti: Air enters the pleural space from rupture of subpleural blebs (primary), underlying lung disease such as COPD, cystic fibrosis or Pneumocystis (secondary), trauma or procedures (iatrogenic).
cli: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea with reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance and reduced chest expansion; tension physiology causes hypotension and shock.
inv: Erect chest radiograph shows a visceral pleural line without distal lung markings; ultrasound (absent lung sliding) and CT help in uncertain or complex cases.
tre: Observation with or without oxygen for small stable cases, needle aspiration or chest drain for larger or symptomatic ones, and VATS pleurodesis for persistent leak or recurrence; smoking cessation.

name: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease)
epi: Rare, about 1 case per million per year, with peaks in young adult men and older adults; causes 10-15% of crescentic glomerulonephritis.
eti: Autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes (type II hypersensitivity), with HLA-DR15 susceptibility and triggers such as smoking and hydrocarbon exposure.
cli: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with hematuria and acute kidney injury, plus pulmonary hemorrhage with hemoptysis in Goodpasture syndrome; older patients often have kidney-only disease.
inv: Serum anti-GBM antibodies and urgent kidney biopsy showing crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence; check ANCA, as double-positive cases occur.
tre: Urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide (rituximab as alternative), plus supportive dialysis and treatment of pulmonary hemorrhage; relapse is uncommon.

name: Crohn disease
epi: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease most common in North America and Northern Europe, rising in newly industrialized countries, with onset peaks at 15-30 and 40-60 years.
eti: Dysregulated immune response to gut microbiota in genetically susceptible people (e.g., NOD2 variants), with smoking a key environmental risk factor; causes transmural, skip-lesion inflammation of any GI segment.
cli: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain (often RLQ from terminal ileitis), weight loss and fatigue; strictures, fistulas, perianal disease, abscesses and extraintestinal features (arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum).
inv: Raised CRP and fecal calprotectin; ileocolonoscopy with biopsies showing skip lesions and noncaseating granulomas, and MR or CT enterography for small bowel and complications.
tre: Corticosteroids (or budesonide) to induce remission, immunomodulators and biologics (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-12/23) for maintenance in moderate-severe disease, smoking cessation, and surgery for complications.

name: Ulcerative colitis
epi: Most common inflammatory bowel disease worldwide, with onset peaks at 15-30 and 50-70 years; more common in nonsmokers and ex-smokers and with a family history.
eti: Immune-mediated mucosal inflammation in genetically susceptible people with altered gut microbiota, starting in the rectum and extending continuously proximally, confined to the colon.
cli: Bloody diarrhea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus and crampy pain; acute severe colitis causes frequent bloody stools, fever, tachycardia and anemia, with toxic megacolon; extraintestinal features include arthritis, erythema nodosum and primary sclerosing cholangitis.
inv: Stool tests including C. difficile to exclude infection, CBC, CRP and fecal calprotectin; colonoscopy with biopsies shows continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum, and abdominal radiograph checks for megacolon in severe flares.
tre: 5-aminosalicylates for mild-moderate disease, corticosteroids for flares, and thiopurines, biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab) or small molecules for moderate-severe disease; acute severe UC needs IV steroids with infliximab or ciclosporin rescue, and colectomy is curative.

name: Celiac disease
epi: Affects about 1% of people worldwide, more common in women, first-degree relatives, type 1 diabetes, Down syndrome and IgA deficiency.
eti: Immune reaction to gluten in people with HLA-DQ2 or DQ8: tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, driving CD4 T-cell inflammation with villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.
cli: Diarrhea, bloating, abdominal pain and weight loss or failure to thrive; extraintestinal features include iron-deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis and fatigue, and many are oligosymptomatic.
inv: IgA anti-tTG with total IgA while eating gluten, then duodenal biopsies showing villous atrophy, intraepithelial lymphocytosis and crypt hyperplasia; HLA testing can rule out disease.
tre: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian support, correcting iron, folate, vitamin D and calcium deficiencies, and monitoring serology, bone health and associated conditions.

name: Graves disease
epi: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism (60-80%), much more common in women, usually aged 20-50; smoking raises risk of eye disease.
eti: Autoimmune TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies drive thyroid growth and hormone overproduction, triggered by genetic susceptibility, stress, smoking, infection, iodine or the postpartum period.
cli: Thyrotoxicosis (weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, atrial fibrillation) with diffuse goiter; specific features are orbitopathy (proptosis, lid retraction) and rare pretibial myxedema.
inv: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and/or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies confirm the cause, with diffusely increased radioiodine uptake if needed.
tre: Beta-blockers for symptoms plus methimazole (propylthiouracil in first-trimester pregnancy), radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy; radioiodine can worsen active orbitopathy, and smoking cessation is important.

name: Cushing syndrome
epi: Iatrogenic glucocorticoid use is by far the most common cause; endogenous Cushing syndrome is rare, mainly affecting adults and more often women.
eti: Prolonged cortisol excess, exogenous or endogenous; endogenous causes are ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma, about 70-80%, or ectopic ACTH) or ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia).
cli: Central obesity, moon face, dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple striae, easy bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, infections and mood change.
inv: Exclude exogenous steroids; screen with late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urine free cortisol or overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression, then ACTH level, high-dose suppression, imaging and petrosal sinus sampling to localize.
tre: Taper exogenous steroids gradually; surgical removal of the pituitary, adrenal or ectopic tumor is first-line, with steroidogenesis inhibitors, pituitary-directed drugs, radiotherapy or bilateral adrenalectomy for persistent disease.

name: Cushing disease
epi: Most common endogenous cause of Cushing syndrome, with about 2-3 new cases per million per year, mainly in women and often diagnosed years after onset.
eti: ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma, usually a microadenoma under 10 mm (often USP8-mutated), drives bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and cortisol excess.
cli: Cushingoid features: central weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump, plethora, purple striae, bruising, proximal weakness, hypertension, diabetes and depression; visual field loss is uncommon.
inv: Confirm hypercortisolism (late-night salivary cortisol, urine free cortisol, dexamethasone suppression), then normal or high ACTH, pituitary MRI and inferior petrosal sinus sampling when MRI is negative or equivocal.
tre: Transsphenoidal adenoma resection is first-line; for persistent disease, repeat surgery, radiotherapy, medical therapy (pasireotide, cabergoline, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) or bilateral adrenalectomy, which risks Nelson syndrome.

name: Addison disease
epi: Rare, affecting about 4-11 per 100,000, usually aged 30-50 and more often women; autoimmune adrenalitis is the main cause in developed countries and tuberculosis elsewhere.
eti: Primary adrenal insufficiency from destruction of the adrenal cortex, mostly autoimmune (21-hydroxylase antibodies), also TB, HIV and fungal infection, hemorrhage, infiltration or drugs, causing cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.
cli: Insidious fatigue, weakness, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, salt craving and postural hypotension, with hyperpigmentation of skin creases, scars and mucosa from high ACTH.
inv: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and sometimes hypoglycemia; low morning cortisol with high ACTH and high renin, confirmed by a blunted ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test, plus 21-hydroxylase antibodies.
tre: Lifelong hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone, with sick-day dose increases, a steroid card and emergency injectable hydrocortisone; adrenal crisis needs IV hydrocortisone and saline.

name: Adrenal crisis
epi: Occurs in about 6-8% of people with adrenal insufficiency each year and carries significant mortality; precipitated by GI illness, infection, surgery, trauma or abrupt steroid withdrawal.
eti: Acute cortisol deficiency, with aldosterone deficiency in primary disease, from known or undiagnosed adrenal insufficiency failing to meet stress demands, causing vasodilatory shock.
cli: Severe weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, dehydration, hypotension or shock, confusion and obtundation, with hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency.
inv: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and raised creatinine; draw cortisol and ACTH if possible, but never delay treatment for tests.
tre: Immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone bolus followed by continued high-dose hydrocortisone, rapid isotonic saline with dextrose as needed, treatment of the trigger, then taper to maintenance and patient education.

name: Primary hyperparathyroidism
epi: Leading cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients, most common in postmenopausal women (3-4:1 female) with a peak at 50-60 years.
eti: Autonomous PTH secretion from a single parathyroid adenoma (80-85%), multigland hyperplasia (10-15%, including MEN1 and MEN2A) or rarely carcinoma.
cli: Usually asymptomatic hypercalcemia on routine testing; symptomatic disease causes kidney stones, osteoporosis and fractures, abdominal pain, constipation, polyuria, fatigue and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
inv: High calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH, low-normal phosphate, 24-hour urine calcium to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, vitamin D, creatinine and DEXA; sestamibi, ultrasound or 4D-CT for surgical localization.
tre: Parathyroidectomy (curative in over 95%) for symptomatic patients or those meeting criteria such as age under 50, osteoporosis, stones or reduced eGFR; otherwise monitoring, with cinacalcet or bisphosphonates if surgery is unsuitable.

name: Parkinson disease
epi: Second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting about 1% of people over 60, about twice as often men; usually begins after age 60.
eti: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies; mostly sporadic, with about 10% genetic (LRRK2, GBA, SNCA) and pesticide exposure as a risk factor.
cli: Asymmetric bradykinesia with rest tremor and/or rigidity, later gait freezing and postural instability; nonmotor features (anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression, dementia) often precede or accompany.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by examination with a sustained levodopa response supporting it; DaT-SPECT for uncertain cases and MRI to exclude other causes.
tre: Levodopa-carbidopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy, with dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors as alternatives or adjuncts, exercise and physiotherapy, and deep brain stimulation for motor fluctuations.

name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
epi: Underdiagnosed, found in about 1-3% of autopsies with most cases missed in life; classically linked to alcohol use disorder but also bariatric surgery, hyperemesis gravidarum, cancer and malnutrition.
eti: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency damages the mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal gray; untreated Wernicke encephalopathy often progresses to chronic Korsakoff amnesia.
cli: Wernicke: confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus and ataxia, with the full triad present in only a minority; Korsakoff: severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation.
inv: Clinical diagnosis (Caine criteria, 2 of 4: dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar signs, altered mental state or memory impairment); MRI changes are specific but insensitive, and treatment must not wait for tests.
tre: Immediate high-dose IV thiamine given before or with glucose, plus magnesium replacement and nutrition, then oral thiamine and alcohol treatment; Korsakoff memory deficits often persist.

name: Malaria
epi: Endemic across many tropical and subtropical regions, with most deaths in sub-Saharan Africa, mainly among young children; travellers returning from endemic areas are also at risk.
eti: Plasmodium protozoa (P. falciparum, vivax, ovale, malariae, knowlesi) transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes; P. falciparum causes most severe disease, while vivax and ovale can relapse from dormant liver hypnozoites.
cli: Fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia and malaise, sometimes with splenomegaly; severe falciparum malaria may cause anemia, jaundice, hypoglycemia, acidosis, respiratory distress, renal failure, seizures or coma.
inv: Urgent thick and thin blood films or rapid diagnostic tests confirm infection, species and parasitemia; repeat testing is needed if initial results are negative but suspicion persists.
tre: Prompt antimalarial therapy chosen by species, severity and regional resistance, typically artemisinin-based combinations for falciparum; severe malaria needs IV artesunate and intensive supportive care, plus primaquine or tafenoquine for vivax/ovale hypnozoites.

name: Lyme disease
epi: Occurs in temperate regions of North America, Europe and Asia where infected Ixodes ticks are established; risk follows outdoor exposure in wooded or brushy areas, peaking in late spring and summer.
eti: Spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex transmitted by Ixodes tick bites, usually after prolonged attachment.
cli: Early localized erythema migrans with fever, fatigue and headache; early disseminated disease causes facial palsy, meningitis or carditis with heart block, and late disease causes migratory or monoarticular arthritis.
inv: Typical erythema migrans in an exposed person is a clinical diagnosis; otherwise two-tier serology is standard, with CSF or synovial fluid testing for neurologic or joint disease.
tre: Oral doxycycline (or amoxicillin or cefuroxime) treats most disease; IV ceftriaxone is used for selected neurologic or high-degree cardiac involvement; arthritis usually responds to an oral course.

name: Tuberculosis
epi: A leading infectious cause of death worldwide, concentrated in low- and middle-income settings; risk rises with HIV, crowding, malnutrition, diabetes, immunosuppression and close contact with infectious cases.
eti: Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei; infection may be contained as latent TB or progress to active disease, most often pulmonary but potentially at any site.
cli: Prolonged cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss and fatigue, sometimes with hemoptysis; extrapulmonary disease may involve lymph nodes, pleura, spine, meninges or other organs.
inv: Chest imaging plus sputum nucleic-acid amplification testing, smear microscopy and culture establish diagnosis and drug susceptibility; IGRA or tuberculin skin testing detects infection but cannot distinguish latent from active TB.
tre: Multidrug therapy, classically isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for drug-susceptible disease, tailored to site and susceptibility, with adherence support, airborne isolation and public-health contact investigation.

name: HIV infection / AIDS
epi: Global pandemic with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa; transmission occurs mainly through sexual contact, shared injecting equipment and perinatal or breastfeeding exposure.
eti: Human immunodeficiency virus (mainly HIV-1) infects CD4 T cells, causing progressive immune depletion; AIDS is defined by a very low CD4 count or an AIDS-defining opportunistic illness.
cli: Acute infection may cause a mononucleosis-like illness with fever, rash, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy, followed by a long asymptomatic phase; advanced disease causes weight loss, opportunistic infections and malignancies.
inv: Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody testing with confirmatory assays, and HIV RNA when very early infection is suspected; CD4 count, viral load and resistance testing guide staging and treatment.
tre: Lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy started promptly after diagnosis, aiming for an undetectable viral load, which prevents sexual transmission; opportunistic-infection prophylaxis is given when CD4 is low.

name: Melanoma
epi: Incidence is highest in fair-skinned populations with high UV exposure; risk rises with sunburn history, many or atypical nevi, family history and immunosuppression, though it occurs in any skin type.
eti: Malignant transformation of melanocytes, often driven by UV-induced DNA damage and oncogenic mutations such as BRAF or NRAS; acral and mucosal subtypes are less UV-related.
cli: A new or changing pigmented lesion showing asymmetry, irregular border, color variation, diameter increase or evolution (ABCDE); may bleed or ulcerate, and advanced disease spreads to nodes and distant organs.
inv: Dermoscopy aids assessment; excisional biopsy with narrow margins gives histology and Breslow thickness, followed by wide local excision, with sentinel node biopsy, staging imaging and BRAF testing by stage.
tre: Wide local excision for localized disease, with sentinel node assessment when indicated; advanced or high-risk resected disease is treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors or BRAF/MEK-targeted therapy.

name: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
epi: Predominantly affects women of childbearing age; more common and often more severe in people of African, Asian and Hispanic ancestry, and lupus nephritis develops in a substantial subset.
eti: Systemic autoimmune disease with loss of immune tolerance, autoantibody production and immune-complex deposition; genetic, hormonal and environmental factors such as UV light contribute.
cli: Fatigue, arthralgia or arthritis, photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, serositis and cytopenias; nephritis causes proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension or renal impairment, and neuropsychiatric involvement can occur.
inv: ANA is highly sensitive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific, while low complement, CBC and urinalysis assess activity; kidney biopsy classifies nephritis when indicated.
tre: Hydroxychloroquine for nearly all patients, with sun protection; glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine or biologics are used for organ-threatening disease, including nephritis by class.

name: Ankylosing spondylitis
epi: Typically begins in late adolescence or early adulthood, usually before age 45, and is more common in men and in people carrying HLA-B27.
eti: Chronic immune-mediated inflammatory arthritis of the axial skeleton (axial spondyloarthritis) with a strong genetic association with HLA-B27 and involvement of the IL-23/IL-17 pathway.
cli: Inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness improving with exercise, buttock pain, enthesitis and reduced spinal mobility; extra-articular features include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.
inv: Raised CRP or ESR in some patients; pelvic radiographs or MRI demonstrate sacroiliitis, and HLA-B27 supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
tre: Regular exercise and physiotherapy plus NSAIDs first-line; TNF or IL-17 inhibitors, or JAK inhibitors, are used for persistent active disease, since conventional DMARDs do not help axial disease.

name: Reactive arthritis
epi: Most common in young adults, usually developing within weeks of genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection; HLA-B27 carriers are at increased risk and of more severe or chronic disease.
eti: Immune-mediated sterile arthritis triggered by infection elsewhere, such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia, rather than direct joint infection.
cli: Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis, enthesitis and dactylitis, sometimes with conjunctivitis, urethritis or cervicitis, and mucocutaneous lesions such as keratoderma blennorrhagicum.
inv: Joint aspiration excludes septic and crystal arthritis; NAAT for chlamydia or stool testing identifies the trigger, with inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 supporting assessment.
tre: NSAIDs and intra-articular corticosteroids, with treatment of any active chlamydial infection; persistent disease may need sulfasalazine or other rheumatology-directed DMARD therapy.

name: Hodgkin lymphoma
epi: Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in young adults and in older adults; a minority of cases are associated with EBV or immunosuppression such as HIV.
eti: B-cell lymphoid neoplasm characterized by Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells within an inflammatory background; EBV contributes to some cases.
cli: Painless lymphadenopathy, often cervical or mediastinal, with B symptoms of fever, night sweats and weight loss, and sometimes pruritus or alcohol-induced nodal pain.
inv: Excisional lymph-node biopsy establishes diagnosis, typically showing CD15/CD30-positive Reed-Sternberg cells; PET-CT stages disease, with CBC, ESR and chemistry for baseline risk.
tre: Stage-adapted combination chemotherapy such as ABVD, often PET-guided, with selective radiotherapy; brentuximab vedotin, checkpoint inhibitors and autologous transplant are used for advanced or relapsed disease.

name: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
epi: Occurs in children and adults; childhood ITP often follows a viral infection and usually resolves, whereas adult ITP is more often persistent or chronic.
eti: Autoantibodies accelerate platelet destruction and impair megakaryocyte platelet production; it may be primary or secondary to HIV, hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disease or drugs.
cli: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding or heavy menstrual bleeding; many patients are asymptomatic, and serious internal bleeding is uncommon.
inv: CBC shows isolated thrombocytopenia and peripheral smear excludes pseudothrombocytopenia or other hematologic disease; diagnosis is by exclusion, with HIV and hepatitis C testing in adults.
tre: Observation for mild disease; corticosteroids or IVIG when treatment is needed; thrombopoietin-receptor agonists, rituximab, fostamatinib or splenectomy for persistent or refractory disease.

name: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
epi: Typically presents at about 2 to 8 weeks of age, is several times more common in boys and firstborns, and is associated with early macrolide exposure.
eti: Idiopathic hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle obstructs gastric outflow; genetic and environmental factors contribute.
cli: Progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds with persistent hunger, dehydration and poor weight gain; an olive-shaped epigastric mass and visible gastric peristalsis may be present.
inv: Ultrasound confirms a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle; blood gas and electrolytes show hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
tre: Correct dehydration and electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities first, then perform pyloromyotomy, usually laparoscopic.

name: Intussusception
epi: Most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and young children, peaking between about 6 months and 3 years; uncommon in adults, where a lead point is usual.
eti: A proximal bowel segment telescopes into a distal segment, most often ileocolic, causing obstruction, venous congestion and ischemia; lymphoid hyperplasia is typical in children and a pathologic lead point in older patients.
cli: Episodic severe colicky abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting and lethargy between episodes; later redcurrant-jelly stool and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass.
inv: Ultrasound is the preferred test, showing a target or doughnut sign; abdominal radiographs assess obstruction or perforation.
tre: Fluid resuscitation and urgent pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction if no peritonitis; surgery for perforation, peritonitis, failed reduction or a pathologic lead point.

name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
epi: Acute life-threatening complication, most common in type 1 diabetes and sometimes the first presentation, but also possible in type 2 diabetes and with SGLT2 inhibitors.
eti: Absolute or relative insulin deficiency with excess counter-regulatory hormones drives hyperglycemia, lipolysis and ketogenesis, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis; infection and missed insulin are common triggers.
cli: Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath and altered mental status.
inv: Raised glucose (normal in euglycemic DKA), ketonemia with beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acidosis with raised anion gap on blood gas; electrolytes, renal function and a search for triggers assess severity.
tre: IV fluids, fixed-rate IV insulin infusion and careful potassium replacement with frequent monitoring, adding dextrose as glucose falls; identify and treat the precipitating cause.

name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
epi: Uncommon ophthalmic emergency, more frequent in older adults, women, people of Asian ancestry and hyperopic eyes with shallow anterior chambers.
eti: Sudden closure of the iridocorneal angle, usually by pupillary block, obstructs aqueous outflow; mydriasis and drugs such as anticholinergics or topiramate can precipitate it.
cli: Sudden severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision, halos, nausea and vomiting with a red eye, hazy cornea and fixed mid-dilated pupil.
inv: Tonometry shows markedly raised intraocular pressure; slit-lamp shows a shallow anterior chamber and corneal edema, and gonioscopy confirms angle closure.
tre: Emergency IOP lowering with topical beta-blocker, alpha-agonist, pilocarpine and systemic acetazolamide or mannitol, then laser peripheral iridotomy, usually also prophylactic in the fellow eye.

name: Peritonsillar abscess
epi: Most common deep neck infection, occurring mainly in older children, adolescents and young adults.
eti: Complication of tonsillitis in which infection spreads into the peritonsillar space; usually polymicrobial with group A streptococcus and oral anaerobes.
