cli: Severe unilateral sore throat, fever, odynophagia, trismus, drooling and muffled hot-potato voice, with a bulging tonsil and uvula deviated away from the affected side.
inv: Diagnosis is mainly clinical; needle aspiration confirms pus, and CT or intraoral ultrasound helps when the diagnosis is unclear or deeper spread is suspected.
tre: Drainage by needle aspiration or incision plus antibiotics covering streptococci and anaerobes, analgesia and hydration; tonsillectomy for selected or recurrent cases, with airway assessment.

name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
epi: The most common vestibular disorder, peaking in the fifth to seventh decades with a female predominance.
eti: Displaced otoconia (canalithiasis) in a semicircular canal, most often posterior, cause abnormal endolymph flow with head movement; most cases are idiopathic, others follow head trauma or labyrinthitis.
cli: Brief episodes of rotatory vertigo, usually under a minute, triggered by rolling in bed, lying down or looking up, often with nausea but no hearing loss or neurologic deficit.
inv: Dix-Hallpike maneuver provokes torsional upbeating nystagmus in posterior-canal BPPV; the supine roll test assesses horizontal-canal disease.
tre: Canalith-repositioning maneuvers such as the Epley maneuver are first-line; vestibular suppressants are not recommended routinely and surgery is reserved for refractory cases.

name: Hashimoto thyroiditis
epi: Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, most often in middle-aged women and those with a family history of thyroid disease.
eti: Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis in which antibody- and T-cell-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue gradually reduces hormone production.
cli: Painless goiter with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, hair loss and low mood as hypothyroidism develops; some patients are euthyroid.
inv: TSH and free T4 define thyroid function; anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies support the autoimmune cause.
tre: Levothyroxine replacement for hypothyroidism, titrated to TSH; euthyroid patients with antibodies are monitored periodically.

name: Budd-Chiari syndrome
epi: Rare disorder, in Western countries usually diagnosed in the third or fourth decade and more often in women.
eti: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow from the hepatic veins to the IVC, most often thrombosis due to myeloproliferative neoplasms or other prothrombotic states; some cases are idiopathic.
cli: Classic triad of abdominal pain, ascites and hepatomegaly; presentation ranges from acute liver failure to chronic portal hypertension and cirrhosis.
inv: Doppler ultrasound is the first-line test, with CT or MRI to define the obstruction; screen for myeloproliferative neoplasm and thrombophilia.
tre: Anticoagulation and treatment of the underlying cause, then stepwise angioplasty or stenting, TIPS and liver transplantation for nonresponders.

name: Behcet disease
epi: Uncommon variable-vessel vasculitis of young adults, most prevalent along the ancient Silk Road (highest in Turkey); disease is often more severe in men.
eti: Multifactorial immune-mediated disease in genetically susceptible people, particularly HLA-B51 carriers, probably triggered by environmental or infectious factors.
cli: Recurrent painful oral aphthae in nearly all patients plus genital ulcers, skin lesions, uveitis and arthritis; vascular thrombosis or aneurysms, neurologic and gastrointestinal disease can occur.
inv: Diagnosis is clinical using classification criteria, as no specific laboratory test exists; a positive pathergy test supports it and imaging assesses organ involvement.
tre: Topical corticosteroids for ulcers and colchicine for mucocutaneous or joint disease; corticosteroids with azathioprine or TNF inhibitors for eye, vascular or neurologic involvement.

name: Hand, foot, and mouth disease
epi: Common viral illness, most frequent in children under 5 years, with outbreaks in childcare settings.
eti: Enterovirus infection, classically coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus A71 (also coxsackievirus A6), spread by saliva, respiratory secretions, blister fluid and feces.
cli: Fever and sore throat followed by painful oral ulcers and a vesicular or papular rash on the hands, feet and often buttocks; most recover in 7-10 days.
inv: Diagnosis is clinical; enterovirus PCR is reserved for atypical, severe or outbreak cases.
tre: Supportive care with fluids and analgesics or antipyretics; no specific antiviral, and hand hygiene limits spread.

name: Myasthenia gravis
epi: Can occur at any age, typically starting in women under 40 and men over 60.
eti: Autoimmune disorder in which antibodies, usually against acetylcholine receptors and less often MuSK or LRP4, impair neuromuscular transmission; thymic hyperplasia or thymoma is common.
cli: Fluctuating fatigable weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, often with ptosis and diplopia, plus bulbar, facial and limb weakness; myasthenic crisis causes respiratory failure.
inv: Acetylcholine-receptor or MuSK antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG support diagnosis; CT or MRI of the chest looks for thymoma.
tre: Pyridostigmine for symptoms with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for selected patients, and IVIG or plasma exchange for crisis.

name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
epi: Can affect any age, somewhat more common in adults and males; often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection by days to weeks.
eti: Acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, often triggered by infection such as Campylobacter jejuni; classic AIDP is demyelinating, with axonal variants.
cli: Rapidly progressive, usually ascending symmetric weakness with reduced or absent reflexes, paresthesias and pain; autonomic instability and respiratory failure can occur.
inv: CSF shows raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation); nerve-conduction studies support diagnosis, and serial vital capacity monitors respiratory function.
tre: IVIG or plasma exchange with supportive care, including respiratory and autonomic monitoring, thromboprophylaxis, pain control and rehabilitation; corticosteroids are not effective.

name: Pheochromocytoma
epi: Rare catecholamine-secreting tumor mainly of adults; about a third of cases are inherited, as in MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau or NF1.
eti: Tumor of adrenal medullary chromaffin cells secreting norepinephrine, epinephrine or both; extra-adrenal counterparts are paragangliomas.
cli: Paroxysmal or sustained hypertension with episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, plus anxiety or pallor; some tumors are found incidentally.
inv: Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines are the first-line biochemical test, followed by CT or MRI to localize the tumor and genetic testing.
tre: Preoperative alpha-blockade, then beta-blockade if needed, with volume expansion before surgical resection; metastatic disease needs specialist systemic or radionuclide therapy.

name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
epi: Mainly affects older adults, with prevalence rising after age 70; it accounts for a small but treatable proportion of dementia.
eti: Communicating hydrocephalus with impaired CSF absorption and reduced intracranial compliance; idiopathic in older adults or secondary to subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis or trauma.
cli: Classic triad of magnetic, shuffling gait disturbance (usually earliest), cognitive slowing and urinary urgency or incontinence.
inv: CT or MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, often with disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid spaces; CSF tap test or external lumbar drainage predicts shunt response.
tre: Ventriculoperitoneal or lumboperitoneal shunting, often with programmable valves; gait responds best, and patients are monitored for shunt complications.

name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
epi: Rare adult-onset neurodegenerative disease, usually beginning after age 50; about 1 in 10 cases is familial.
eti: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons; most cases are sporadic, and familial cases involve genes such as C9orf72 and SOD1.
cli: Progressive asymmetric limb or bulbar weakness with wasting, fasciculations, spasticity and hyperreflexia, dysarthria and dysphagia, eventually respiratory failure; sensation is spared.
inv: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG/nerve conduction showing widespread denervation; MRI and blood tests exclude mimics, and genetic testing is offered when appropriate.
tre: Riluzole modestly slows progression; edaravone is used in some countries and tofersen for SOD1-ALS, with multidisciplinary respiratory (noninvasive ventilation), nutritional and communication support.

name: Cardiac tamponade
epi: Life-threatening emergency that can develop acutely after trauma, cardiac surgery or myocardial rupture, or subacutely from malignant, infectious or inflammatory effusions.
eti: Pericardial fluid, blood or pus raises intrapericardial pressure and impairs diastolic filling, reducing cardiac output; rapid accumulation of small volumes can cause it.
cli: Beck triad of hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, with tachycardia, dyspnea and pulsus paradoxus; it can progress to obstructive shock.
inv: Bedside echocardiography shows effusion with diastolic right-chamber collapse; ECG may show low voltage or electrical alternans.
tre: Urgent pericardiocentesis, ideally echo-guided, or surgical drainage such as a pericardial window, especially for trauma; support circulation with fluids and treat the cause.

name: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
epi: Mainly affects people over about 60-70 years, more often men and smokers; family history and dust exposure increase risk.
eti: Chronic progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern; smoking, metal or wood dust and genetic factors are associated.
cli: Insidious progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough with fatigue, bibasilar velcro crackles and finger clubbing.
inv: High-resolution CT shows a UIP pattern with basal subpleural reticulation and honeycombing; PFTs show restriction with reduced DLCO, and other ILD causes are excluded.
tre: Antifibrotics pirfenidone or nintedanib slow decline; supportive oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation and early lung-transplant referral, with palliative care in advanced disease.

name: Interstitial pulmonary fibrosis
epi: Umbrella term for fibrotic interstitial lung disease, more common in older adults and men.
eti: Fibrosis of the alveolar interstitium that may be idiopathic or due to connective-tissue disease, occupational exposure such as asbestos or silica, drugs such as amiodarone, bleomycin or methotrexate, or hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
cli: Progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough with fine inspiratory crackles, exertional desaturation and sometimes clubbing.
inv: High-resolution CT and PFTs (restriction, low DLCO) characterize fibrosis; exposure history, autoimmune serology and sometimes biopsy identify the cause.
tre: Remove exposures and treat the underlying cause, such as immunosuppression for connective-tissue disease; nintedanib for progressive pulmonary fibrosis, plus oxygen, rehabilitation and transplant referral.

name: Sarcoidosis
epi: Can affect any age but usually begins in adults aged 20-40, more often in women and people of African or Scandinavian descent.
eti: Multisystem disorder of unknown cause with noncaseating granulomas, probably an exaggerated immune response to an unidentified antigen in genetically susceptible people.
cli: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, dry cough and dyspnea, fatigue, erythema nodosum, uveitis and arthralgia; cardiac, neurologic or hypercalcemic disease can occur.
inv: Chest radiography or CT shows hilar adenopathy or interstitial disease; biopsy (often EBUS) showing noncaseating granulomas after excluding TB and fungi, with ECG, eye exam and calcium.
tre: Many cases resolve without treatment; oral corticosteroids for significant organ involvement, with methotrexate or other immunosuppressants as steroid-sparing therapy.

name: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
epi: Rare, affecting men in about two thirds of cases with peak diagnosis at 25-45 years; most patients have inflammatory bowel disease, usually ulcerative colitis.
eti: Chronic immune-mediated inflammation and fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, causing multifocal strictures and eventually biliary cirrhosis.
cli: Often asymptomatic with cholestatic liver tests; fatigue, pruritus, jaundice and episodes of bacterial cholangitis, with high cholangiocarcinoma risk.
inv: Raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT; MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilations (beading), with biopsy for suspected small-duct disease and colonoscopy for IBD.
tre: No proven disease-modifying therapy; ursodeoxycholic acid may improve tests, dominant strictures are dilated endoscopically, and liver transplantation treats advanced disease, with cancer surveillance.

name: Wilson disease
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 30,000), usually presenting between childhood and age 40.
eti: ATP7B mutations impair biliary copper excretion and incorporation into ceruloplasmin, causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain and cornea.
cli: Liver disease ranging from hepatitis to cirrhosis or acute liver failure, with tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, psychiatric symptoms and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
inv: Low serum ceruloplasmin, raised 24-hour urinary copper, slit-lamp Kayser-Fleischer rings and raised hepatic copper on biopsy; ATP7B testing confirms.
tre: Lifelong chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine, zinc for maintenance or presymptomatic patients, a low-copper diet and liver transplantation for acute liver failure or end-stage disease.

name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
epi: Most common ANCA-associated vasculitis, peaking at age 45-60 with a slight male predominance.
eti: Necrotizing granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis associated with ANCA, usually PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in about three quarters of patients.
cli: Chronic sinusitis, bloody nasal discharge, crusting or saddle-nose deformity, lung nodules or alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with constitutional symptoms.
inv: PR3-ANCA, urinalysis for hematuria and casts, renal function and chest or sinus CT; biopsy showing necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis confirms (renal biopsy shows pauci-immune GN).
tre: Induction with high-dose glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, then maintenance usually with rituximab; plasma exchange is considered in selected severe cases.

name: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
epi: Rare autoimmune connective-tissue disease about five times more common in women, usually beginning at age 20-50.
eti: Autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculopathy and fibroblast activation cause excess collagen deposition in skin and internal organs; genetic and environmental factors contribute.
cli: Raynaud phenomenon, puffy fingers, sclerodactyly, digital ulcers and telangiectasia, with esophageal dysmotility, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension and scleroderma renal crisis.
inv: ANA is positive in most patients; anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I), anticentromere and anti-RNA polymerase III define subsets, with PFTs, HRCT, echocardiography and BP monitoring.
tre: Organ-based therapy: calcium-channel blockers for Raynaud, immunosuppression such as mycophenolate for skin or lung disease, proton-pump inhibitors for reflux and prompt ACE inhibitors for renal crisis.

name: Multiple myeloma
epi: Plasma-cell malignancy of older adults, median age at diagnosis around 70, about twice as common in Black people and slightly more in men.
eti: Clonal malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) or free light chains and activate osteoclasts, causing lytic bone disease; it is preceded by MGUS.
cli: Bone pain (often back) and pathologic fractures, anemia, recurrent infections, renal failure and hypercalcemia (CRAB features).
inv: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains, CBC, calcium and creatinine, bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells and whole-body imaging (low-dose CT, MRI or PET-CT).
tre: Combination therapy with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, anti-CD38 antibodies and corticosteroids, autologous stem-cell transplant in eligible patients and BCMA-directed therapies for relapse.

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
epi: Rare idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics, more common in young adult men and with high-potency first-generation agents.
eti: Dopamine D2-receptor blockade by antipsychotics or antiemetics, or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs in Parkinson disease, disrupts central thermoregulation and muscle tone.
cli: Develops over 1-3 days with fever, severe lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis).
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by markedly raised creatine kinase, leukocytosis, renal function and electrolytes; exclude serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, infection and heat stroke.
tre: Stop the causative drug (or restart dopaminergic therapy), give intensive supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, benzodiazepines and bromocriptine or dantrolene in moderate-to-severe cases.

name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
epi: Most common neonatal gastrointestinal emergency, affecting mainly premature and very-low-birth-weight infants, with high mortality.
eti: Multifactorial ischemic and inflammatory bowel necrosis in an immature gut, involving abnormal bacterial colonization and invasion; formula feeding increases risk while breast milk is protective.
cli: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and tenderness, bilious aspirates, bloody stools, lethargy, apnea and temperature instability, progressing to shock.
inv: Abdominal radiographs show dilated loops and pneumatosis intestinalis, with portal venous gas or free air in advanced disease; labs show thrombocytopenia, acidosis and raised CRP.
tre: Stop enteral feeds, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, parenteral nutrition and broad-spectrum antibiotics; surgery or peritoneal drainage for perforation or clinical deterioration.

name: Thyroid storm
epi: Rare life-threatening thyrotoxicosis, about 1-2% of hyperthyroidism admissions, usually with underlying Graves disease.
eti: Decompensated thyrotoxicosis precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, iodine load, childbirth or stopping antithyroid drugs.
cli: High fever, marked tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, heart failure, agitation, delirium or coma, and vomiting, diarrhea or jaundice.
inv: Clinical diagnosis aided by the Burch-Wartofsky score; suppressed TSH with raised free T4/T3 support it, and treatment must not await results.
tre: ICU care with a beta-blocker (propranolol), a thionamide (PTU often preferred) followed at least an hour later by iodine, glucocorticoids, cooling and treatment of the precipitant.

name: Erdheim-Chester disease
epi: Very rare histiocytic neoplasm, slightly more common in men, typically diagnosed at 40-60 years.
eti: Clonal proliferation of foamy CD68+, CD1a-negative histiocytes driven by MAPK-pathway mutations, BRAF V600E in over half of cases.
cli: Bone pain in the legs and arms, diabetes insipidus, exophthalmos, hairy-kidney retroperitoneal fibrosis, aortic coating and neurologic or cardiac involvement; severity varies widely.
inv: Imaging shows bilateral symmetric diaphyseal osteosclerosis of long bones; biopsy with immunohistochemistry and BRAF/MAPK testing confirms, and whole-body imaging stages disease.
tre: BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib) for BRAF-mutant disease or MEK inhibitors (cobimetinib), with interferon-alpha or other agents when targeted therapy is not suitable.

name: Tetanus
epi: Rare where vaccination is widespread; occurs mainly in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people, older adults and in neonates where maternal vaccination is lacking.
eti: Clostridium tetani spores enter wounds and produce tetanospasmin, which blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA, glycine) in the spinal cord.
cli: After 3-21 days, trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, dysphagia, generalized painful muscle spasms and opisthotonus with autonomic instability.
inv: Diagnosis is clinical based on signs and wound or vaccination history; no laboratory test confirms tetanus.
tre: Human tetanus immune globulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines for spasms and airway or ventilatory support; give tetanus vaccine since disease does not confer immunity.

name: Rabies
epi: Causes tens of thousands of deaths a year worldwide, mostly from dog bites in Asia and Africa; bats cause most human cases in the US.
eti: Rabies virus (a lyssavirus) in the saliva of infected mammals enters through bites or scratches and travels along peripheral nerves to the CNS.
cli: After an incubation of weeks to months, fever and pain or paresthesia at the bite site progress to encephalitis with agitation, hydrophobia, hypersalivation or ascending paralysis.
inv: Antemortem testing uses saliva PCR, nuchal skin biopsy and serum and CSF antibodies; management of exposure never waits for testing.
tre: Post-exposure prophylaxis with thorough wound washing, rabies immune globulin and a rabies vaccine series is nearly 100% effective; once symptoms appear, disease is almost always fatal.

name: Acute rheumatic fever
epi: Peak incidence in children aged 5-15 years, mainly in low-resource and crowded settings; prior rheumatic fever raises recurrence risk.
eti: Delayed autoimmune reaction 1-5 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis (and possibly skin infection) via molecular mimicry.
cli: Fever with migratory polyarthritis, carditis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; carditis can lead to chronic rheumatic heart disease.
inv: Revised Jones criteria plus evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASO or anti-DNase B, throat culture); ECG and echocardiography assess carditis, and ESR/CRP are raised.
tre: Antibiotics to eradicate streptococci, aspirin or NSAIDs for arthritis and heart-failure treatment when needed, then long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin.

name: Kawasaki disease
epi: Mainly affects children under 5 years, more often boys and children of East Asian ancestry; leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries.
eti: Acute medium-vessel vasculitis of unknown cause, probably an abnormal immune response to an infectious trigger in genetically susceptible children.
cli: Fever for 5 days or more with bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, hand and foot swelling then peeling and cervical lymphadenopathy.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by raised CRP and ESR, leukocytosis and later thrombocytosis; echocardiography assesses coronary arteries at diagnosis and follow-up.
tre: IVIG plus aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset; corticosteroids or other immunomodulators for high-risk or IVIG-resistant disease, with echo follow-up.

name: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
epi: Rare systemic vasculitis of middle-aged adults; a minority of cases are associated with hepatitis B (or C).
eti: Necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized and sometimes small muscular arteries causing microaneurysms and infarction; it spares the lungs, causes no glomerulonephritis and is ANCA-negative.
cli: Fever, weight loss, myalgia, mononeuritis multiplex, abdominal pain from mesenteric ischemia, livedo or skin nodules and ulcers, testicular pain and renal-artery hypertension.
inv: Raised inflammatory markers, negative ANCA and hepatitis B/C serology; biopsy showing necrotizing arteritis or angiography showing renal or mesenteric microaneurysms confirms.
tre: Corticosteroids, adding cyclophosphamide for severe disease or methotrexate or azathioprine otherwise; HBV-associated PAN is treated with antivirals plus short steroids and plasma exchange.

name: Leptospirosis
epi: Worldwide zoonosis, most common in tropical regions and after flooding; risk is linked to freshwater recreation, farming, sanitation and veterinary work.
eti: Leptospira spirochetes shed in the urine of infected animals, especially rodents, enter through abraded skin or mucous membranes from contaminated water or soil.
cli: After 2-30 days, often biphasic fever, headache, severe myalgia (calves) and conjunctival suffusion; severe disease (Weil disease) causes jaundice, acute kidney injury, pulmonary hemorrhage or meningitis.
inv: PCR of blood or urine early and serology (MAT or IgM ELISA) later, with CBC, renal and liver tests; culture is slow and specialized.
tre: Doxycycline for mild disease and IV penicillin or ceftriaxone for severe disease, with supportive care including dialysis when needed; doxycycline can be used as prophylaxis for high-risk exposure.

name: Hepatic encephalopathy
epi: Common complication of cirrhosis, affecting a large proportion of patients during their illness; minimal (covert) encephalopathy is even more frequent, and it also occurs in acute liver failure.
eti: Neurotoxins, mainly gut-derived ammonia, bypass hepatic clearance through liver failure and portosystemic shunting, with inflammation contributing; precipitants include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, electrolyte disturbance and sedatives.
cli: Spectrum graded by West Haven criteria from subtle attention and sleep changes to lethargy, disorientation, asterixis, confusion and coma.
inv: Clinical diagnosis after excluding other causes and searching for precipitants (infection screen, electrolytes, glucose, GI bleeding); raised ammonia supports but does not grade the disorder.
tre: Treat precipitants and give lactulose, adding rifaximin for recurrence prevention; protect the airway in high grades, maintain nutrition and consider liver transplantation.

name: Alport syndrome
epi: Rare inherited disorder (about 1 in 50,000 newborns); about two thirds of cases are X-linked, with males most severely affected.
eti: Pathogenic variants in COL4A5 (X-linked) or COL4A3/COL4A4 (autosomal recessive or dominant) disrupt type IV collagen in glomerular, cochlear and ocular basement membranes.
cli: Persistent hematuria progressing to proteinuria, hypertension and kidney failure, with sensorineural hearing loss in late childhood or adolescence and anterior lenticonus or retinal flecks.
inv: Urinalysis and renal function, audiology and eye examination; genetic testing confirms, and kidney biopsy shows thinning and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane.
tre: Early ACE inhibitor or ARB to slow kidney decline, hearing aids and eye care, and dialysis or kidney transplantation for kidney failure.

name: Fabry disease
epi: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder estimated at 1 in 1,000 to 9,000; later-onset forms are more common than the classic form, and females are often affected more mildly.
eti: GLA variants cause alpha-galactosidase A deficiency with accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in vascular endothelium, kidney, heart and nerves.
cli: Classic disease begins in childhood with acroparesthesia, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis and corneal verticillata, later kidney failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and stroke.
inv: Low alpha-galactosidase A activity confirms males; females need GLA genetic testing, plus plasma lyso-Gb3 and assessment of kidney, heart and brain.
tre: Enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase) or oral migalastat for amenable variants, with pain control and management of kidney, cardiac and cerebrovascular complications.

name: MELAS syndrome
epi: Rare maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder; most patients develop symptoms between ages 2 and 40, often in childhood.
eti: Mitochondrial DNA variants, about 80% m.3243A>G in MT-TL1, impair oxidative phosphorylation; heteroplasmy causes variable expression.
cli: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes with seizures, migraine-like headaches, hemianopia, hearing loss, short stature, myopathy and diabetes.
inv: Raised blood and CSF lactate; MRI during episodes shows lesions not respecting vascular territories, and mtDNA testing confirms.
tre: IV arginine for acute stroke-like episodes and oral arginine or citrulline to reduce recurrences, with antiseizure therapy, supportive care and avoidance of mitochondrial toxins such as valproate.

name: Tuberous sclerosis complex
epi: Autosomal dominant disorder affecting about 1 in 6,000 to 10,000 people; about two thirds of cases arise from new variants.
eti: Pathogenic TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) variants cause mTOR overactivity and benign hamartomas in many organs.
cli: Seizures including infantile spasms, intellectual disability and autism, hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas and LAM.
inv: Clinical diagnostic criteria and genetic testing, with brain MRI, renal imaging, echocardiography, EEG, skin and eye examination.
tre: Antiseizure therapy (vigabatrin for infantile spasms), mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus or topical sirolimus for selected lesions, and lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance.

name: Neurofibromatosis type 1
epi: Common autosomal dominant disorder affecting about 1 in 3,000 to 4,000 people; about half of cases arise from new variants.
eti: Loss-of-function NF1 variants reduce neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor that negatively regulates RAS signaling.
cli: Cafe-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, skeletal dysplasias and learning difficulties, with increased cancer risk.
inv: Diagnosis uses clinical criteria; genetic testing for uncertain cases, with ophthalmologic examination and imaging guided by symptoms.
tre: Regular surveillance and symptom-directed care; surgery for symptomatic tumors and MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib for inoperable plexiform neurofibromas.

name: Sturge-Weber syndrome
epi: Rare sporadic congenital neurocutaneous disorder affecting about 1 in 20,000 to 50,000 people.
eti: Somatic (postzygotic, non-inherited) GNAQ variant causes capillary malformations of the facial skin, leptomeninges and eye.
cli: Facial port-wine stain in the ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution, leptomeningeal angioma with seizures, stroke-like episodes, hemiparesis and intellectual disability, and glaucoma.
inv: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement; regular eye-pressure checks for glaucoma.
tre: Antiseizure drugs with epilepsy surgery for refractory cases, glaucoma treatment, low-dose aspirin in some patients, pulsed-dye laser for the birthmark and developmental support.

name: Marfan syndrome
epi: Autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder affecting about 1 in 5,000 people; about three quarters inherit it from a parent.
eti: Pathogenic FBN1 variants disrupt fibrillin-1 and increase TGF-beta signaling, weakening connective tissue.
cli: Tall stature, long limbs and arachnodactyly, chest wall and spinal deformities, upward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), mitral valve prolapse and aortic root dilation with dissection risk.
inv: Clinical assessment with the Ghent criteria, echocardiography of the aortic root, slit-lamp eye examination and FBN1 genetic testing.
tre: Beta-blockers or ARBs to slow aortic dilation, regular aortic imaging, avoidance of strenuous or contact sports and elective aortic root surgery when thresholds are reached.

name: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal dominant disorder (estimated 1 in 20,000 to 150,000); about half of cases are de novo.
eti: Heterozygous pathogenic COL3A1 variants cause deficient type III collagen in blood vessels, skin and hollow organs.
cli: Arterial dissection or rupture, bowel perforation and uterine rupture in pregnancy, with thin translucent skin, extensive bruising and characteristic facial features; median survival is about 50 years.
inv: COL3A1 molecular testing confirms; noninvasive arterial imaging (ultrasound, MRA or CTA) for surveillance.
tre: Celiprolol is used in some centers, with blood-pressure control and noninvasive vascular surveillance; avoid contact sports, conventional angiography and elective surgery.

name: Angelman syndrome
epi: Rare neurogenetic disorder affecting about 1 in 12,000 to 24,000 people, usually recognized in infancy or early childhood.
eti: Loss of maternally expressed UBE3A on 15q11.2-q13, most often a maternal deletion (about 70%), with UBE3A variants, paternal uniparental disomy or imprinting defects.
cli: Severe developmental delay, absent or minimal speech, ataxic gait with tremor, happy demeanor with frequent laughter and hand-flapping, seizures, microcephaly and sleep problems.
inv: DNA methylation analysis of 15q11.2-q13 detects most cases, followed by UBE3A sequencing if normal, with EEG for seizures.
tre: No cure; antiseizure medication, physical, occupational and speech therapy with nonverbal communication, behavioral and sleep management.

name: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion)
epi: Most common microdeletion syndrome, affecting about 1 in 4,000 people, with highly variable expression.
eti: Usually de novo deletion of 22q11.2 including TBX1, disrupting development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches (thymus, parathyroids, heart outflow tract, palate).
cli: Conotruncal heart defects, hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism, T-cell immunodeficiency from thymic hypoplasia, palatal abnormalities, facial features, learning difficulties and psychiatric illness.
inv: Chromosomal microarray or FISH confirms the deletion; assess calcium and PTH, T-cell counts, echocardiography, hearing and development.
tre: Multidisciplinary care including cardiac surgery, calcium and vitamin D, infection management and avoidance of live vaccines until T-cell function is assessed, palate and speech therapy, and thymus transplant for complete athymia.

name: Fanconi anemia
epi: Rare inherited bone-marrow-failure syndrome (about 1 in 100,000 to 160,000), more common in Ashkenazi Jewish, Roma and Afrikaner populations.
eti: Usually autosomal recessive (rarely X-linked) variants in more than 20 FANC genes, most often FANCA, impair DNA interstrand-crosslink repair.
cli: Progressive pancytopenia in childhood with short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, cafe-au-lait spots, renal and genital malformations, and high risk of AML and head-and-neck or genital squamous cancers.
inv: Chromosome breakage testing with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C is diagnostic, followed by genetic testing; CBC and marrow examination assess marrow failure.
tre: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for marrow failure or leukemia, with transfusions and androgens as bridging therapy and lifelong cancer surveillance.

name: Erythropoietic protoporphyria
epi: Third most common porphyria (about 2-5 per million) and the most common in children; symptoms begin in early childhood.
eti: Ferrochelatase deficiency, usually from a FECH loss-of-function variant plus a common low-expression allele, causes protoporphyrin accumulation; ALAS2 gain-of-function causes the X-linked form.
cli: Painful burning and stinging of sun-exposed skin within minutes of exposure, with redness and swelling but little blistering; 20-30% have liver dysfunction and a few develop cholestatic liver failure.
inv: Markedly raised free erythrocyte protoporphyrin confirms, with FECH or ALAS2 genetic testing and liver tests.
tre: Sun avoidance and protective clothing; afamelanotide increases sun tolerance, with vitamin D supplementation and liver transplantation for severe liver disease.

name: Ataxia-telangiectasia
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 40,000 to 100,000), with onset of ataxia usually before age 5.
eti: Biallelic ATM variants impair DNA double-strand-break repair, causing neurodegeneration, immunodeficiency and radiosensitivity.
cli: Progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculomotor apraxia and dysarthria, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and high risk of leukemia and lymphoma.
inv: Elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein, low immunoglobulins (IgA, IgG2) and lymphopenia; ATM genetic testing confirms.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care with physical therapy, infection prevention and immunoglobulin replacement when indicated; minimize ionizing radiation and monitor for cancer.

name: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
epi: Rare acquired clonal disorder (about 16 per million) usually presenting at age 30-40, often associated with aplastic anemia.
eti: Somatic PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell causes loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 and CD59, leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
cli: Hemolytic anemia with dark morning urine, fatigue, abdominal pain, dysphagia and erectile dysfunction, venous thrombosis at unusual sites (hepatic, mesenteric, cerebral) and marrow failure.
inv: High-sensitivity flow cytometry showing GPI-anchored protein deficiency (CD55/CD59 or FLAER) is diagnostic; raised LDH, low haptoglobin and hemoglobinuria support hemolysis.
tre: Complement C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) for symptomatic disease, with proximal inhibitors as options; anticoagulation for thrombosis and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation as the only cure.

name: Hereditary hemochromatosis
epi: Common inherited disorder in people of northern European, especially Celtic, ancestry; symptoms usually appear at age 30-60, earlier in men.
eti: Usually homozygous HFE C282Y variants reduce hepcidin, increasing intestinal iron absorption and causing iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, joints and pituitary.
cli: Fatigue, arthralgia (especially second and third MCP joints), skin bronzing, diabetes, hepatomegaly and cirrhosis, hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy.
inv: Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin, then HFE genotyping; liver tests, MRI or biopsy assess iron load and fibrosis.
tre: Regular venesection to target ferritin levels is first-line, with chelation if phlebotomy is not possible; avoid iron supplements and excess alcohol, and screen for HCC in cirrhosis.

name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
epi: Rare X-linked immunodeficiency (about 1-10 per million males) affecting boys.
eti: WAS gene variants impair WASP, an actin-cytoskeleton regulator in blood cells, causing immune dysfunction and small, short-lived platelets.
cli: Triad of eczema, recurrent infections and microthrombocytopenia with bleeding, plus increased autoimmunity and lymphoma risk.
inv: CBC shows thrombocytopenia with low mean platelet volume; immunologic testing, WASP flow cytometry and WAS genetic testing confirm.
tre: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is curative, with gene therapy in some centers; infection prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement and eczema care meanwhile.

name: Phenylketonuria (PKU)
epi: Autosomal recessive metabolic disorder (about 1 in 10,000 to 25,000 newborns) detected by newborn screening in many countries.
eti: PAH variants cause phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (rarely BH4 defects), so phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine is reduced.
cli: Untreated: intellectual disability, seizures, behavioral problems, eczema, musty odor and fair skin and hair; early-treated children develop normally.
inv: Newborn screening shows raised blood phenylalanine, confirmed with plasma amino acids, BH4 defect testing and PAH genetic testing.
tre: Lifelong low-phenylalanine diet with phenylalanine-free medical formula and strict control in pregnancy; sapropterin for responsive patients and pegvaliase for adults.

name: Alkaptonuria
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 250,000 to 1 million), more common in Slovakia and the Dominican Republic; usually recognized in adulthood.
eti: HGD variants cause homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency, so homogentisic acid accumulates and is deposited as pigment in connective tissue (ochronosis).
cli: Urine darkening on standing from infancy, bluish-black pigmentation of ear cartilage and sclera, early spine and large-joint arthritis, heart-valve calcification and kidney or prostate stones.
inv: Raised urinary homogentisic acid on gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirms, with HGD testing and imaging of joints and heart valves.
tre: Nitisinone reduces homogentisic acid production; supportive care with analgesia, physiotherapy, joint replacement and valve surgery when needed.

name: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 185,000 worldwide), far more common in Old Order Mennonites; usually detected by newborn screening.
eti: Variants in BCKDHA, BCKDHB or DBT cause branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, so leucine, isoleucine, valine and their ketoacids accumulate; leucine is neurotoxic.
cli: Classic form presents in the first days of life with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, abnormal movements and encephalopathy with sweet maple-syrup odor of urine or cerumen; untreated it causes seizures, coma and death.
inv: Newborn screening and plasma amino acids show raised branched-chain amino acids with alloisoleucine (diagnostic); urine shows branched-chain ketoacids, and genetic testing confirms.
tre: Lifelong dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids with special formula, emergency high-calorie management of catabolic crises and occasionally dialysis; thiamine for responsive variants and liver transplantation in selected cases.

name: Menkes disease
epi: Rare X-linked recessive disorder (about 1 in 100,000 newborns) affecting mainly boys, presenting at 2-3 months; about a third of cases are new mutations.
eti: ATP7A variants impair intestinal copper absorption and distribution, causing copper deficiency in the brain and reduced activity of copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase.
cli: Sparse, kinky, hypopigmented hair, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental regression, connective-tissue laxity and tortuous arteries; most die by age 3, while occipital horn syndrome is a milder form.
inv: Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin (interpret carefully in newborns), raised plasma dopamine-to-norepinephrine ratio and ATP7A genetic testing.
tre: Early subcutaneous copper histidinate, ideally started in the neonatal period before neurologic damage, with supportive neurologic, nutritional and seizure care.

name: Tay-Sachs disease
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder, more common in Ashkenazi Jewish, French-Canadian, Cajun and Old Order Amish populations; carrier screening has reduced incidence.
eti: HEXA variants cause beta-hexosaminidase A deficiency and GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons.
cli: Infantile form begins at 3-6 months with developmental regression, exaggerated startle, hypotonia then spasticity, seizures, blindness, macrocephaly and a macular cherry-red spot, without hepatosplenomegaly; death in early childhood. Juvenile and late-onset forms are milder.
inv: Low hexosaminidase A enzyme activity and HEXA genetic testing confirm; fundoscopy shows the cherry-red spot.
tre: No curative therapy; supportive care with seizure control, nutrition, respiratory care and genetic counseling with carrier screening.

name: Niemann-Pick disease type C
epi: Rare autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder (about 1 in 100,000-150,000), presenting from the perinatal period to adulthood.
eti: Biallelic NPC1 (about 95%) or NPC2 variants impair intracellular cholesterol trafficking, causing unesterified cholesterol and glycolipid accumulation in lysosomes.
cli: Neonatal cholestatic jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly, then childhood ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, gelastic cataplexy, dysarthria, dysphagia, seizures and cognitive decline; adults may present with psychiatric illness or dementia.
inv: Plasma oxysterols or lysosphingolipid biomarkers screen for disease, confirmed by NPC1 or NPC2 genetic testing; filipin staining of fibroblasts is now rarely used.
tre: Multidisciplinary supportive care; miglustat in many countries, and arimoclomol (with miglustat) and levacetylleucine were FDA-approved in 2024.

name: Niemann-Pick disease
epi: Group of rare autosomal recessive lysosomal disorders; types A/B (acid sphingomyelinase deficiency) affect about 1 in 250,000, more often Ashkenazi Jews, and type C about 1 in 150,000.
eti: Types A and B (ASMD) result from SMPD1 variants causing sphingomyelin accumulation; type C results from NPC1/NPC2 variants impairing cholesterol trafficking.
cli: Type A: infantile hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration and cherry-red spot with death in early childhood; type B: hepatosplenomegaly, lung disease and dyslipidemia into adulthood; type C: ataxia, vertical gaze palsy and cognitive decline.
inv: Low acid sphingomyelinase activity and SMPD1 testing for types A/B; oxysterol biomarkers and NPC1/NPC2 testing for type C.
tre: Supportive care; olipudase alfa enzyme replacement for non-neurologic manifestations of ASMD, and miglustat, arimoclomol or levacetylleucine for type C.

name: Gaucher disease
epi: Most common lysosomal storage disorder (about 1 in 50,000-100,000), with type 1 especially common in Ashkenazi Jews (about 1 in 500-1,000).
eti: Biallelic GBA1 variants cause glucocerebrosidase deficiency and glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages (Gaucher cells).
cli: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic): splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia with bruising, bone pain, crises and fractures; types 2 and 3 add neurologic involvement.
inv: Low glucocerebrosidase activity in leukocytes confirmed by GBA1 testing; biomarkers and MRI assess disease burden.
tre: Enzyme replacement therapy (imiglucerase and related agents) or substrate reduction therapy (eliglustat, miglustat) for type 1; ERT does not treat neurologic disease.

name: Hurler syndrome (MPS I)
epi: Severe MPS I (Hurler) affects about 1 in 100,000 newborns, presenting in infancy; attenuated forms are rarer.
eti: Autosomal recessive IDUA variants cause alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency with lysosomal accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate.
cli: Coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, joint stiffness, umbilical or inguinal hernias, airway obstruction, cardiac valve disease and developmental decline from about age 1.
inv: Raised urinary glycosaminoglycans, deficient alpha-L-iduronidase activity and IDUA genetic testing confirm diagnosis.
tre: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation before age 2 to 2.5 for severe disease, with laronidase enzyme replacement and multidisciplinary supportive care.

name: Hunter syndrome (MPS II)
epi: Rare X-linked recessive disorder affecting about 1 in 100,000-170,000 males.
eti: IDS variants cause iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency with lysosomal accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate.
cli: Coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, hepatosplenomegaly, joint contractures, airway and heart-valve disease and pebbly skin, without corneal clouding; neuronopathic and attenuated forms.
inv: Raised urinary glycosaminoglycans, deficient iduronate-2-sulfatase activity and IDS genetic testing confirm diagnosis.
tre: Idursulfase enzyme replacement for somatic features (it does not cross the blood-brain barrier), with multidisciplinary supportive care.

name: Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 100,000), usually presenting at 3-4 months of age.
eti: Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (G6PC1, type Ia, about 80%) or its transporter (SLC37A4, type Ib) blocks glucose release from glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
cli: Severe fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, massive hepatomegaly, doll-like facies, growth failure, hyperlipidemia and hyperuricemia; type Ib adds neutropenia, infections and IBD-like colitis, and hepatic adenomas develop later.
inv: Fasting hypoglycemia with raised lactate, triglycerides and uric acid; G6PC1 or SLC37A4 genetic testing confirms diagnosis.
tre: Frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch with avoidance of fasting, allopurinol and lipid management, G-CSF or empagliflozin for type Ib neutropenia, and liver transplantation in selected cases.

name: Pompe disease (GSD II)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (about 1 in 40,000) with classic infantile-onset and late-onset forms.
eti: GAA variants cause acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency, so glycogen accumulates in lysosomes of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.
cli: Classic infantile form: floppy baby with hypotonia, macroglossia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure, fatal in the first year untreated; late-onset form: progressive proximal and respiratory muscle weakness without major heart disease.
inv: Low GAA activity on dried blood spot or leukocytes with GAA genetic testing; raised CK, and ECG (short PR, large QRS) and echocardiography in infants.
tre: Enzyme replacement therapy (alglucosidase or avalglucosidase alfa) started early, with immune tolerance induction for CRIM-negative infants plus respiratory and rehabilitation support.

name: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
epi: Very rare X-linked recessive disorder (about 1 in 235,000-380,000) almost exclusively affecting males.
eti: HPRT1 variants cause severe hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency, blocking purine salvage and causing uric acid overproduction.
cli: Orange sand-like crystals in diapers, developmental delay, dystonia and choreoathetosis, spasticity, compulsive self-injury such as lip and finger biting, gouty arthritis and urate kidney stones.
inv: Raised serum and urine uric acid; low HPRT enzyme activity and HPRT1 genetic testing confirm diagnosis.
tre: Allopurinol and hydration for hyperuricemia (does not improve neurologic features), protective devices, dental extraction if needed, and behavioral and neurologic management.

name: Pityriasis versicolor
epi: Common superficial fungal infection of adolescents and young adults, highly prevalent in hot humid climates and much less common in cold regions.
eti: Overgrowth of Malassezia yeast, part of normal skin flora, converting to its hyphal form; heat, sweating and oily skin predispose.
cli: Oval, finely scaling hypo- or hyperpigmented macules and patches on the trunk, neck and upper arms, usually asymptomatic or mildly itchy.
inv: Usually clinical; KOH microscopy shows the spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of yeast and hyphae, and Wood lamp may show yellow-green fluorescence.
tre: Topical ketoconazole shampoo, selenium sulfide or azole creams; oral itraconazole or fluconazole for extensive disease, with prophylaxis for frequent recurrence.

name: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)
epi: Occurs almost exclusively in tobacco users, mainly men aged 30-45, with highest prevalence in Asia and the Middle East.
eti: Nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory thrombosis of small and medium arteries and veins of the limbs, strongly linked to tobacco exposure; immune mechanisms are suspected.
cli: Distal limb ischemia with foot or hand claudication, rest pain, cold sensitivity, Raynaud phenomenon, ischemic ulcers and gangrene, often with migratory superficial thrombophlebitis.
inv: Clinical diagnosis after excluding atherosclerosis, embolism and autoimmune disease; angiography shows segmental distal occlusions with corkscrew collaterals.
tre: Complete cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products is essential, with wound care, cold avoidance, iloprost in some patients and amputation for nonhealing gangrene.

name: Susac syndrome
epi: Rare disorder, most common in young adult women aged 20-40.
eti: Autoimmune endotheliopathy causing microvascular occlusion in the brain, retina and cochlea.
cli: Triad of subacute encephalopathy with headache, branch retinal artery occlusions and low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; the full triad is often absent at onset.
inv: MRI shows central corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions; fluorescein angiography shows branch retinal artery occlusions and wall hyperfluorescence, and audiometry documents hearing loss.
tre: Early immunosuppression with high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG and steroid-sparing agents such as mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide or rituximab in severe disease.

name: Castleman disease
epi: Rare group of lymphoproliferative disorders: unicentric disease affects all ages, HHV-8-associated multicentric disease mainly people with HIV, and idiopathic multicentric disease (iMCD) is rarer.
eti: Dysregulated cytokine signaling, especially IL-6, causes lymph-node hyperplasia; HHV-8 drives some multicentric cases while unicentric and iMCD causes are unknown.
cli: Unicentric disease is often an asymptomatic solitary mass; multicentric disease causes fever, night sweats, weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, edema and cytopenias.
inv: Excisional lymph-node biopsy with characteristic histology after excluding lymphoma, infection and autoimmune disease; CRP, CBC, HIV and HHV-8 testing and PET-CT for extent.
tre: Surgical excision for unicentric disease; siltuximab (anti-IL-6) first-line for iMCD and rituximab-based therapy for HHV-8-associated disease with antiretrovirals in HIV.

name: Gestational diabetes mellitus
epi: Common pregnancy complication, more prevalent in Asian/Pacific Islander and Hispanic women; affected women have increased future risk of type 2 diabetes.
eti: Pregnancy-related insulin resistance, driven by placental hormones, exceeds the mother's pancreatic insulin reserve, causing hyperglycemia first recognized during pregnancy.
cli: Usually asymptomatic; risks include preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, fetal macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, stillbirth and neonatal hypoglycemia, respiratory distress and hyperbilirubinemia.
inv: Universal screening at 24-28 weeks with a 50-g glucose challenge, confirmed by oral glucose tolerance test; repeat 75-g OGTT postpartum to check for persistent diabetes.
tre: Diet and exercise first, adding insulin (preferred) or metformin if glycemic targets are not met, with fetal surveillance and postpartum diabetes screening.

name: Allergic conjunctivitis
epi: Very common, affecting a large share of the population, often under age 20 and frequently coexisting with allergic rhinitis and asthma.
eti: IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity: allergens such as pollen, dust mites or pet dander trigger conjunctival mast-cell degranulation and histamine release.
cli: Bilateral itching (hallmark), redness, clear watery discharge, eyelid edema and chemosis, often with sneezing and rhinorrhea; pain or vision loss suggests another diagnosis.
inv: Clinical diagnosis from history and examination; conjunctival scraping may show eosinophils and fluorescein staining excludes corneal abrasion when needed.
tre: Allergen avoidance, cool compresses and artificial tears, with topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizer drops as mainstay; short courses of antihistamine-vasoconstrictor drops for mild cases.

name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
epi: Most common adult leukemia in Western countries, affecting older adults (median age about 70) with slight male predominance; rare in Asian populations.
eti: Clonal proliferation of mature CD5+ B lymphocytes, typically arising from monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis through acquired genetic abnormalities and B-cell receptor signaling.
cli: Often asymptomatic lymphocytosis found incidentally; may cause lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, B symptoms, cytopenias, autoimmune hemolysis/thrombocytopenia and recurrent infections from hypogammaglobulinemia.
inv: CBC shows sustained B-lymphocytosis with smudge cells on smear; flow cytometry confirms CD5, CD19, CD23 coexpression; FISH/TP53 and IGHV status guide prognosis.
tre: Watch-and-wait for asymptomatic early disease; treat active disease with targeted therapy such as BTK inhibitors or venetoclax-obinutuzumab, chosen by genetic risk and fitness.

name: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)
epi: Uncommon myeloproliferative neoplasm of adults, with incidence rising with age, slight male predominance and median diagnosis in the mid-50s.
eti: Reciprocal t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase driving myeloid proliferation.
cli: Often asymptomatic; fatigue, weight loss and splenomegaly with early satiety or left upper quadrant pain; progresses from chronic to accelerated and blast phase if untreated.
inv: CBC shows leukocytosis with left-shifted granulocytes and basophilia; bone marrow, cytogenetics/FISH and quantitative PCR for BCR-ABL1 confirm diagnosis and monitor response.
tre: Oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib or second-generation agents such as dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib) with molecular monitoring; stem-cell transplantation for resistant or advanced disease.

name: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia
epi: Rare indolent lymphoproliferative disorder of older adults (median age about 60), making up most large granular lymphocytic leukemia cases.
eti: Clonal expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells resisting apoptosis through JAK/STAT activation, often from STAT3 gain-of-function mutations; strongly associated with autoimmunity.
cli: Chronic neutropenia with recurrent infections, anemia, mild splenomegaly and lymphocytosis; frequently associated with rheumatoid arthritis; many patients are asymptomatic.
inv: Persistent circulating large granular lymphocytes on smear; flow cytometry shows CD3+, CD8+, CD57+ T cells and TCR gene rearrangement confirms clonality; STAT3 testing supports diagnosis.
tre: Observation if asymptomatic; immunosuppression for cytopenias or symptoms, with methotrexate or cyclophosphamide first-line and cyclosporine as an alternative.

name: Cryptococcal meningitis
epi: Major opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, causing over 100,000 HIV-related deaths yearly, also affecting transplant recipients and others on immunosuppression.
eti: Inhaled Cryptococcus neoformans (from bird droppings/soil) or C. gattii disseminates to the CNS in patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity.
cli: Subacute meningoencephalitis with headache, fever, altered mental status, nausea and vomiting, visual disturbance and cranial nerve palsies; neck stiffness may be absent.
inv: Brain imaging before lumbar puncture; CSF shows high opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose; cryptococcal antigen, India ink and culture confirm diagnosis.
tre: Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole consolidation and maintenance; therapeutic lumbar punctures for raised pressure and delayed ART start to reduce IRIS.

name: Hepatorenal syndrome
epi: Serious complication of advanced cirrhosis with ascites, accounting for a substantial share of acute kidney injury in hospitalized cirrhotic patients, with high short-term mortality.
eti: Portal hypertension causes splanchnic vasodilation and effective arterial hypovolemia, activating RAAS and sympathetic systems and causing intense renal vasoconstriction; infections such as SBP often precipitate.
cli: Progressive oliguria and rising creatinine in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis showing jaundice, ascites, coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy.
inv: Diagnosis of exclusion: rising creatinine not improving after albumin volume expansion, without shock, nephrotoxins, or structural kidney disease (bland urine, minimal proteinuria, normal ultrasound).
tre: Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins, treat precipitants, give terlipressin plus albumin first-line (norepinephrine or midodrine-octreotide alternatives); liver transplantation is definitive.

name: Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori disease)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder, more frequent in founder populations; type IIIa (liver and muscle) is far more common than IIIb (liver only).
eti: Biallelic AGL gene variants cause glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency, so abnormal limit-dextrin-like glycogen accumulates in liver and muscle.
cli: Infantile hepatomegaly, fasting ketotic hypoglycemia and growth failure; later progressive skeletal myopathy, cardiomyopathy and liver fibrosis, cirrhosis or adenomas.
inv: Hypoglycemia with ketosis, elevated transaminases, lipids and CK; molecular testing for AGL variants confirms, with enzyme assay if genetics inconclusive.
tre: Frequent feeds with cornstarch and a high-protein diet to prevent hypoglycemia, with liver, cardiac and muscle surveillance; liver transplant for cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.

name: Acute bacterial meningitis
epi: Medical emergency affecting all ages; causative organisms vary by age and vaccination, and meningococcal disease particularly affects young children, adolescents and young adults.
eti: Bacterial invasion of the meninges, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, with group B streptococcus and E. coli in neonates and Listeria in infants, older adults and the immunocompromised.
cli: Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and altered mental status; seizures, focal deficits or shock may occur, and meningococcal disease may cause a petechial or purpuric rash.
inv: Blood cultures and lumbar puncture when safe, with CSF typically showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose and high protein plus Gram stain, culture and PCR; imaging precedes LP in selected patients.
tre: Immediate empiric IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, adding vancomycin or ampicillin by age and risk, without delaying for LP; dexamethasone when indicated, supportive care, and chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal contacts.

name: Meningitis (overview)
epi: Occurs at all ages; incidence and causative pathogens vary with age, vaccination, geography and immune status, with viral meningitis more common but bacterial more dangerous.
eti: Inflammation of the meninges, usually from viral, bacterial or fungal infection, and less commonly from noninfectious causes such as drugs, malignancy or autoimmune disease.
cli: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and altered mental status; seizures, focal deficits, rash or shock suggest severe or bacterial disease.
inv: Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture and PCR when safe distinguishes causes; blood cultures and neuroimaging are used according to presentation.
tre: Suspected bacterial meningitis needs immediate empiric antibiotics and supportive care; treatment is then tailored to the identified cause, with antivirals or antifungals where indicated.

name: Viral meningitis
epi: The most common form of meningitis, occurring at any age with summer and autumn peaks for enteroviruses; it is usually milder than bacterial meningitis.
eti: Viral infection of the meninges, most often enteroviruses, with HSV-2, VZV, HIV, mumps and arboviruses among other causes.
cli: Fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea and sometimes rash, usually with preserved consciousness.
inv: Lumbar puncture typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and normal or mildly raised protein; CSF PCR identifies many causes while bacterial meningitis is excluded.
tre: Supportive care for most cases, usually with full recovery; IV aciclovir is used when HSV or VZV is suspected or confirmed, and empiric antibiotics until bacterial infection is excluded.

name: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
epi: A common form of heart failure that increases with age, most often following ischemic heart disease, with hypertension, cardiomyopathy and valve disease as other causes.
eti: Reduced left-ventricular systolic function with ejection fraction 40% or less, caused by ischemic, hypertensive, valvular, toxic, inflammatory or genetic myocardial injury.
cli: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue and peripheral edema; signs include raised JVP, crackles and a third heart sound, and decompensation causes pulmonary edema.
inv: Echocardiography documents reduced ejection fraction; ECG, natriuretic peptides, renal and electrolyte testing and ischemic evaluation identify cause and guide treatment.
tre: Four foundational drug classes when tolerated: ARNI or ACE inhibitor/ARB, evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor; diuretics relieve congestion, with ICD or CRT in selected patients.

name: Acute decompensated heart failure (pulmonary edema)
epi: A common emergency and leading cause of hospitalization in older adults, occurring in people with known heart failure or as a first presentation of cardiac disease.
eti: Acute rise in cardiac filling pressures with congestion, often triggered by ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled hypertension, valve disease, medication or dietary nonadherence.
cli: Severe dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, hypoxemia, edema and sometimes pink frothy sputum; hypertensive pulmonary edema may develop abruptly, and hypoperfusion indicates cardiogenic shock.
inv: ECG, chest radiograph, BNP or NT-proBNP, troponin, renal and electrolyte tests and echocardiography identify the cause and severity.
tre: Oxygen and noninvasive ventilation when needed, IV loop diuretics for congestion and vasodilators such as nitrates in hypertensive patients; inotropes or mechanical support for shock, and treat the precipitant.

name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
epi: Occurs mainly in older adults with type 2 diabetes, often undiagnosed, and is usually precipitated by infection, medications or another acute illness; mortality is higher than in DKA.
eti: Relative insulin deficiency causes severe hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis and profound dehydration with hyperosmolality; residual insulin limits ketogenesis, so significant ketoacidosis is absent.
cli: Insidious polyuria, polydipsia, weakness and profound dehydration with progressive neurologic changes from confusion to coma; seizures and thrombosis can occur.
inv: Very high glucose and raised effective serum osmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis; electrolytes, renal function and infection screening identify severity and trigger.
tre: Careful IV fluid replacement first, then low-dose IV insulin once glucose stops falling with fluids alone, with electrolyte replacement, thromboprophylaxis and treatment of the trigger; avoid rapid osmolality shifts.

name: Myxedema coma
epi: Rare, life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism, most often in older women during winter; despite its name, coma is often absent.
eti: Longstanding severe hypothyroidism decompensated by a precipitant such as infection, cold exposure, sedatives, surgery or stopping thyroid replacement, impairing thermoregulation, ventilation and circulation.
cli: Altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia, with features of hypothyroidism such as non-pitting edema and dry skin.
inv: Low free T4 with markedly elevated TSH in primary disease, or low or normal TSH in central disease; cortisol, glucose, sodium, blood gases and infection screening assess precipitants.
tre: Immediate IV thyroid hormone plus empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, with ventilatory and circulatory support, passive rewarming and treatment of the trigger.

name: Acute diverticulitis
epi: Common, increasing with age and in people with colonic diverticulosis; obesity, low-fiber diet, smoking and physical inactivity raise risk.
eti: Inflammation, often with microperforation, of a colonic diverticulum, usually in the sigmoid colon in Western populations, with right-sided disease more common in Asian populations.
cli: Left-lower-quadrant pain and tenderness, fever and altered bowel habit; complicated disease causes abscess, perforation with peritonitis, fistula, stricture or obstruction.
inv: CT abdomen and pelvis confirms diagnosis and detects complications when uncertain or severe; CBC and CRP support assessment, and colonoscopy is deferred until recovery when indicated.
tre: Uncomplicated disease is managed with analgesia, diet modification and selective rather than routine antibiotics; complicated disease needs IV antibiotics, percutaneous drainage of suitable abscesses or surgery.

name: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
epi: Common functional gastrointestinal disorder, more frequent in women and usually beginning before middle age; it may follow gastroenteritis.
eti: Disorder of gut-brain interaction involving visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility, microbiota changes and central pain processing, without structural disease explaining symptoms.
cli: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation with altered stool frequency or form, classified as constipation-, diarrhea-predominant or mixed subtypes; bloating is common.
inv: Diagnosis uses Rome symptom-based criteria after screening for alarm features; limited testing such as CBC, CRP, celiac serology and fecal calprotectin is guided by presentation.
tre: Education, diet changes such as a supervised low-FODMAP trial, exercise and psychological therapies; soluble fiber, antispasmodics, laxatives or antidiarrheals and low-dose tricyclics are chosen by subtype.

name: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
epi: Common in adolescents and young adults; most people acquire EBV in childhood, when infection is often mild or silent.
eti: Primary infection with Epstein-Barr virus, a herpesvirus spread mainly through saliva that infects B cells and persists latently for life.
cli: Fever, severe pharyngitis with tonsillar enlargement, marked fatigue and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; splenomegaly, mild hepatitis and a rash after amoxicillin may occur.
inv: CBC shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes; heterophile antibody (Monospot) or EBV-specific serology confirms diagnosis, and liver enzymes are often raised.
tre: Supportive care with hydration, analgesia and rest; avoid contact sports while the spleen is enlarged because of rupture risk, and avoid unnecessary antibiotics, which do not treat EBV.

name: Lung cancer
epi: A leading cause of cancer death worldwide; risk rises strongly with tobacco exposure and age, and occupational exposures, radon and air pollution also contribute.
eti: Malignant tumors of bronchial or pulmonary epithelium, mainly non-small-cell carcinomas (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell) and small-cell carcinoma; smoking is the major preventable cause.
cli: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, recurrent pneumonia and weight loss; may cause paraneoplastic syndromes or symptoms of local spread and metastases, and early disease is often asymptomatic.
inv: CT chest characterizes lesions and tissue biopsy confirms histology; PET-CT and brain imaging stage disease, and molecular and PD-L1 testing guide therapy in non-small-cell cancer.
tre: Stage-, histology- and biomarker-directed treatment including resection, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy; smoking cessation, and low-dose CT screening for eligible high-risk people.

name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
epi: A major cause of cancer death worldwide; risk is highest in cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B or C, alcohol-related liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
eti: Malignant transformation of hepatocytes, usually in a chronically diseased liver; hepatitis B can cause HCC even without cirrhosis, and aflatoxin exposure contributes in some regions.
cli: Often asymptomatic early; later right-upper-quadrant pain, weight loss, hepatomegaly, jaundice or decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis.
inv: Surveillance ultrasound with or without AFP every six months in at-risk patients; multiphase CT or MRI can diagnose typical lesions, with biopsy used selectively.
tre: Stage-based treatment including resection, ablation, liver transplantation, transarterial chemoembolization and systemic immunotherapy or targeted therapy for advanced disease.

name: Migraine
epi: Very common primary headache disorder, about three times more common in women, often beginning in adolescence or early adulthood.
eti: Neurovascular disorder involving trigeminovascular activation and CGRP release, with genetic and environmental influences; aura reflects cortical spreading depression.
cli: Recurrent attacks of often unilateral, pulsating moderate-to-severe headache worsened by activity, with nausea and light or sound sensitivity; some attacks are preceded by reversible visual, sensory or speech aura.
inv: Clinical diagnosis using ICHD criteria; neuroimaging is reserved for red flags, atypical features or a new neurologic deficit.
tre: Acute NSAIDs or triptans, with antiemetics, while limiting overuse; preventive therapy such as beta-blockers, topiramate, amitriptyline or CGRP-targeted drugs for frequent or disabling attacks.

name: Measles (rubeola)
epi: One of the most contagious human infections; outbreaks occur where vaccination coverage falls, with highest morbidity in young children, the malnourished and the immunocompromised.
eti: Measles virus, a paramyxovirus, spread by airborne droplets and particles; infection causes transient immunosuppression.
cli: Prodrome of high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots, followed by a maculopapular rash starting at the hairline and spreading downward; complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and late SSPE.
inv: Clinical suspicion plus measles PCR from respiratory or urine samples and/or IgM serology; notify public health for confirmation and contact tracing.
tre: Supportive care, vitamin A for children, airborne isolation and treatment of complications; MMR vaccination prevents disease, and post-exposure vaccine or immunoglobulin protects selected contacts.

name: Varicella (chickenpox)
epi: Highly contagious childhood infection where vaccination is not routine; adults, pregnant women, neonates and immunocompromised people are at risk of severe disease.
eti: Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus spread by respiratory droplets and contact with lesions; the virus then remains latent in sensory ganglia and can reactivate as shingles.
cli: Fever and malaise with an intensely itchy rash of macules, papules and vesicles crusting over, in successive crops at different stages with a central (truncal) predominance.
inv: Usually clinical; PCR of vesicle fluid is the preferred confirmatory test when the diagnosis is uncertain.
tre: Supportive and antipruritic care for uncomplicated disease, avoiding aspirin in children; aciclovir for adults, high-risk or severe cases, with immunoglobulin for exposed high-risk contacts and vaccination for prevention.

name: Roseola (exanthem subitum)
epi: Common viral illness of infants and young children, mostly between about 6 months and 2 years of age.
eti: Primary infection with human herpesvirus 6, less often HHV-7, spread through saliva from asymptomatic carriers.
cli: Abrupt high fever for several days in an otherwise well child, followed by a blanching pink maculopapular rash on the trunk as the fever resolves; febrile seizures may occur.
inv: Clinical diagnosis in typical cases; testing is rarely needed in uncomplicated disease.
tre: Supportive care with fluids and antipyretics for comfort; evaluate and manage febrile seizures appropriately.

name: Acute glomerulonephritis
epi: Occurs at any age depending on cause; post-streptococcal disease is most common in children in low-resource settings, while IgA nephropathy and vasculitis predominate in adults.
eti: Immune-mediated glomerular inflammation, including post-infectious (classically post-streptococcal) immune-complex disease, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis.
cli: Nephritic syndrome with hematuria and cola-colored urine, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, oliguria and reduced kidney function; post-streptococcal disease follows throat or skin infection after a latent interval.
inv: Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria; creatinine, complement, ASO or anti-DNase B, ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and often kidney biopsy establish cause.
tre: Control blood pressure and fluid overload with salt restriction and diuretics, and treat the underlying cause; antibiotics clear residual streptococcal infection, and immunosuppression is used for immune-mediated forms.

name: Cataract
epi: A leading cause of visual impairment and reversible blindness worldwide, very common in older adults; congenital cataract also occurs.
eti: Opacification of the crystalline lens, usually from age-related protein changes; diabetes, corticosteroids, smoking, UV exposure, trauma and congenital or metabolic causes increase risk.
cli: Gradual painless blurred vision, glare, halos, reduced contrast and color perception and difficulty with night driving; myopic shift may occur, and an altered red reflex is seen.
inv: Visual acuity testing and slit-lamp examination after pupil dilation confirm lens opacity and assess severity and other eye disease.
tre: Updated glasses and better lighting may help early disease; definitive treatment is cataract surgery with phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation when vision affects daily life.

name: Batten disease
epi: Rare group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses); onset ranges from infancy to adulthood depending on subtype, with childhood forms most typical.
eti: Pathogenic variants in one of many CLN genes cause lysosomal accumulation of lipopigment and neuronal loss; most forms are autosomal recessive, though adult CLN4 disease can be autosomal dominant.
cli: Progressive vision loss, seizures, cognitive and motor decline and behavioral change; the order and pace vary by subtype (e.g. vision loss first in juvenile CLN3 disease).
inv: Genetic testing establishes the subtype; enzyme assays (e.g. TPP1, PPT1), ophthalmologic examination, EEG, neuroimaging and electron microscopy support the diagnosis.
tre: Largely supportive and multidisciplinary, with symptomatic treatment of seizures, movement and behavioral problems; intraventricular cerliponase alfa enzyme replacement is approved for CLN2 disease.

name: Athlete's foot (tinea pedis)
epi: Very common superficial fungal infection, more frequent in adult males; risk rises with occlusive footwear, sweating, diabetes and use of communal wet areas such as pools and showers.
eti: Dermatophyte infection of keratinized foot skin, most often Trichophyton rubrum; spread by direct contact or contaminated floors and footwear.
cli: Itching, scaling, fissuring and maceration between the toes; moccasin-type dry scaling of the soles or vesicular/bullous lesions can occur, often with coexisting onychomycosis.
inv: Often clinical; KOH microscopy of skin scrapings shows fungal hyphae, with fungal culture when diagnosis is uncertain or disease is refractory.
tre: Topical azoles or terbinafine are first-line, with oral terbinafine, itraconazole or fluconazole for extensive or resistant disease; keep feet dry and treat associated nail infection.

name: Pierre Robin sequence
epi: Congenital craniofacial sequence recognized at birth; it can occur in isolation or as part of a genetic syndrome.
eti: Underdevelopment of the mandible displaces the tongue backward (glossoptosis), which can block the airway and interfere with palatal closure, producing a U-shaped cleft palate; the exact cause is often unknown.
cli: Micrognathia, glossoptosis and frequently cleft palate, with noisy breathing, upper-airway obstruction, feeding difficulty and choking.
inv: Clinical examination plus airway and feeding assessment; sleep studies, airway endoscopy and genetic evaluation assess severity and associated syndromes.
