tre: Prone or lateral positioning and feeding support for mild cases; nasopharyngeal airway for moderate obstruction and surgery such as mandibular distraction or tongue-lip adhesion for severe obstruction, with multidisciplinary care.

name: Jaundice
epi: A clinical sign rather than a disease; occurs at any age and is very common, often physiological, in newborns during the first week of life.
eti: Bilirubin accumulates from excess production (hemolysis), impaired hepatic uptake or conjugation, hepatocellular injury or biliary obstruction.
cli: Yellow skin and sclerae; dark urine, pale stools and itching suggest conjugated (cholestatic) causes, while other features reflect the underlying disorder.
inv: Total and direct bilirubin, liver enzymes, CBC and hemolysis tests separate the major mechanisms; ultrasound is first-line imaging for suspected biliary obstruction.
tre: Treat the underlying cause; neonatal jaundice may need phototherapy or exchange transfusion, and cholangitis or acute liver failure needs urgent care.

name: Koplik spots
epi: Pathognomonic early sign of measles, seen in roughly 60-70% of patients; they appear during the prodrome, about a day before the rash, and fade within a few days.
eti: Measles virus infection; the white centers reflect necrosis of submucosal gland epithelium, surrounded by dilated vessels that give the red halo.
cli: Tiny bluish-white spots on an erythematous base ('grains of salt'), usually on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, with fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
inv: Recognized clinically; measles is confirmed with RT-PCR of throat/nasopharyngeal swab or urine and/or measles IgM serology, with prompt public-health notification.
tre: The spots need no treatment; measles care is supportive with vitamin A for children, isolation and complication management, and MMR vaccination prevents disease.

name: Constipation
epi: Very common symptom in children and adults, more frequent in older adults, during pregnancy and with low fibre intake, inactivity or constipating medicines.
eti: Usually functional and multifactorial, from low fibre or fluid intake, inactivity, ignoring the urge to defecate, slow transit or medication effects; secondary causes include hypothyroidism and colorectal disease.
cli: Fewer than three bowel movements a week, hard or lumpy stools, straining, bloating and a sense of incomplete emptying; blood in stool or weight loss are alarm features.
inv: Usually clinical; tests such as blood tests or colonoscopy are guided by alarm features, age, persistence and suspected secondary causes.
tre: Increase fibre, fluids and activity and keep a regular toilet routine; laxatives (bulk-forming or osmotic first) are used when lifestyle measures fail.

name: Dyspepsia
epi: Very common upper-gastrointestinal symptom in adults; most people with persistent symptoms and normal investigations have functional dyspepsia.
eti: Causes include functional dyspepsia (altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity), peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori infection, NSAIDs, reflux and, rarely, upper-GI cancer.
cli: Epigastric pain or burning, early satiety, post-meal fullness, bloating, belching or nausea; weight loss, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, anemia or GI bleeding are alarm features.
inv: Clinical assessment guides testing; H. pylori test-and-treat is used for uncomplicated symptoms, with endoscopy for alarm features or older age per local guidance.
tre: Lifestyle changes and stopping NSAIDs where possible; antacids or proton pump inhibitors relieve symptoms, and H. pylori eradication is given when positive.

name: Acute mechanical low back pain
epi: Very common in adults and a leading cause of disability; most acute episodes improve within a few weeks.
eti: Usually nonspecific strain of muscles, ligaments, discs or facet joints without serious underlying disease, often after lifting or awkward movement.
cli: Localized low-back pain worse with movement and eased by rest, with paraspinal tenderness and no neurological deficit; fever, weight loss, bladder/bowel change or major trauma are red flags.
inv: Routine imaging is not recommended without red flags; imaging is considered when red flags are present or symptoms persist beyond about 6 weeks of conservative care.
tre: Education, staying active and superficial heat, with short-term NSAIDs; avoid bed rest, and use physical therapy for recovery and recurrence prevention.

name: Dysmenorrhea
epi: Very common menstrual pain, especially in adolescents; primary dysmenorrhea accounts for about 90% of cases.
eti: Primary dysmenorrhea results from prostaglandin-mediated uterine contractions and ischemia without pelvic disease; secondary dysmenorrhea is due to conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis or fibroids.
cli: Crampy lower-abdominal or pelvic pain beginning with menses and usually lasting up to 72 hours, sometimes with nausea, vomiting, headache, back pain or fatigue.
inv: Primary dysmenorrhea is diagnosed clinically; transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging for suspected secondary causes, with MRI for deep endometriosis.
tre: NSAIDs are first-line, with heat and regular exercise; hormonal contraceptives are effective alternatives, and secondary causes are treated specifically.

name: Calcium channel blocker adverse effects
epi: Common in people taking calcium-channel blockers for hypertension, angina or arrhythmia; the pattern depends on whether the drug is a dihydropyridine or a non-dihydropyridine.
eti: Dihydropyridines (e.g. amlodipine, nifedipine) cause arteriolar vasodilation, while verapamil and diltiazem depress cardiac conduction and contractility.
cli: Dihydropyridines cause ankle edema, flushing, headache and dizziness (and gingival hyperplasia); verapamil/diltiazem cause constipation, bradycardia, AV block, hypotension and may worsen heart failure.
inv: Medication history, blood pressure and heart rate; ECG for suspected bradycardia or AV block, and liver tests with non-dihydropyridines.
tre: Reduce the dose, switch class or stop the drug when appropriate; significant bradycardia, hypotension or overdose needs urgent supportive and specific treatment.

name: Gangrene
epi: Occurs with severe ischemia, infection or trauma; risk is highest with diabetes, peripheral arterial disease/atherosclerosis, smoking and serious injury.
eti: Tissue death from loss of blood supply; dry gangrene is ischemic, wet gangrene adds bacterial infection, and gas gangrene is a Clostridium infection of deep tissue.
cli: Pain or numbness, blue-black discoloration, swelling and foul-smelling discharge; fever, crepitus or systemic toxicity suggest wet or gas gangrene and sepsis.
inv: Clinical examination and vascular assessment; blood tests, cultures and imaging (including for gas in tissue) when infection is suspected, and angiography to plan revascularization.
tre: Urgent surgical debridement or amputation of dead tissue, antibiotics for infected gangrene and revascularization when possible; hyperbaric oxygen is sometimes used, with control of diabetes and vascular disease.

name: Tumor lysis syndrome
epi: Oncologic emergency seen most often after starting treatment for high-burden, rapidly proliferating cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, ALL with high white count, bulky DLBCL and AML; it can occur spontaneously.
eti: Rapid tumor-cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (metabolized to uric acid); uric acid and calcium phosphate deposit in renal tubules, and phosphate binds calcium.
cli: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hyperuricemia causing nausea, weakness, muscle cramps or tetany, arrhythmias, seizures and acute kidney injury; may be laboratory-only initially.
inv: Serial potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, creatinine and urine output with ECG monitoring; Cairo-Bishop criteria define laboratory and clinical TLS.
tre: Prevention with aggressive IV hydration and allopurinol, or rasburicase for high-risk patients (avoid in G6PD deficiency); correct electrolytes and use dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, oliguria or severe AKI.

name: Superior vena cava syndrome
epi: Malignancy, especially small-cell lung cancer and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, is the leading cause, but benign device-related thrombosis (catheters, pacemaker leads) now causes about 40% of cases.
eti: External compression, tumor invasion or thrombosis of the superior vena cava obstructs venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs.
cli: Facial and neck swelling, upper-limb edema, dilated chest-wall veins, dyspnea, cough and headache worse lying down; laryngeal or cerebral edema is life-threatening.
inv: Contrast-enhanced chest CT identifies the obstruction and cause; venography is the reference standard, and tissue diagnosis of suspected cancer guides therapy.
tre: Treat airway or cerebral compromise urgently; endovascular stenting (with thrombolysis if needed) gives rapid relief, alongside anticoagulation for thrombosis and cancer-directed chemotherapy or radiation.

name: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
epi: Rare, life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction at the severe end of the SJS/TEN spectrum; mortality is substantial and predicted by SCORTEN.
eti: Medications cause over 80% of cases (e.g. allopurinol, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, NSAIDs), triggering T-cell-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis and full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
cli: Fever and malaise followed by painful dusky or targetoid macules, flaccid bullae and sheet-like epidermal detachment over 30% of body surface area, with Nikolsky sign and mucosal erosions.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by skin biopsy showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis with negative immunofluorescence; monitor fluids, electrolytes, infection and organ function and calculate SCORTEN.
tre: Stop the culprit drug immediately and give supportive care in a burn or intensive care unit with wound, eye and mucosal care; cyclosporine, IVIG, corticosteroids or TNF inhibitors are used selectively and remain debated.

name: Urosepsis (sepsis from urinary source)
epi: About a quarter of sepsis cases arise from the urogenital tract; risk is higher in older adults and with urinary obstruction, catheters or instrumentation.
eti: Dysregulated host response to urinary tract infection causing organ dysfunction; Escherichia coli causes about half of cases, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter and Pseudomonas.
cli: Fever or hypothermia, chills, tachycardia, hypotension and confusion with dysuria, flank pain or costovertebral-angle tenderness; organ dysfunction may include AKI, ARDS or DIC.
inv: Urinalysis and urine culture, blood cultures, lactate, CBC and metabolic panel; imaging (CT or ultrasound) looks for obstruction or abscess, without delaying antibiotics.
tre: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour, IV crystalloid resuscitation and vasopressors for persistent hypotension; urgent source control such as decompressing an obstructed kidney or replacing catheters.

name: Typhoid fever
epi: Most common where sanitation is poor, especially South Asia, Africa and Latin America; most cases in high-income countries occur in returning travelers.
eti: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, spread by food or water contaminated with feces of an infected person or chronic carrier.
cli: Gradually rising sustained fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain and constipation or diarrhea, sometimes with rose spots, relative bradycardia and hepatosplenomegaly; intestinal perforation or bleeding can occur.
inv: Blood culture is the main diagnostic test early in illness, with stool, urine or bone-marrow culture as adjuncts; susceptibility testing is essential because of drug resistance.
tre: Antibiotics chosen by local resistance and travel history (e.g. azithromycin, ceftriaxone or carbapenems for extensively drug-resistant strains), with supportive care; vaccination, safe food/water and sanitation prevent disease.

name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
epi: Rare hematologic emergency, most often acquired immune-mediated TTP in adults; congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome) is rare. Untreated mortality is about 90%.
eti: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (usually autoantibody-mediated, rarely inherited ADAMTS13 variants) leaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers that form platelet microthrombi.
cli: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia with neurologic symptoms, fever and renal injury; fewer than 5% have the full pentad.
inv: CBC and smear with schistocytes, raised LDH and low haptoglobin; PLASMIC score estimates likelihood, and ADAMTS13 activity below 10% confirms TTP, but treatment should not await results.
tre: Urgent plasma exchange plus corticosteroids, with caplacizumab and rituximab in immune TTP; avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding.

name: Septic arthritis
epi: Orthopedic emergency with peak incidence in young children; adult risk rises with older age, prosthetic joints, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, injection drug use and immunosuppression.
eti: Bacterial infection of a joint, usually hematogenous; Staphylococcus aureus is most common, with Kingella kingae in young children and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active adults.
cli: Acute painful, hot, swollen joint with restricted movement and fever, usually monoarticular and most often the knee, followed by the hip.
inv: Urgent arthrocentesis before antibiotics for cell count (often over 50,000 WBC/µL with neutrophil predominance), Gram stain and culture; blood cultures and inflammatory markers support evaluation.
tre: Empiric IV antibiotics after aspiration (e.g. vancomycin for gram-positive cover) tailored to cultures, plus joint drainage by needle aspiration, arthroscopy or open surgery.

name: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
epi: Most common hip disorder of pre-adolescents and adolescents (average onset 11-12 years); obesity is the strongest risk factor, with male sex, rapid growth and endocrine disease also contributing.
eti: Shear stress across a weakened proximal femoral growth plate lets the femoral neck displace anteriorly and superiorly relative to the epiphysis, which stays in the acetabulum.
cli: Hip, groin, thigh or referred knee pain with limp and limited internal rotation; obligatory external rotation on hip flexion (Drehmann sign); unstable slips prevent weight bearing.
inv: Bilateral AP and frog-leg lateral hip radiographs show the slip (Klein line abnormality); MRI can detect pre-slip changes.
tre: Urgent surgical stabilization, usually in situ screw fixation, with no weight bearing until fixed; monitor or consider fixing the contralateral hip and evaluate endocrine causes in atypical cases.

name: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
epi: Autosomal-dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome affecting about 1 in 36,000 births; roughly 20% of cases arise from new variants.
eti: Germline VHL tumor-suppressor variants; loss of the second allele stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factors, driving angiogenesis and tumor growth.
cli: CNS and retinal hemangioblastomas, clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (leading cause of death), pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors, and endolymphatic sac tumors.
inv: VHL genetic testing plus lifelong surveillance with eye exams, plasma/urine metanephrines, brain and spine MRI and abdominal imaging from childhood.
tre: Surveillance with organ-specific surgery or ablation timed to tumor size and symptoms; the HIF-2α inhibitor belzutifan treats VHL-associated tumors, with genetic counseling and family testing.

name: Hereditary coproporphyria
epi: Rare acute hepatic porphyria with reduced penetrance, so many carriers never have symptoms; attacks usually begin after puberty and are more common in women.
eti: Autosomal-dominant CPOX variants reduce coproporphyrinogen oxidase activity; attacks are triggered by porphyrinogenic drugs, fasting and hormonal changes that induce hepatic heme synthesis.
cli: Acute neurovisceral attacks with severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, psychiatric symptoms and proximal motor neuropathy; about 20% also have blistering photosensitivity.
inv: Markedly raised urine porphobilinogen during attacks; fecal porphyrins with predominant coproporphyrin III distinguish HCP, and CPOX genetic testing confirms it.
tre: Stop triggering drugs, give carbohydrate/glucose, fluids and analgesia, and IV hemin for significant attacks; givosiran reduces attack frequency in recurrent disease.

name: Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS III)
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal disorder and the most common mucopolysaccharidosis (about 1 in 70,000 births); symptoms begin in early childhood after normal infancy.
eti: Deficiency of one of four enzymes that degrade heparan sulfate (SGSH, NAGLU, HGSNAT or GNS; types IIIA-IIID) causes accumulation mainly in the central nervous system.
cli: Early speech and developmental delay followed by hyperactivity, aggressive behavior, sleep disturbance, cognitive regression, seizures and loss of mobility; somatic features are mild.
inv: Urinary glycosaminoglycans with raised heparan sulfate, then enzyme assay and molecular testing to define the subtype.
tre: No approved disease-modifying therapy; supportive multidisciplinary care for behavior, sleep, seizures, nutrition and mobility, with clinical trials of gene and enzyme therapies.

name: CARASIL
epi: Very rare autosomal-recessive cerebral small-vessel disease, reported mainly in Japan and China; onset is in the 20s or 30s.
eti: Biallelic HTRA1 variants disrupt regulation of TGF-beta signaling, causing arteriopathy of small cerebral vessels; heterozygous HTRA1 variants can cause a milder later-onset dominant small-vessel disease.
cli: Gait disturbance with leg spasticity, stroke or stroke-like episodes and progressive cognitive and mood decline, with early scalp alopecia and low-back pain from spondylosis/disc degeneration.
inv: Brain MRI shows diffuse white-matter hyperintensities and lacunar infarcts; HTRA1 molecular testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy; supportive care with vascular-risk management, rehabilitation and treatment of pain, spasticity and psychiatric symptoms.

name: Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome
epi: Extremely rare familial prion disease with autosomal-dominant inheritance; onset is usually in mid-adulthood and the course spans several years.
eti: Pathogenic PRNP variants produce misfolded prion protein that accumulates as amyloid plaques and progressively damages the brain, particularly the cerebellum.
cli: Slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria, later with dementia, behavioral change, pyramidal signs and abnormal movements; fatal over months to years.
inv: Family history and neurologic assessment with brain MRI; PRNP genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, and genetic counseling is offered to relatives.
tre: No disease-modifying treatment; supportive multidisciplinary care including mobility and speech therapy, fall prevention, symptom control and palliative care.

name: Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula
epi: Congenital anomaly in about 1 in 3,500 births; the most common form (type C, proximal atresia with distal fistula) accounts for about 84%, and associated anomalies such as VACTERL are frequent.
eti: Abnormal separation of the embryonic foregut into trachea and esophagus leaves a blind esophageal pouch with an abnormal tracheal connection.
cli: Excess drooling, choking, coughing and cyanosis with feeds and aspiration; prenatal polyhydramnios is common, while isolated H-type fistula may present later with recurrent pneumonia.
inv: An orogastric tube cannot pass beyond about 10-15 cm and coils on chest radiograph, with gas in the stomach indicating a distal fistula; echocardiography and renal, spinal and limb imaging screen for VACTERL anomalies.
tre: Keep the infant upright, suction the upper pouch and avoid feeds to prevent aspiration, then surgical fistula ligation and esophageal anastomosis; follow up for strictures, reflux and tracheomalacia.

name: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal-dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome affecting skin, lungs and kidneys; features usually appear in the 20s or 30s.
eti: Pathogenic variants in the FLCN tumor-suppressor gene (folliculin); a second somatic hit in kidney cells allows tumor growth.
cli: Multiple fibrofolliculomas on the face, neck and upper trunk, basal lung cysts with recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, and increased risk of renal tumors (often chromophobe or hybrid oncocytic).
inv: Skin examination with biopsy of lesions, chest CT for cysts and FLCN genetic testing; regular renal MRI surveillance detects tumors early.
tre: Treat pneumothorax (pleurodesis for recurrence), remove skin lesions for cosmesis and manage renal tumors with surveillance and nephron-sparing surgery; offer family testing.

name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
epi: Congenital defect in about 2.3 per 10,000 live births, often detected on prenatal ultrasound; the left-sided posterolateral (Bochdalek) type is most common.
eti: A diaphragmatic defect lets abdominal organs enter the chest during development, causing pulmonary hypoplasia, pulmonary hypertension and cardiac dysfunction.
cli: Respiratory distress soon after birth, scaphoid abdomen, reduced breath sounds on the affected side and heart sounds displaced to the opposite side.
inv: Prenatal ultrasound and fetal MRI estimate severity; postnatal chest radiograph shows bowel loops in the chest with mediastinal shift.
tre: Avoid bag-mask ventilation; intubate, decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube, use gentle ventilation and treat pulmonary hypertension, with ECMO for high-risk infants and surgical repair after stabilization.

name: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
epi: Rare autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder; about 60% of cases are paraneoplastic, mostly with small-cell lung cancer, and the rest are autoimmune.
eti: Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium-dependent acetylcholine release.
cli: Proximal, especially leg, weakness, reduced or absent reflexes and autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth and constipation; strength and reflexes briefly improve after sustained contraction.
inv: P/Q-type VGCC antibodies; nerve conduction shows low motor amplitudes that increase markedly after brief exercise or high-rate repetitive stimulation; screen for small-cell lung cancer with chest CT/PET.
tre: Treat any underlying cancer; amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) is first-line symptomatic therapy, with IVIG or other immunotherapy for refractory disease.

name: Primary biliary cholangitis
epi: Chronic autoimmune liver disease mainly of middle-aged women (female-to-male about 9:1), often with other autoimmune disorders such as Sjögren syndrome or thyroid disease.
eti: Autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts causes chronic cholestasis that can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis.
cli: Often asymptomatic at diagnosis; fatigue and pruritus are common, later jaundice, xanthelasma, osteoporosis and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
inv: Raised alkaline phosphatase with positive antimitochondrial antibodies is diagnostic in most cases; ultrasound excludes obstruction and biopsy is reserved for AMA-negative or atypical cases.
tre: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line; inadequate responders receive second-line therapy such as the PPAR agonists elafibranor or seladelpar, or fibrates, plus itch and bone management and transplantation for end-stage disease.

name: POEMS syndrome
epi: Rare paraneoplastic syndrome due to a plasma-cell disorder, usually affecting middle-aged adults; about 15% have associated Castleman disease.
eti: A monoclonal (usually lambda) plasma-cell clone drives raised VEGF and other cytokines, causing multisystem damage.
cli: Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein and skin changes (hyperpigmentation, thickening, hemangiomas), often with edema/effusions, papilledema and sclerotic bone lesions.
inv: Mandatory polyneuropathy plus monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, with a major criterion (Castleman disease, raised VEGF or sclerotic bone lesions) and a minor criterion; immunofixation, VEGF, skeletal imaging, nerve studies and marrow biopsy.
tre: Radiation for isolated bone lesions and systemic therapy (e.g. lenalidomide- or melphalan-based) with autologous stem-cell transplantation for disseminated disease, plus supportive neuropathy and endocrine care.

name: Multiple sclerosis
epi: Most common chronic demyelinating CNS disease, usually beginning between 20 and 40 years and about three times more common in women; relapsing-remitting disease accounts for 70-80% at onset.
eti: Immune-mediated CNS demyelination and neurodegeneration arising from genetic susceptibility (e.g. HLA-DRB1*15:01) and environmental factors such as Epstein-Barr virus, low vitamin D and smoking.
cli: Episodes of optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, weakness, diplopia, ataxia or bladder dysfunction separated in time and space; progressive forms cause accumulating disability, fatigue and cognitive impairment.
inv: MRI of brain and spine shows periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal T2 lesions; McDonald criteria require dissemination in space and time, with CSF oligoclonal bands and evoked potentials as support.
tre: Disease-modifying therapies (e.g. interferon-beta, glatiramer, fingolimod, natalizumab, anti-CD20 antibodies) reduce relapses and progression; high-dose corticosteroids treat disabling relapses, plus rehabilitation and symptom management.

name: Porphyria cutanea tarda
epi: The most common porphyria overall, usually presenting in adulthood; about 80% of cases are sporadic (acquired) and 20% familial.
eti: Reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) activity causes uroporphyrin accumulation, triggered by iron overload, alcohol, smoking, hepatitis C, HIV and estrogens.
cli: Photosensitive skin fragility with painless blisters, erosions and scarring on the backs of the hands and other sun-exposed areas, plus milia, hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation; no acute neurovisceral attacks.
inv: Raised plasma or urinary porphyrins with predominant uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin; check ferritin, HFE genotype, liver tests and hepatitis C/HIV status.
tre: Avoid sunlight, alcohol, smoking and estrogens and treat hepatitis C; serial phlebotomy to reduce iron or low-dose hydroxychloroquine induce remission.

name: MERRF syndrome
epi: Rare maternally inherited mitochondrial encephalomyopathy; onset is usually in childhood to adulthood after normal early development.
eti: Mitochondrial DNA variants, most often m.8344A>G in MT-TK (over 80% of typical cases), impair oxidative phosphorylation; heteroplasmy explains variable severity.
cli: Myoclonus, often the first sign, followed by generalized epilepsy, ataxia, weakness, exercise intolerance and dementia; hearing loss, optic atrophy, neuropathy, cardiomyopathy and lipomas may occur.
inv: Molecular mtDNA testing (blood, urine or muscle) confirms the diagnosis; raised lactate and ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy support it.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care; anticonvulsants with levetiracetam or clonazepam for myoclonus, avoiding valproate, plus rehabilitation, hearing aids and cardiac surveillance.

name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
epi: Rare clonal myeloid neoplasm, most common in children under 15 but also seen in adults; adult pulmonary LCH occurs almost exclusively in smokers.
eti: Clonal proliferation of CD1a+/CD207+ myeloid dendritic cells driven by MAPK-pathway mutations, most commonly BRAF V600E.
cli: Lytic bone lesions (often skull), seborrheic-like rash, lymphadenopathy, lung cysts and nodules, hepatosplenomegaly and diabetes insipidus from pituitary involvement.
inv: Biopsy shows cells with grooved 'coffee-bean' nuclei that express CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy; BRAF/MAPK testing and staging imaging define extent.
tre: Single-site disease may need only curettage, local steroid or radiation; multisystem disease is treated with vinblastine-prednisone-based chemotherapy or MAPK-pathway inhibitors, and smoking cessation for pulmonary LCH.

name: Familial Mediterranean fever
epi: Most common monogenic autoinflammatory disease, frequent in Armenian, Turkish, Arab and Jewish populations; first attacks usually occur in childhood or adolescence.
eti: Usually autosomal-recessive MEFV variants alter pyrin, causing inflammasome overactivity and recurrent sterile inflammation; some patients have only one detectable variant.
cli: Recurrent 12-72-hour attacks of fever with peritonitis, pleuritis, arthritis or erysipelas-like rash; AA amyloidosis causing kidney failure is the main long-term risk.
inv: Raised CRP, ESR and serum amyloid A during attacks; diagnosis is clinical, supported by MEFV genetic testing and a response to colchicine, with urine protein screening for amyloidosis.
tre: Lifelong daily colchicine prevents attacks and amyloidosis; IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) are used when colchicine is ineffective or not tolerated.

name: Congenital lobar emphysema
epi: Rare lung malformation (about 1 in 20,000-30,000 births) with male predominance; half present at birth and most of the rest within 6 months.
eti: Deficient bronchial cartilage or bronchial obstruction creates a ball-valve effect, causing progressive overinflation of a lobe, most often the left upper lobe, then the right middle lobe.
cli: Neonatal or infant respiratory distress, tachypnea, wheeze and cyanosis, with reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance over the affected side and mediastinal shift.
inv: Chest radiograph shows a hyperlucent, overdistended lobe with compression of adjacent lung and mediastinal shift; CT defines anatomy and excludes other lesions.
tre: Mild or moderate cases can be observed; infants with significant respiratory compromise need lobectomy, which has excellent outcomes.

name: Alstrom syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive multisystem ciliopathy (over 900 reported cases) with onset in infancy or early childhood.
eti: Biallelic ALMS1 variants disrupt a protein involved in primary cilia function.
cli: Cone-rod retinal dystrophy with nystagmus and photophobia in infancy, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, childhood obesity, insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes, acanthosis nigricans and dilated cardiomyopathy, with later renal and hepatic disease.
inv: Ophthalmologic examination with electroretinography, audiology, echocardiography and metabolic tests; ALMS1 genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: No curative therapy; multidisciplinary surveillance and management of vision, hearing, diabetes, cardiac, renal and hepatic complications.

name: Dry eye disease
epi: Very common, especially in older adults and women, and with screen use, contact lenses, dry environments and autoimmune disease.
eti: Loss of tear-film homeostasis from evaporative causes (mainly meibomian gland dysfunction, the commoner type) or aqueous deficiency (e.g. Sjögren syndrome), with ocular-surface inflammation.
cli: Burning, gritty or foreign-body sensation, redness, fluctuating blurred vision and paradoxical reflex tearing, often worse late in the day or with visual tasks.
inv: Clinical assessment with tear breakup time, Schirmer test and fluorescein or lissamine green staining; tear osmolarity may grade severity.
tre: Stepwise care: environmental changes and artificial tears, then preservative-free lubricants and punctal plugs, then anti-inflammatory drops such as cyclosporine or lifitegrast; lid hygiene for meibomian gland dysfunction.

name: Acne vulgaris
epi: Very common, mainly in adolescents and young adults around puberty, though it can persist or begin in adulthood.
eti: Androgen-driven sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization and plugging, Cutibacterium acnes proliferation and inflammation.
cli: Open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules and pustules and, in severe disease, nodules and cysts on the face, chest and back; may cause scarring, pigmentation change and psychological distress.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; no routine tests, though hormonal evaluation is considered when features suggest hyperandrogenism such as polycystic ovary syndrome.
tre: Topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide (with or without topical antibiotic) are first-line; oral antibiotics such as doxycycline (limited courses, with benzoyl peroxide), combined oral contraceptives, and isotretinoin for severe or scarring acne.

name: Hemorrhoids
epi: Very common in adults, associated with constipation, straining, low-fibre diet, pregnancy and aging.
eti: Engorgement and downward displacement of the anal vascular cushions from raised pressure; internal hemorrhoids arise above and external below the dentate line.
cli: Painless bright-red bleeding and prolapse with internal hemorrhoids; itching, perianal lumps and sudden severe pain with thrombosed external hemorrhoids.
inv: Inspection, digital rectal examination and anoscopy; persistent or unexplained bleeding needs colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.
tre: High-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners and avoidance of straining, with sitz baths and topical agents; rubber-band ligation or surgery for persistent or high-grade disease.

name: Aphthous ulcer
epi: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis is the most common oral ulcer condition, affecting up to a quarter of people and usually beginning in childhood or young adulthood; minor aphthae make up over 70% of cases.
eti: Multifactorial immune-mediated ulceration with genetic predisposition; triggers include local trauma, stress, smoking cessation and iron, B12 or folate deficiency, and ulcers may signal celiac disease, Crohn disease, Behçet disease or HIV.
cli: Painful round or oval ulcers with a yellow-grey base and red halo on non-keratinized mucosa; minor ulcers (<5-10 mm) heal in about 2 weeks without scarring, while major and herpetiform types are larger or more numerous.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; frequent, severe or atypical ulcers warrant CBC, iron, B12, folate and celiac serology and assessment for systemic disease.
tre: Topical corticosteroids are first-line, with topical analgesics and antiseptic rinses; correct deficiencies and treat underlying disease, reserving systemic steroids or immunomodulators for severe recurrent disease.

name: Acute myeloid leukemia
epi: The most common acute leukemia in adults, with a median age at diagnosis of about 68 years and slight male predominance; risk rises with prior chemotherapy or radiation, benzene, smoking, myelodysplasia and Down syndrome.
eti: Acquired genetic alterations in myeloid progenitors cause clonal expansion of immature myeloblasts that replace normal hematopoiesis.
cli: Fatigue and pallor from anemia, infections from neutropenia and bruising or bleeding from thrombocytopenia developing over days to weeks; leukostasis, gum infiltration or DIC (especially in APL) may occur.
inv: CBC and smear show blasts, sometimes with Auer rods; bone-marrow aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular testing (e.g. FLT3, NPM1, IDH) confirm the diagnosis (generally ≥20% blasts) and define risk.
tre: Fit patients receive intensive induction (cytarabine plus an anthracycline, '7+3') then consolidation, with targeted agents for specific mutations; unfit patients often receive venetoclax with a hypomethylating agent, APL is treated with ATRA plus arsenic trioxide, and allogeneic transplant is curative for selected patients.

name: Aortic dissection
epi: Uncommon but life-threatening emergency; incidence rises with age and hypertension, while inherited aortopathies such as Marfan syndrome cause disease at younger ages.
eti: An intimal tear lets blood dissect through the aortic media, creating a false lumen; hypertension, atherosclerosis, connective-tissue disorders, bicuspid aortic valve, trauma and cocaine are risk factors.
cli: Abrupt severe tearing or sharp chest or back pain, pulse or blood-pressure differences between arms, syncope, neurologic deficits, aortic regurgitation, malperfusion or shock.
inv: CT angiography is first-line in stable patients, with transesophageal echocardiography or MRI as alternatives; ECG and chest radiograph (widened mediastinum) cannot exclude dissection.
tre: Immediate IV beta-blockade to lower heart rate and blood pressure plus analgesia; Stanford type A needs emergency surgery, while uncomplicated type B is managed medically with endovascular repair for complications.

name: Cauda equina syndrome
epi: Rare neurosurgical emergency from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris; most common in adults with lumbar disc disease.
eti: Large central lumbar disc herniation is the commonest cause (about 45%), followed by spinal stenosis, tumor, epidural abscess, hematoma and trauma.
cli: Low-back pain with unilateral or bilateral sciatica, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and leg weakness with reduced reflexes.
inv: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the gold standard, with neurologic examination, perianal sensation testing and post-void bladder scanning.
tre: Urgent surgical decompression (laminectomy or discectomy), ideally within 48 hours of presentation, with treatment of abscess, tumor or hematoma as appropriate.

name: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
epi: Rare type of stroke (about 3-4 per million per year), three times more common in women, mainly of childbearing age; risk is higher in pregnancy and postpartum.
eti: Thrombosis of dural sinuses or cerebral veins impairs venous drainage, raising intracranial pressure and causing venous infarcts or hemorrhage; risks include oral contraceptives, pregnancy, thrombophilia, infection, inflammatory disease and cancer.
cli: Headache, often progressive over days, in most patients; seizures, focal deficits, papilledema, visual disturbance or reduced consciousness may occur.
inv: MRI with MR venography is the gold standard, with CT venography as an alternative; thrombophilia and other risk-factor testing are chosen by context.
tre: Anticoagulation with heparin is the cornerstone even with hemorrhagic infarction, followed by warfarin or a DOAC for 3-12 months; treat seizures and raised intracranial pressure, with endovascular therapy for deterioration.

name: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
epi: Rare, uniformly fatal prion disease (about 1 per million per year); about 85% of cases are sporadic, 10-15% genetic and under 1% acquired (iatrogenic or variant).
eti: Misfolded prion protein induces misfolding of normal prion protein, causing spongiform neurodegeneration; genetic forms arise from PRNP variants.
cli: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia, visual disturbance and behavioral change, progressing to akinetic mutism; most die within a year.
inv: MRI diffusion-weighted imaging shows cortical ribboning or basal ganglia hyperintensity; EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes, CSF 14-3-3/tau and RT-QuIC support the diagnosis, with PRNP testing for genetic forms.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy; supportive and palliative care, symptomatic treatment of myoclonus, and infection-control precautions for instruments and tissue.

name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
epi: Acquired secondary syndrome complicating sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications, cancer (especially acute promyelocytic leukemia), pancreatitis and liver disease.
eti: Systemic activation of coagulation causes widespread microthrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors, leading to organ ischemia and bleeding.
cli: Bleeding from multiple sites (venipuncture sites, mucosa), bruising and petechiae, thrombosis and organ dysfunction; chronic DIC with cancer may be mainly thrombotic.
inv: Low or falling platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and aPTT, raised D-dimer and schistocytes on smear; scoring systems (e.g. ISTH) combine serial results with clinical context.
tre: Treat the underlying cause urgently; give platelets, plasma, fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate for bleeding or high bleeding risk, and heparin only in thrombosis-predominant cases.

name: Miller Fisher syndrome
epi: Rare variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome (about 1-2 per million), more common in men and in East Asia, usually following a viral or bacterial infection.
eti: Post-infectious autoimmune neuropathy in which anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies (positive in most patients) target oculomotor nerves and sensory pathways.
cli: Classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, often with ptosis or facial weakness; limb weakness is mild or absent unless overlapping with GBS.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by serum anti-GQ1b antibodies; CSF albuminocytologic dissociation and nerve conduction studies may help.
tre: Most patients recover spontaneously within weeks to months with supportive care and monitoring; IVIG or plasma exchange is reserved for severe disease or GBS overlap.

name: Ingrown toenail
epi: Common foot problem, peaking in adolescence and young adulthood with male predominance; the great toe is affected in about 80% of cases.
eti: Improper nail trimming, tight footwear, sweating, trauma and obesity drive the nail edge into the lateral nail fold, causing inflammation and sometimes infection.
cli: Pain worsened by footwear, with tenderness, redness and swelling of the nail fold and, in later stages, drainage and granulation tissue.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; no routine tests are needed unless deep infection or osteomyelitis is suspected.
tre: Conservative care (proper trimming, footwear, soaks, lifting the nail edge) for mild cases; partial nail avulsion with phenol matrixectomy for moderate, severe or recurrent cases, as simple avulsion often recurs.

name: Molluscum contagiosum
epi: Common viral skin infection, most frequent in children aged 1-10 and in people with eczema or immune suppression; in adults it is often sexually transmitted.
eti: Molluscum contagiosum virus, a poxvirus, spreads by direct skin contact, autoinoculation, shared objects such as towels, and sexual contact.
cli: Small, firm, skin-colored, pink or pearly dome-shaped papules with central umbilication, often in clusters; widespread or giant lesions suggest immune compromise.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; biopsy showing molluscum bodies is rarely needed for atypical lesions, and STI screening is appropriate for genital lesions in adults.
tre: Usually resolves without scarring within 6-12 months, so treatment is often unnecessary; curettage, cryotherapy or topical agents (e.g. cantharidin) are options for persistent, symptomatic or genital lesions.

name: Neurofibromatosis type 2
epi: Rare autosomal-dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome (about 1 in 33,000), usually presenting in adolescence or early adulthood; about half of cases arise from new variants, often mosaic.
eti: Pathogenic variants in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene (merlin); a second somatic hit leads to schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas.
cli: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas causing progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance, plus other cranial, spinal and peripheral schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas and juvenile cataracts.
inv: MRI of brain with internal auditory canals and of the spine, audiology and ophthalmology; NF2 genetic testing (including tumor tissue for mosaicism) supports diagnosis.
tre: Surveillance, microsurgery or stereotactic radiosurgery depending on tumor growth and hearing; bevacizumab can shrink progressive vestibular schwannomas, with hearing rehabilitation and specialist multidisciplinary care.

name: Osgood-Schlatter disease
epi: Common overuse condition of active adolescents during growth spurts, especially in jumping and running sports; more frequent in boys.
eti: Repetitive traction from the quadriceps via the patellar tendon on the immature tibial tubercle apophysis causes microinjury and inflammation.
cli: Pain, tenderness and a bony swelling over the tibial tubercle, worse with running, jumping, stairs and kneeling; often bilateral.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; radiographs are reserved for atypical, unilateral or severe pain and may show tubercle fragmentation or soft-tissue swelling.
tre: Activity modification, ice, simple analgesia and quadriceps/hamstring stretching, with knee padding or brief bracing if needed; symptoms usually resolve when growth ends and surgery is rarely required.

name: Pancreatic cancer
epi: A leading cause of cancer death with 5-year survival under about 10-15%; most cases occur after 55, and only about 20% are resectable at diagnosis.
eti: About 90% are ductal adenocarcinomas arising from precursor lesions with KRAS and other mutations; risks include smoking, diabetes, obesity, chronic pancreatitis and hereditary syndromes (e.g. BRCA2, Lynch, Peutz-Jeghers).
cli: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), weight loss, epigastric pain radiating to the back, anorexia and new-onset diabetes; body/tail tumors present late.
inv: Pancreas-protocol multiphase CT is the key staging test, with MRI/MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy; CA 19-9 supports monitoring but is not diagnostic.
tre: Resection (Whipple for head tumors, distal pancreatectomy for body/tail) with neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy such as FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine-nab-paclitaxel; unresectable disease receives systemic therapy plus biliary stenting and palliative care.

name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
epi: Autosomal-dominant vascular disorder affecting about 1 in 5,000; nosebleeds usually begin in childhood and telangiectases increase with age.
eti: Heterozygous variants in TGF-beta/BMP pathway genes, mainly ACVRL1 and ENG (SMAD4 with juvenile polyposis), cause fragile telangiectases and arteriovenous malformations.
cli: Recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, telangiectases of lips, tongue, fingers and GI tract, iron-deficiency anemia and AVMs in lungs, liver or brain that can cause stroke, brain abscess or hemorrhage.
inv: Curaçao criteria (3 of 4: epistaxis, telangiectases, visceral AVMs, affected first-degree relative) plus genetic testing; transthoracic contrast echocardiography screens for pulmonary AVMs and brain MRI for cerebral AVMs.
tre: Iron replacement, nasal humidification and local therapy for epistaxis, tranexamic acid or systemic bevacizumab for severe bleeding, and embolization of pulmonary AVMs; antibiotic prophylaxis for procedures when pulmonary AVMs are present.

name: Osteomyelitis
epi: Can occur at any age; children usually develop hematogenous disease of long bones, while adults are at risk from diabetes, vascular disease, trauma, surgery, implants, hemodialysis and injection drug use.
eti: Bone infection, usually bacterial and most often Staphylococcus aureus, arising from bloodstream spread, contiguous spread (e.g. diabetic foot ulcers) or direct inoculation from trauma or surgery.
cli: Localized bone pain, swelling, warmth and fever; chronic disease may produce draining sinus tracts and dead bone (sequestrum), while vertebral disease causes back pain.
inv: ESR, CRP and blood cultures; MRI is the most sensitive imaging, plain radiographs show later changes, and bone biopsy with culture identifies the pathogen.
tre: Prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics (often 4-6 weeks, initially IV) plus surgical debridement of necrotic bone or infected hardware when needed; optimize blood supply and diabetes control.

name: Acute intermittent porphyria
epi: The most common acute hepatic porphyria; penetrance is low (most carriers never have attacks), and attacks usually start after puberty and are several times more frequent in women.
eti: Autosomal-dominant HMBS variants reduce porphobilinogen deaminase activity; attacks are triggered by porphyrinogenic drugs, fasting, alcohol, smoking, infection and hormonal changes.
cli: Severe diffuse abdominal pain without peritonitis, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia and hypertension, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, motor neuropathy and dark or reddish urine; hyponatremia (SIADH) is common, with no skin photosensitivity.
inv: Markedly raised urine porphobilinogen during an attack is the key first-line test; HMBS genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and enables family screening.
tre: Stop triggers, give carbohydrate, analgesia and antiemetics, correct sodium and give IV hemin for significant attacks; givosiran prophylaxis reduces attacks in recurrent disease.

name: Breast cancer
epi: The most common cancer in women worldwide (about 1 in 8 US women over a lifetime) and rare in men; risk rises with age (median diagnosis around 61).
eti: Malignant proliferation of breast ductal or lobular epithelium; risks include age, family history, BRCA1/2 variants, prolonged estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, hormone therapy), radiation, obesity and alcohol.
cli: Often asymptomatic and found on screening; otherwise a painless breast lump, skin dimpling, nipple retraction or discharge, peau d'orange or axillary lymphadenopathy.
inv: Triple assessment with clinical examination, mammography/ultrasound and core-needle biopsy; pathology reports estrogen/progesterone receptor and HER2 status, and staging is guided by stage and symptoms.
tre: Stage- and subtype-directed: breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy with sentinel node assessment and radiation, plus endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-targeted therapy for HER2-positive, and chemotherapy or immunotherapy as indicated.

name: Bronchiectasis
epi: Chronic airway disease that increases with age and is more common in women; many cases are post-infectious or idiopathic, and exacerbations drive hospitalization.
eti: A cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance causes permanent bronchial dilation; causes include prior infection (e.g. TB), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, ABPA, connective-tissue disease and airway obstruction.
cli: Chronic productive cough with daily purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections, dyspnea, fatigue and hemoptysis; crackles and sometimes clubbing; exacerbations bring increased cough, sputum and breathlessness.
inv: High-resolution CT is diagnostic (bronchus wider than its artery, lack of tapering); sputum cultures, immunoglobulins, ABPA tests, sweat or CF genetic testing and spirometry identify cause and severity.
tre: Daily airway clearance and exercise, treat the underlying cause, culture-guided antibiotics for exacerbations (often 14 days), long-term macrolides or inhaled antibiotics for frequent exacerbations, and Pseudomonas eradication.

name: Achalasia
epi: Rare primary esophageal motility disorder, usually presenting between 25 and 60 years, affecting men and women equally.
eti: Loss of inhibitory neurons in the esophageal myenteric plexus causes failed lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis; usually idiopathic, while Chagas disease and malignancy (pseudoachalasia) can mimic it.
cli: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, weight loss, nocturnal cough and aspiration.
inv: High-resolution esophageal manometry confirms the diagnosis; barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus with 'bird-beak' narrowing, and endoscopy excludes malignancy.
tre: Pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with fundoplication or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) are definitive options; botulinum toxin or nitrates/calcium-channel blockers for patients unfit for these.

name: Hepatitis A
epi: Common worldwide where sanitation is poor; outbreaks occur among close contacts, travelers, people who use drugs and people experiencing homelessness, and severity increases with age and pre-existing liver disease.
eti: Hepatitis A virus, an RNA picornavirus spread fecal-orally by person-to-person contact or contaminated food and water; it does not cause chronic infection.
cli: After an incubation of about 2-7 weeks: fatigue, fever, nausea, anorexia and abdominal pain followed by jaundice, dark urine and pale stools; young children are often asymptomatic and acute liver failure is rare.
inv: IgM anti-HAV confirms acute infection; aminotransferases are markedly raised, with bilirubin and INR to assess severity.
tre: Supportive care with rest, nutrition and hydration and avoidance of alcohol and hepatotoxins; vaccination or post-exposure prophylaxis prevents infection.

name: Hepatitis B
epi: Hundreds of millions of people live with chronic hepatitis B, mostly in Asia and Africa; prevalence depends on vaccination coverage, perinatal transmission and exposure risk.
eti: Hepatitis B virus, a DNA virus spread by blood and body fluids through perinatal, sexual and parenteral routes; chronic infection is likely after perinatal infection but uncommon after adult infection.
cli: Acute infection may be asymptomatic or cause fatigue, nausea, right-upper-quadrant pain, dark urine and jaundice, rarely acute liver failure; chronic infection may lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
inv: HBsAg identifies infection, with IgM anti-HBc in acute disease; HBeAg, HBV DNA, liver enzymes and fibrosis assessment stage chronic disease, and HBsAg persisting beyond six months defines chronicity.
tre: Acute infection is usually managed supportively; chronic hepatitis B with active disease or cirrhosis is treated with entecavir or tenofovir, with HCC surveillance; vaccination and birth-dose prophylaxis prevent infection.

name: CADASIL
epi: Rare but the most common inherited cerebral small-vessel disease, typically presenting in young to middle adulthood.
eti: Autosomal dominant NOTCH3 variants cause degeneration of vascular smooth-muscle cells with granular osmiophilic material deposits in small arteries.
cli: Migraine with aura, recurrent subcortical lacunar strokes or TIAs, mood disturbance, apathy and progressive cognitive decline leading to subcortical dementia.
inv: Brain MRI shows white-matter hyperintensities, characteristically in the anterior temporal poles and external capsules, with lacunes; NOTCH3 genetic testing confirms, with skin biopsy selectively.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy; management addresses vascular risk factors, antiplatelet therapy after ischemic events, migraine and mood symptoms, and genetic counseling, avoiding smoking.

name: Allergic rhinitis
epi: Very common allergic disorder affecting children and adults, often alongside asthma, eczema and allergic conjunctivitis; seasonal and perennial forms occur.
eti: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to inhaled allergens such as pollens, house dust mites, molds or animal dander, causing mast cell release of histamine and other mediators.
cli: Sneezing, nasal itching, clear rhinorrhea and congestion, often with itchy, watery eyes; pale boggy turbinates and allergic shiners may be seen, and sleep and quality of life can suffer.
inv: Diagnosis is usually clinical; skin-prick or specific IgE testing identifies relevant allergens when the diagnosis is uncertain or immunotherapy is considered.
tre: Allergen avoidance and saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroids as the most effective therapy, and oral or intranasal antihistamines; allergen immunotherapy is an option for selected patients.

name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
epi: Common inherited disorder, most frequent in people of Northern European ancestry, but underdiagnosed; consider in early COPD, emphysema in non-smokers or unexplained liver disease.
eti: Codominant SERPINA1 variants, most importantly the Z allele, reduce circulating alpha-1 antitrypsin, allowing unopposed neutrophil elastase lung damage, while misfolded protein accumulating in hepatocytes causes liver disease.
cli: Early-onset, basal-predominant panacinar emphysema with dyspnea, worsened greatly by smoking; liver disease ranges from neonatal cholestasis to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
inv: Low serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level followed by phenotype or genotype testing confirms diagnosis; spirometry, CT chest and liver tests assess organ involvement.
tre: Smoking cessation, vaccination and standard COPD therapy; IV augmentation therapy for selected patients with severe deficiency and emphysema, and liver transplantation for end-stage liver disease.

name: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
epi: Rare but among the most common autoimmune encephalitides, mainly affecting children and young women; it can follow HSV encephalitis.
eti: IgG antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of NMDA receptors, associated with ovarian teratoma in a proportion of young women, but often without a tumor.
cli: Viral-like prodrome followed by psychiatric and behavioral change, memory loss, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, speech disturbance, autonomic instability, central hypoventilation and reduced consciousness.
inv: Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in CSF (more sensitive than serum) confirm diagnosis; CSF pleocytosis, nonspecific or normal MRI, abnormal EEG, and pelvic imaging for teratoma.
tre: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, and removal of any tumor; rituximab or cyclophosphamide for inadequate response, with supportive and rehabilitative care.

name: Antiphospholipid syndrome
epi: Can affect adults of any age, more common in women, either as a primary disorder or secondary to autoimmune disease, especially SLE.
eti: Persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I) cause a prothrombotic state and placental dysfunction.
cli: Venous or arterial thrombosis such as DVT, PE or stroke, recurrent pregnancy loss, preeclampsia, thrombocytopenia and livedo reticularis; catastrophic APS causes rapid multiorgan thrombosis.
inv: Diagnosis requires a clinical event plus persistently positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies on testing at least 12 weeks apart.
tre: Long-term warfarin after thrombotic APS, with DOACs avoided especially in high-risk or arterial disease; obstetric APS is managed with heparin and low-dose aspirin.

name: Aplastic anemia
epi: Rare marrow-failure disorder occurring at any age, with peaks in adolescents/young adults and older adults, and higher incidence in East Asia.
eti: Most acquired cases involve immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells; drugs, toxins such as benzene, radiation, seronegative hepatitis and inherited syndromes such as Fanconi anemia are other causes.
cli: Fatigue and pallor from anemia, infections from neutropenia, and bruising, petechiae or bleeding from thrombocytopenia; splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are usually absent.
inv: CBC shows pancytopenia with low reticulocytes; bone marrow biopsy shows hypocellular fatty marrow without malignant infiltration, with tests excluding PNH, inherited syndromes and other causes.
tre: Supportive transfusions and infection management; severe disease is treated with allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in suitable patients or immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin plus ciclosporin, often with eltrombopag.

name: Balo concentric sclerosis
epi: Rare inflammatory demyelinating disease, usually affecting young to middle-aged adults, reported more often in East Asian populations.
eti: Considered a variant of multiple sclerosis in which lesions form concentric alternating bands of demyelinated and myelinated tissue; immune-mediated mechanisms are suspected.
cli: Subacute focal neurologic deficits such as hemiparesis, aphasia, cognitive or behavioral change, headache or seizures; the course can be monophasic or evolve into relapsing MS.
inv: MRI shows characteristic concentric onion-ring lesions; CSF analysis and exclusion of tumor, infection and other demyelinating disorders support the diagnosis.
tre: High-dose corticosteroids for acute attacks, with plasma exchange or other immunotherapy for refractory cases, and MS disease-modifying therapy if a relapsing course develops.

name: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
epi: The most common congenital overgrowth syndrome, usually recognized prenatally or in infancy; increased with assisted reproductive technologies.
eti: Genetic or epigenetic imprinting abnormalities of chromosome 11p15, such as loss of methylation at IC2, paternal uniparental disomy or CDKN1C variants, dysregulate growth genes; most cases are sporadic.
cli: Macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele or umbilical hernia, lateralized overgrowth, neonatal hypoglycemia, ear creases and organomegaly, with increased risk of embryonal tumors such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.
inv: Clinical scoring with methylation and genetic testing of 11p15; tumor surveillance with regular abdominal ultrasound and AFP in early childhood depending on molecular subtype.
tre: Manage neonatal hypoglycemia, airway and feeding issues, surgical repair of abdominal-wall defects or macroglossia, and follow tumor-surveillance protocols with multidisciplinary care.

name: Hereditary angioedema
epi: Rare autosomal dominant disorder; attacks often begin in childhood or adolescence and recur throughout life, sometimes triggered by trauma, stress, infection or estrogens.
eti: Most often C1-inhibitor deficiency (type 1) or dysfunction (type 2) from SERPING1 variants, causing excess bradykinin and increased vascular permeability; rarer forms have normal C1-inhibitor.
cli: Recurrent non-pitting, non-itchy swelling of skin, gut or airway without urticaria, causing painful abdominal attacks and potentially fatal laryngeal edema.
inv: Low C4 with low C1-inhibitor level or function confirms types 1 and 2; genetic testing helps in normal-C1-inhibitor forms.
tre: Attacks need on-demand C1-inhibitor concentrate, icatibant or ecallantide with airway protection, as antihistamines, steroids and adrenaline are ineffective; long-term prophylaxis with lanadelumab, berotralstat or C1-inhibitor for frequent attacks.

name: Alexander disease
epi: Rare leukodystrophy; the classic infantile form presents in the first years of life, while juvenile and adult-onset forms present later with slower progression.
eti: Gain-of-function GFAP variants, usually arising de novo and autosomal dominant, cause astrocyte dysfunction with Rosenthal fiber accumulation.
cli: Infantile disease causes macrocephaly, seizures, developmental delay and spasticity; adult-onset disease causes progressive bulbar dysfunction (dysarthria, dysphagia, palatal myoclonus), ataxia and spastic paraparesis.
inv: Brain MRI shows frontal-predominant white-matter changes in infants or medullary and cervical cord atrophy in adults; GFAP genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy is established; care is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing seizures, nutrition and swallowing, spasticity and mobility.

name: Myotonic dystrophy
epi: The most common adult-onset muscular dystrophy, with variable age of onset from congenital to late adult, and type 1 more common than type 2.
eti: Autosomal dominant repeat expansions: CTG in DMPK causes type 1, showing anticipation, and CCTG in CNBP causes type 2; toxic RNA disrupts splicing of many genes.
cli: Distal and facial weakness with myotonia, ptosis, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, insulin resistance, hypogonadism and daytime sleepiness; congenital DM1 causes neonatal hypotonia.
inv: Genetic testing for the repeat expansion confirms diagnosis, with EMG showing myotonic discharges; ECG, Holter, eye, respiratory and endocrine assessments screen complications.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy; multidisciplinary supportive care with cardiac surveillance and pacemaker or ICD when indicated, mexiletine for troublesome myotonia, and respiratory, anesthetic and endocrine care.

name: Essential tremor
epi: The most common adult movement disorder; prevalence rises with age, and a positive family history is frequent.
eti: Usually idiopathic; familial cases often show autosomal-dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, though no single causative gene accounts for most cases.
cli: Bilateral, largely symmetric action/postural tremor of the hands, sometimes head or voice; often improves transiently with alcohol and worsens with stress, caffeine or fatigue.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by neurologic examination; check thyroid function and review drugs or other secondary causes; DaT-SPECT can help when Parkinson disease is uncertain.
tre: Observation for mild disease; propranolol or primidone first line when function is impaired; botulinum toxin, deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound thalamotomy for refractory disabling tremor.

name: Sjogren syndrome
epi: Common systemic autoimmune disease, strongly female-predominant and usually diagnosed in middle age; may be primary or secondary to RA, SLE or systemic sclerosis.
eti: Lymphocytic infiltration and immune-mediated dysfunction of exocrine glands, chiefly salivary and lacrimal, with B-cell hyperactivity and autoantibody production.
cli: Dry eyes and dry mouth with dental caries and parotid swelling; fatigue, arthralgia, and extraglandular disease (lung, kidney, neuropathy, vasculitis) may occur, with increased lymphoma risk.
inv: Schirmer test and ocular surface staining, salivary flow testing, anti-Ro/SSA (and anti-La/SSB) antibodies, and minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
tre: Artificial tears, saliva substitutes, secretagogues such as pilocarpine and meticulous dental care; hydroxychloroquine or immunosuppression for significant systemic disease; monitor for lymphoma.

name: Renal artery stenosis
epi: Atherosclerotic disease accounts for most cases, mainly in older adults with vascular risk factors; fibromuscular dysplasia predominates in younger women.
eti: Narrowing of a renal artery reduces renal perfusion, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and causing renovascular hypertension and ischemic nephropathy.
cli: Often asymptomatic; resistant or new-onset severe hypertension, abdominal bruit, unexplained renal decline (especially after ACE inhibitor/ARB start) or recurrent flash pulmonary edema suggest disease.
inv: Duplex ultrasound, CT angiography or MR angiography assess stenosis; renal function and cardiovascular risk are evaluated, with catheter angiography if intervention is planned.
tre: Risk-factor control with statin, antiplatelet therapy and antihypertensives (ACE inhibitor/ARB with renal monitoring) for atherosclerotic disease; revascularization for selected cases; angioplasty is preferred for fibromuscular dysplasia.

name: Heerfordt syndrome
epi: Rare form of sarcoidosis (uveoparotid fever), usually seen in young to middle-aged adults.
eti: Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation of sarcoidosis involving the uveal tract, parotid glands and facial nerve.
cli: Classic tetrad of anterior uveitis, bilateral parotid enlargement, facial nerve palsy and low-grade fever; dry eyes or mouth may occur.
inv: Chest imaging for hilar lymphadenopathy, serum ACE and calcium, ophthalmologic examination, and biopsy of accessible tissue showing noncaseating granulomas after excluding infection.
tre: Systemic corticosteroids for ocular, neurologic or systemic involvement, with topical steroids for uveitis; steroid-sparing immunosuppressants for chronic disease.

name: Epilepsy
epi: Common neurologic disorder at any age, with highest incidence in early childhood and older adults; risk rises with genetic, structural, infectious, metabolic and acquired brain disorders.
eti: Enduring predisposition to unprovoked seizures from abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal activity; causes include genetic, structural, infectious, metabolic and immune, though many remain unknown.
cli: Recurrent unprovoked focal or generalized seizures, with altered awareness, motor, sensory or autonomic features; postictal confusion or fatigue may follow.
inv: Eyewitness history and examination; EEG supports classification; MRI is preferred for structural causes, and glucose, electrolytes and ECG exclude mimics and provoked seizures.
tre: Antiseizure medication selected by seizure type and patient factors; rescue therapy for prolonged seizures; surgery, neurostimulation or dietary therapy for drug-resistant cases; address driving and safety.

name: Fibromuscular dysplasia
epi: Uncommon nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease, predominantly affecting young to middle-aged women; renal and extracranial carotid/vertebral arteries are most involved.
eti: Abnormal cellular proliferation and fibrous change in the arterial wall cause stenosis, aneurysm, dissection or tortuosity; not atherosclerotic or inflammatory.
cli: May cause hypertension, headache, pulsatile tinnitus, neck pain, TIA or stroke, or arterial dissection; some patients are asymptomatic.
inv: CTA, MRA or duplex ultrasound; catheter angiography when intervention is planned may show the multifocal string-of-beads pattern; screen other vascular beds once diagnosed.
tre: Blood-pressure control and antiplatelet therapy; percutaneous angioplasty without stenting for selected renal lesions; aneurysm and dissection need individualized vascular care.

name: Hemophilia A
epi: The most common severe inherited bleeding disorder, affecting mainly males; about one-third of cases arise from new mutations; severity follows factor VIII activity.
eti: X-linked recessive deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation factor VIII due to F8 variants, commonly an intron 22 inversion in severe disease.
cli: Spontaneous hemarthroses and deep muscle hematomas in severe disease, with prolonged bleeding after trauma or procedures; recurrent joint bleeds cause hemophilic arthropathy.
inv: Prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing, normal PT and platelet count, low factor VIII activity; Bethesda assay detects inhibitors; emicizumab interferes with aPTT-based assays.
tre: Factor VIII replacement or emicizumab prophylaxis; prompt factor replacement for bleeds; desmopressin for some mild cases; bypassing agents or immune tolerance induction for inhibitors; avoid NSAIDs and IM injections.

name: Primary myelofibrosis
epi: Chronic Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm, usually diagnosed in older adults.
eti: Clonal stem-cell disorder driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations; abnormal megakaryocytes release cytokines causing marrow fibrosis and extramedullary hematopoiesis.
cli: Anemia, fatigue, massive splenomegaly with early satiety, hepatomegaly, weight loss, night sweats, fever and bone pain; risk of leukemic transformation.
inv: Leukoerythroblastic blood film with teardrop cells; dry tap on aspiration with reticulin/collagen fibrosis on trephine biopsy; JAK2/CALR/MPL testing and risk scoring.
tre: Risk-adapted: observation for low-risk disease; JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib for splenomegaly and symptoms; transfusion and anemia therapies; allogeneic stem-cell transplantation is the only cure.

name: Farber disease
epi: Very rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder, usually beginning in infancy or early childhood, with milder later-onset forms.
eti: ASAH1 variants cause acid ceramidase deficiency, leading to ceramide accumulation in tissues.
cli: Classic triad of painful swollen joints with contractures, subcutaneous nodules and progressive hoarseness; severe forms involve lungs, liver, nervous system and other organs.
inv: Reduced acid ceramidase activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts and ASAH1 molecular testing confirm diagnosis; imaging and organ assessment define disease burden.
tre: No curative therapy; multidisciplinary supportive care; hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can help joint and nodule disease in forms without major neurologic involvement.

name: Melasma
epi: Common acquired facial hyperpigmentation, especially in women, during pregnancy or hormonal contraceptive use, and in darker skin phototypes.
eti: Increased melanocyte activity driven by UV and visible light exposure, estrogen/progesterone influence and genetic susceptibility.
cli: Symmetric light-to-dark brown or gray-brown macules and patches on the forehead, cheeks, upper lip, nose or chin.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; Wood lamp and dermoscopy help characterize pigment depth and distinguish mimics.
tre: Strict broad-spectrum (preferably tinted) sun protection and topical depigmenting therapy such as hydroquinone, triple combination cream, azelaic acid or tranexamic acid; recurrence is common.

name: Omphalocele
epi: Congenital midline abdominal-wall defect, often detected on prenatal ultrasound; associated with advanced maternal age and chromosomal anomalies.
eti: Failure of the physiologically herniated midgut to return to the abdomen, leaving viscera in a sac of peritoneum and amnion into which the umbilical cord inserts.
cli: Newborn with a central membrane-covered sac containing bowel and often liver; associated cardiac defects, trisomies 13/18/21 and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are common.
inv: Prenatal ultrasound and maternal AFP, fetal echocardiography and karyotype; postnatal echocardiography, genetic testing and glucose monitoring for Beckwith-Wiedemann.
tre: Cover and protect the sac, prevent heat and fluid loss, decompress stomach and support breathing; primary closure for small defects, staged closure or epithelialization for giant omphaloceles.

name: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal-dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome; many cases are inherited from an affected parent but a substantial minority arise de novo.
eti: Heterozygous pathogenic STK11 variants cause hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract (especially small bowel) and a markedly increased lifetime risk of GI and non-GI cancers.
cli: Dark blue-brown mucocutaneous macules around the mouth, eyes, nostrils, buccal mucosa and perianal area in childhood; small-bowel polyps cause intussusception, obstruction, bleeding and anemia; risk of colorectal, gastric, breast, pancreatic and gonadal tumors.
inv: Diagnosis by histologically confirmed Peutz-Jeghers polyps with pigmentation or family history, confirmed by STK11 genetic testing; surveillance uses upper endoscopy, colonoscopy and small-bowel imaging (capsule or MR enterography) from childhood.
tre: Endoscopic polypectomy of larger polyps to prevent intussusception and bleeding, surgery for obstruction or intussusception, and lifelong multisite cancer surveillance with genetic counseling of relatives.

name: Classic galactosemia
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive disorder detected by newborn screening in many countries; affected infants become ill within days of starting breast milk or lactose-containing formula.
eti: Biallelic GALT pathogenic variants cause near-absent galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase activity, so galactose-1-phosphate and other galactose metabolites accumulate in liver, brain, lens and other tissues.
cli: Neonatal poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, jaundice, hypoglycemia, hepatocellular damage, bleeding diathesis, E. coli sepsis and cataracts; long-term speech, cognitive and motor problems and premature ovarian insufficiency can occur despite treatment.
inv: Newborn screening (elevated galactose/galactose-1-phosphate, low GALT activity) followed by erythrocyte GALT enzyme assay and GALT molecular testing; liver tests, glucose, coagulation and cultures assess acute complications.
tre: Stop breast milk and switch immediately to lactose-free (e.g. soy) formula, then lifelong galactose/lactose restriction; treat sepsis, coagulopathy and hypoglycemia, and monitor development, speech, eyes and ovarian function.

name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
epi: Most common childhood malignancy, peaking between about 2 and 10 years of age, with a second smaller rise in older adults; more common in males.
eti: Malignant clonal proliferation of B- or T-lineage lymphoid precursors with acquired genetic abnormalities; risk is increased by Down syndrome, other genetic syndromes, ionizing radiation and prior chemotherapy.
cli: Marrow failure causes fatigue, pallor, bruising/bleeding and infections, with fever, bone pain, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly; CNS involvement or a mediastinal mass (T-ALL) may occur.
inv: CBC and smear may show blasts and cytopenias; bone marrow with at least 20% lymphoblasts, flow cytometry immunophenotyping and cytogenetic/molecular testing (e.g. BCR-ABL1) classify disease; lumbar puncture assesses CNS involvement.
tre: Risk-adapted multiagent chemotherapy in induction, consolidation and prolonged maintenance phases with intrathecal CNS prophylaxis; tyrosine kinase inhibitors for Philadelphia-positive disease, and immunotherapy, CAR-T cells or stem-cell transplantation for high-risk or relapsed disease.

name: Schnitzler syndrome
epi: Very rare acquired autoinflammatory disorder, usually beginning in middle-aged or older adults.
eti: Chronic IL-1-driven autoinflammation associated with a monoclonal gammopathy, usually IgM (occasionally IgG); a minority progress to lymphoproliferative disease such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.
cli: Chronic recurrent non-pruritic or mildly pruritic urticarial rash with recurrent fever, bone pain, arthralgia/arthritis, fatigue and lymphadenopathy.
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation shows the monoclonal protein; raised CRP and neutrophilia are typical, imaging may show bone sclerosis and skin biopsy shows neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis; diagnosis uses Strasbourg criteria.
tre: IL-1 blockade, especially anakinra, produces rapid and sustained remission; long-term monitoring of the gammopathy for lymphoproliferative transformation.

name: Osteoarthritis
epi: Most common form of arthritis; prevalence rises steeply with age, and most people over 65 have radiographic changes although not all are symptomatic.
eti: Degeneration of the whole joint, with cartilage loss, subchondral bone remodeling and osteophytes; primary disease is age-related, while secondary disease follows injury, inflammatory arthritis, obesity or metabolic disorders.
cli: Activity-related joint pain, morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes, crepitus, bony swelling and reduced range of motion; hand disease causes Heberden and Bouchard nodes.
inv: Diagnosis is usually clinical; radiographs show joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, but radiographic severity correlates poorly with symptoms.
tre: Exercise, weight loss, activity modification and bracing first; topical or oral NSAIDs and acetaminophen, intra-articular corticosteroid injection for flares, and joint replacement for severe hip or knee disease.

name: Infantile colic
epi: Common in healthy babies; typically begins in the first few weeks of life and resolves by about 3-4 months of age.
eti: Cause is unknown; immature digestion, gut sensitivity and, in a minority, cow's milk protein intolerance have been suggested.
cli: Excessive inconsolable crying (classically more than 3 hours a day, 3 days a week) often in the late afternoon or evening, with flushing, clenched fists, drawing up of the knees or back arching, in an infant who otherwise feeds and grows normally.
inv: Clinical diagnosis after history and examination exclude illness, injury, feeding problems or poor weight gain; investigations are not routinely needed.
tre: Reassurance and caregiver support, holding, rocking, upright feeding and burping; continue normal feeding and avoid unproven remedies or spinal/cranial manipulation, reviewing if symptoms persist beyond 4 months or weight gain is poor.

name: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
epi: Very common benign rash affecting roughly half or more of term newborns, appearing in the first week of life (peak around day 2); less common in preterm infants.
