eti: Cause is unknown; it may be an immune response to microbial colonization of hair follicles and is not an infection.
cli: Firm yellow-white 1-3 mm papules or pustules on an irregular red base on the face, trunk and limbs, usually sparing palms and soles, in a well infant; lesions resolve within 1-2 weeks without scarring.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; if uncertain, a Wright-stained smear of pustule contents shows predominantly eosinophils, helping exclude infection.
tre: No treatment needed; reassure parents and use gentle skin care, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics or topical agents.

name: Diaper dermatitis
epi: Very common in infants in diapers, especially with frequent stools, diarrhea, antibiotic use or infrequent changes.
eti: Irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged moisture, friction, urine ammonia and stool enzymes/acids; secondary Candida infection is common, especially after antibiotics or when rash persists.
cli: Red, sometimes scaly rash on convex diaper-contact skin; candidal rash is bright red, involves skin folds and has satellite papules or pustules.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; KOH preparation can confirm Candida when uncertain.
tre: Frequent diaper changes, gentle water cleansing, diaper-free time and barrier creams (zinc oxide or petrolatum); topical antifungal such as nystatin or miconazole for candidal rash, and a brief low-potency hydrocortisone only for severe inflammation.

name: Hirschsprung disease
epi: Occurs in about 1 in 5,000 live births with a male predominance; usually diagnosed in the neonatal period, and associated with Down syndrome.
eti: Failed craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells leaves a distal aganglionic segment (rectosigmoid in about 80%) that remains tonically contracted; RET variants are the main genetic factor.
cli: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and chronic constipation; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis causes fever, explosive diarrhea and distension and can be life-threatening.
inv: Rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells (with calretinin immunohistochemistry) is the gold standard; contrast enema shows a transition zone and anorectal manometry shows an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex.
tre: Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure, sometimes staged with a temporary stoma; enterocolitis needs decompression/rectal washouts, fluids and antibiotics.

name: Head lice (pediculosis capitis)
epi: Common worldwide in children aged about 3-12 years, more often girls, across all socioeconomic groups; spread mainly by head-to-head contact.
eti: Infestation by Pediculus humanus capitis, an obligate human parasite that crawls but cannot jump or fly; itching results from hypersensitivity to louse saliva.
cli: Scalp pruritus, often behind the ears and at the nape, with excoriations and possible secondary impetigo; many infestations are asymptomatic.
inv: Diagnosis requires seeing a live louse, ideally by wet combing with a fine-toothed comb; nits alone do not prove active infestation.
tre: Topical pediculicide such as permethrin, spinosad, malathion, benzyl alcohol or topical ivermectin, or repeated wet combing, usually with a second treatment after 7-10 days; check and treat infested household contacts.

name: Zellweger syndrome
epi: Zellweger spectrum disorders affect about 1 in 50,000 people; classic Zellweger syndrome is the severe end, presenting at birth, and affected infants usually do not survive beyond the first year.
eti: Autosomal-recessive variants in PEX genes (PEX1 in about 70%) impair peroxisome biogenesis, causing accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids and other metabolites and defective myelination.
cli: Profound neonatal hypotonia, poor feeding, seizures, distinctive face (high forehead, flat face, broad nasal bridge, large fontanelle), hepatomegaly/liver dysfunction, renal cysts, stippled epiphyses, cataracts/retinopathy and hearing loss.
inv: Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids with other peroxisomal biochemical markers (e.g. plasmalogens, bile-acid intermediates) suggest the diagnosis; PEX gene molecular testing confirms it.
tre: No curative therapy; supportive multidisciplinary care for feeding, seizures, liver disease, vision and hearing, with genetic counseling of the family.

name: Vitiligo
epi: Affects about 0.5-2% of people worldwide, with no clear sex or racial predilection; often begins in childhood or young adulthood.
eti: Autoimmune, CD8+ T-cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes driven by interferon-gamma/JAK-STAT signaling, on a background of genetic susceptibility.
cli: Asymptomatic, well-demarcated depigmented macules and patches, often on the face, hands and anogenital area, with Koebner phenomenon and possible leukotrichia; associated with autoimmune thyroid disease.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by Wood lamp (bright blue-white fluorescence) and dermoscopy; thyroid function and antibody screening because of associated autoimmunity.
tre: Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors or ruxolitinib cream for limited disease, narrowband UVB phototherapy for widespread disease, oral JAK inhibitors in selected cases and grafting for stable lesions, plus sun protection.

name: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
epi: Mainly affects preterm infants, with incidence inversely related to gestational age (nearly universal at 24 weeks, uncommon by 34 weeks and rare at term); maternal diabetes and male sex increase risk.
eti: Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant in immature lungs raises alveolar surface tension, causing diffuse alveolar collapse, reduced compliance, impaired gas exchange and inflammatory lung injury.
cli: Tachypnea, expiratory grunting, nasal flaring, retractions and cyanosis starting within minutes to hours of birth, worsening over 48-72 hours without treatment.
inv: Chest radiograph shows low lung volumes with diffuse ground-glass reticulogranular pattern and air bronchograms; blood gases and oxygen saturation assess severity, with sepsis evaluation as indicated.
tre: Antenatal corticosteroids for women at risk of preterm birth prevent RDS; early nasal CPAP with selective surfactant replacement, careful oxygen targeting and supportive care, with mechanical ventilation if needed.

name: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome
epi: Onset is usually in the first year of life, peaking at about 3-7 months; treatment is urgent because delay worsens developmental outcome.
eti: Most cases have an identifiable structural, genetic, metabolic or acquired cause (e.g. tuberous sclerosis, cortical malformation, hypoxic-ischemic injury); the remainder have no identified cause.
cli: Clusters of brief flexor, extensor or mixed spasms of neck, trunk and limbs, often on waking, with developmental arrest or regression.
inv: Video EEG typically shows hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-voltage slow waves and multifocal spikes); brain MRI, then metabolic and genetic testing if no cause is found.
tre: Urgent first-line therapy with hormonal treatment (ACTH or high-dose oral prednisolone) or vigabatrin, with vigabatrin preferred in tuberous sclerosis; ketogenic diet or other options for refractory spasms under specialist care.

name: Onychomycosis (fungal nail infection)
epi: Common, affecting a few percent to over 8% of people, more often toenails than fingernails; risk rises with age, diabetes, immunodeficiency and peripheral vascular disease.
eti: Dermatophytes, mainly Trichophyton rubrum, cause about 90% of cases; Candida (mostly fingernails) and nondermatophyte molds cause the rest.
cli: Thickened, discolored (white-yellow), brittle or crumbly nails with onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis; distal lateral subungual type is most common, and proximal subungual disease suggests immunosuppression.
inv: Confirm before systemic therapy with KOH microscopy, fungal culture, PAS-stained nail clipping (most sensitive) or PCR, since many dystrophic nails are not fungal.
tre: Oral terbinafine is most effective for dermatophyte disease, with itraconazole as an alternative; topical efinaconazole, ciclopirox or tavaborole for mild disease, plus debridement; recurrence is common.

name: Stauffer syndrome (nephrogenic hepatic dysfunction)
epi: Rare paraneoplastic syndrome classically associated with renal cell carcinoma, reported in a minority of RCC patients and occasionally with other tumors.
eti: Tumor-related cytokines, especially IL-6, cause reversible intrahepatic cholestasis/hepatic dysfunction without liver metastases or biliary obstruction.
cli: Elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGT and sometimes bilirubin with prolonged prothrombin time, often with fever, weight loss, fatigue and hepatosplenomegaly; a rarer icteric variant causes jaundice and pruritus.
inv: Cholestatic liver tests with imaging that excludes hepatic metastases and biliary obstruction; abdominal CT identifies the renal mass, and liver biopsy, if done, shows nonspecific hepatitis.
tre: Treat the underlying tumor, usually by nephrectomy; liver abnormalities typically normalize after resection, and their recurrence may signal tumor relapse.

name: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)
epi: Rare ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (about 1-3 per million adults) with onset typically in middle age and equal sex distribution.
eti: Th2/IL-5-driven eosinophilic tissue injury plus ANCA-mediated vasculitis; MPO-ANCA is found in about one-third to 40%, and ANCA-negative patients more often have cardiac involvement.
cli: Asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, followed by peripheral eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates and systemic vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex, purpura, cardiomyopathy and sometimes glomerulonephritis.
inv: CBC shows marked eosinophilia; ANCA (usually MPO), inflammatory markers, urinalysis, cardiac assessment and imaging, with biopsy showing eosinophil-rich necrotizing vasculitis or granulomas where feasible.
tre: Glucocorticoids for all; add cyclophosphamide or rituximab for severe organ-threatening disease, and maintain remission with mepolizumab, azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab (benralizumab is an alternative anti-IL-5 option).

name: Canavan disease
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive leukodystrophy most common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry; the neonatal/infantile form usually presents by 3-5 months of age.
eti: ASPA variants reduce aspartoacylase activity, so N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA) accumulates in the brain and causes spongy degeneration and failure of myelin formation and maintenance.
cli: Infantile form: initially normal infant who develops hypotonia, poor head control, macrocephaly, developmental delay, irritability, feeding difficulty, seizures and later spasticity and blindness; a mild/juvenile form causes only mild delays.
inv: Markedly elevated urinary NAA, MRI/MR spectroscopy showing diffuse white-matter disease with high NAA peak, and ASPA molecular testing confirm the diagnosis; carrier screening is offered to at-risk populations.
tre: No curative therapy; supportive care for nutrition, seizures, spasticity, respiratory problems and development, with genetic counseling.

name: Chalazion
epi: Common benign eyelid lesion, affecting both sexes equally with peak incidence in adults aged about 30-50 years.
eti: Obstruction of a meibomian (or Zeis) gland causes a sterile chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation; it is inflammatory rather than infectious.
cli: Painless, firm, slowly enlarging nodule within the eyelid, more often upper lid; large lesions may cause blurred vision or astigmatism, and acute inflammation can make it tender.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; recurrent or atypical lesions should be biopsied to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.
tre: Warm compresses and lid massage resolve most within weeks; persistent lesions may receive intralesional corticosteroid injection or incision and curettage.

name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
epi: Most common inherited peripheral neuropathy, usually beginning in childhood or early adulthood and progressing slowly.
eti: Mostly autosomal-dominant (also recessive and X-linked) gene defects; CMT1 (demyelinating, most often PMP22 duplication) is commonest, while CMT2 is axonal (e.g. MFN2).
cli: Slowly progressive distal leg weakness and wasting ('stork legs'), foot drop, pes cavus and hammertoes, distal sensory loss and reduced or absent reflexes, later involving the hands.
inv: Nerve-conduction studies distinguish demyelinating (slowed velocities) from axonal forms; family history and genetic testing (PMP22 analysis, gene panels or exome) confirm the subtype.
tre: No disease-modifying therapy; ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, orthopedic surgery for severe foot deformity, and genetic counseling.

name: Choanal atresia
epi: Congenital posterior nasal obstruction in about 1 in 5,000-8,000 live births; unilateral disease is more common than bilateral, and about half of cases are syndromic, most notably CHARGE syndrome.
eti: Failure of recanalization of the posterior nasal passage (persistent bucconasal/nasopharyngeal membrane) during early fetal development, leaving a bony, membranous or mixed atretic plate.
cli: Bilateral atresia is a neonatal airway emergency because newborns are obligate nasal breathers, causing cyclical (paradoxical) cyanosis that improves with crying and worsens with feeding or rest; unilateral disease causes persistent one-sided nasal obstruction and discharge, often diagnosed later in childhood.
inv: Inability to pass a nasal catheter suggests the diagnosis; nasal endoscopy confirms it and CT defines the atretic plate; screen for CHARGE and other associated anomalies.
tre: Bilateral atresia needs immediate oral airway (e.g. McGovern nipple) or intubation followed by early endoscopic transnasal repair; unilateral atresia is repaired electively, often later in childhood.

name: Congenital hypothyroidism
epi: Affects about 1 in 2,000-4,000 newborns, more often girls; one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability, detected by newborn screening.
eti: Thyroid dysgenesis (absent, hypoplastic or ectopic gland) causes about 80-85% of cases, with dyshormonogenesis (e.g. TPO, TG, DUOX2 defects) most of the rest; iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide and transient forms follow maternal antibodies or drugs.
cli: Most infants look normal at birth; untreated disease causes prolonged jaundice, lethargy, poor feeding, constipation, hypotonia, large tongue, umbilical hernia, large fontanelles and later growth failure and intellectual disability.
inv: Abnormal newborn screening (TSH and/or T4) must be confirmed promptly with serum TSH and free T4; thyroid ultrasound or scintigraphy may define the cause but should not delay treatment.
tre: Start levothyroxine as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, ideally within the first 2 weeks of life, with frequent TSH and free T4 monitoring during early childhood to protect neurodevelopment.

name: Dermatomyositis
epi: Rare idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with female predominance; adult peak around 40-60 years and a separate juvenile form in children.
eti: Complement-mediated microangiopathy of muscle capillaries and skin causes perifascicular muscle injury; adult disease is associated with malignancy, especially in the first years after diagnosis (anti-TIF1-gamma).
cli: Subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness with heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl/V sign and periungual changes; dysphagia and interstitial lung disease (especially anti-MDA5) may occur, and some patients are amyopathic.
inv: Elevated CK/aldolase, myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Mi-2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma), EMG, muscle MRI and biopsy showing perifascicular atrophy; screen for ILD and age-appropriate malignancy.
tre: High-dose glucocorticoids with steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate; IVIG, rituximab or other agents for refractory disease, plus photoprotection and physiotherapy.

name: Gastroschisis
epi: Occurs in about 1 in 4,000 live births with rising prevalence; strongly associated with young maternal age (under 20) and maternal smoking.
eti: Full-thickness paraumbilical abdominal-wall defect, usually to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, through which bowel herniates without a covering membrane and is damaged by amniotic fluid exposure.
cli: Exposed, often thickened and inflamed bowel outside the abdomen at birth with no sac; associated intestinal atresia, stenosis, perforation or volvulus in up to a quarter, but extraintestinal anomalies are uncommon (unlike omphalocele).
inv: Detected prenatally by elevated maternal serum AFP and ultrasound showing free-floating bowel; postnatal examination confirms it, with assessment for bowel atresia or ischemia.
tre: Delivery at a center with neonatal surgery; cover bowel in sterile wrap, keep warm, gastric decompression, IV fluids and antibiotics, then primary closure or staged silo reduction and parenteral nutrition until feeds establish.

name: Friedreich ataxia
epi: Most common inherited ataxia in people of European ancestry; onset usually at 10-15 years, though late-onset forms occur.
eti: Autosomal-recessive, usually biallelic GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in intron 1 of FXN reduce frataxin, causing mitochondrial iron accumulation and oxidative damage.
cli: Progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, absent lower-limb reflexes with extensor plantars, loss of vibration and proprioception, scoliosis and pes cavus; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in about two-thirds and diabetes in up to 30%.
inv: FXN GAA repeat testing (plus sequencing if only one expansion) confirms diagnosis; nerve conduction shows sensory axonal neuropathy, and ECG/echocardiography and glucose screening detect complications.
tre: Omaveloxolone is approved for patients aged 16 and older; multidisciplinary supportive care with physiotherapy, mobility aids, speech therapy, scoliosis management and treatment of cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

name: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
epi: Rare life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome; primary (familial) HLH usually presents in infancy and early childhood, while secondary HLH predominates in adults.
eti: Uncontrolled activation of cytotoxic T cells, NK cells and macrophages; primary HLH results from mutations in cytotoxicity genes (e.g. PRF1, UNC13D, STXBP2), and secondary HLH is triggered by infection (especially EBV), malignancy (especially lymphoma) or autoimmune disease (macrophage activation syndrome).
cli: Persistent high fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hepatitis, coagulopathy, rash and neurologic symptoms, progressing to multiorgan failure.
inv: HLH-2004 criteria (5 of 8): fever, splenomegaly, bicytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia, ferritin over 500 ng/mL, low NK-cell activity, raised soluble CD25 and hemophagocytosis; search for the trigger and genetic testing.
tre: Urgent HLH-directed therapy with dexamethasone and etoposide (HLH-94 based) plus treatment of the trigger; emapalumab or ruxolitinib for refractory disease, and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation for familial, relapsed or refractory HLH.

name: Herpangina
epi: Common in infants and children, mostly under 10 years, with outbreaks in summer and early autumn, especially in childcare settings.
eti: Enteroviruses, chiefly coxsackievirus A serotypes (also coxsackie B, echovirus and enterovirus A71), spread by fecal-oral, respiratory droplet and direct contact.
cli: Sudden fever, sore throat, odynophagia and drooling with small vesicles or shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars and posterior pharynx; rarely aseptic meningitis, encephalitis or myocarditis (especially EV-A71).
inv: Clinical diagnosis; RT-PCR for enterovirus is reserved for severe or complicated cases and outbreaks.
tre: Supportive care with fluids, soft foods and antipyretic analgesics to maintain hydration; antibiotics and antivirals are not indicated; hand hygiene limits spread.

name: Corn (clavus)
epi: Very common, especially on the feet and toes; more frequent with ill-fitting or high-heeled shoes and foot deformities.
eti: Repeated pressure or friction over a bony prominence causes focal hyperkeratosis with a dense central keratin core (hard corns on toe tops, soft corns between toes).
cli: Small, round, well-circumscribed, tender area of hard skin with a central core that is painful with direct pressure.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; paring reveals a central core (versus pinpoint capillaries in a plantar wart), and footwear and foot biomechanics should be assessed.
tre: Remove the cause with well-fitting footwear and padding, soften and file the skin; podiatrist paring or orthotics for persistent lesions, and people with diabetes or poor circulation should not self-treat.

name: Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive disorder with two forms: infantile-onset Wolman disease (rarest, fatal in infancy if untreated) and the more common later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease presenting from childhood to adulthood.
eti: Biallelic LIPA variants reduce lysosomal acid lipase activity, so cholesteryl esters and triglycerides accumulate in liver, spleen, gut, adrenals and vessel walls.
cli: Wolman disease: vomiting, diarrhea, malabsorption, massive hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive and adrenal calcification in the first weeks; later-onset disease: hepatomegaly, raised transaminases, dyslipidemia (high LDL, low HDL), fibrosis/cirrhosis and early atherosclerosis.
inv: Low LAL enzyme activity on dried blood spot and LIPA genetic testing confirm diagnosis; lipid profile, liver tests and imaging assess organ involvement.
tre: Enzyme replacement with sebelipase alfa plus dietary and supportive care; stem-cell or liver transplantation have been used in selected cases.

name: Neonatal jaundice (physiological)
epi: Clinical jaundice occurs in about 60% of term and 80% of preterm newborns in the first week, and physiologic jaundice accounts for most neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
eti: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from high red-cell mass with shorter red-cell lifespan, low hepatic UGT1A1 conjugating activity and increased enterohepatic circulation.
cli: Yellow skin and sclerae appearing after 24 hours, peaking around days 3-5 and resolving by 2-3 weeks in a well, feeding infant; jaundice in the first 24 hours or rapidly rising bilirubin suggests a pathologic cause.
inv: Transcutaneous or total serum bilirubin plotted on hour-specific nomograms with risk factors; blood group, Coombs test and conjugated bilirubin when jaundice is early, severe or prolonged.
tre: Usually observation and support of adequate feeding; phototherapy when bilirubin exceeds age- and risk-specific thresholds, and exchange transfusion for severe hyperbilirubinemia unresponsive to phototherapy.

name: Nursemaid's elbow
epi: Very common upper-limb injury in children aged about 1-4 years, uncommon after 5 years as the annular ligament strengthens; recurrence occurs in about 20%.
eti: Sudden axial traction on an extended, pronated forearm (e.g. lifting or swinging a child by the hand) lets the annular ligament slip over the radial head and become trapped between the radial head and capitellum.
cli: Child abruptly stops using the arm, holding it at the side slightly flexed or extended with the forearm pronated, and resists supination; there is no swelling, bruising or deformity.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with a typical mechanism; radiographs only if there is swelling, deformity, focal bony tenderness, an atypical mechanism or failed reduction, to exclude fracture.
tre: Closed reduction by hyperpronation (higher first-attempt success) or supination-flexion, often with a palpable click; most children use the arm normally within 30 minutes, and caregivers are advised to avoid pulling on the arm.

name: Perioral dermatitis
epi: Common facial eruption, mainly in women aged about 20-45 years, but increasingly seen in children of either sex.
eti: Strongly associated with topical (and inhaled/nasal) corticosteroid use; cosmetics, heavy moisturizers, fluorinated toothpaste, barrier dysfunction and microbial factors may contribute.
cli: Small erythematous papules, pustules or scaly pink patches around the mouth, nose or eyes, typically with a narrow spared zone along the lip vermilion border; burning or stinging is common.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; biopsy is rarely needed, mainly for atypical or granulomatous variants.
tre: Taper and stop topical corticosteroids and simplify skin products ('zero therapy'); topical metronidazole, erythromycin, azelaic acid or pimecrolimus, with oral tetracycline-class antibiotics (erythromycin in young children or pregnancy) for more extensive disease.

name: Whipple disease
epi: Very rare multisystem infection (about 1-3 per million), predominantly in middle-aged white men (around 4:1), with higher risk in farmers and others with soil exposure.
eti: Chronic infection with Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinomycete, in genetically susceptible hosts with impaired macrophage function; it can involve the small intestine, joints, heart, CNS and eyes.
cli: Migratory arthralgia often precedes diarrhea/steatorrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain and fever; lymphadenopathy, culture-negative endocarditis and CNS disease (cognitive change, oculomasticatory myorhythmia) may occur.
inv: Duodenal biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria; T. whipplei PCR or immunohistochemistry on tissue confirms, and CSF PCR should be checked for CNS involvement.
tre: Induction with IV ceftriaxone or penicillin G for 2 weeks followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for at least 12 months; monitor for relapse and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

name: Subdural hematoma
epi: Acute subdural hematoma follows significant head trauma at any age; chronic subdural hematoma is increasingly common in older adults, especially with anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, alcohol misuse and brain atrophy.
eti: Tearing of bridging veins that cross the subdural space releases blood between the dura and arachnoid; atrophy stretches these veins so minor or forgotten trauma can suffice.
cli: Acute: headache, decreasing consciousness, focal deficits and signs of herniation; chronic: insidious headache, confusion, cognitive decline, gait disturbance, hemiparesis or seizures over weeks.
inv: Noncontrast CT head shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection that crosses suture lines but not dural reflections, hyperdense when acute and hypodense or mixed when chronic; coagulation studies are checked.
tre: Reverse anticoagulation; urgent craniotomy for symptomatic acute hematomas with mass effect, burr-hole drainage for symptomatic chronic hematomas, observation for small stable collections, and middle meningeal artery embolization as an adjunct to reduce recurrence.

name: Syringomyelia
epi: Uncommon (roughly 1-8 per 100,000), most often associated with Chiari I malformation; other cases follow spinal cord trauma, tumors or arachnoiditis, and some are asymptomatic.
eti: Disturbed CSF flow, most often at the foramen magnum, leads to a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, usually cervical, that damages crossing spinothalamic fibers and anterior horn cells as it expands.
cli: Cape-like dissociated loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and proprioception over the shoulders and arms, hand weakness and wasting, neuropathic pain, and later lower-limb spasticity, scoliosis and bladder dysfunction.
inv: MRI of the whole spine and craniocervical junction is the gold standard to show the syrinx and its cause, with cine MRI to assess CSF flow.
tre: Treat the cause: foramen magnum (posterior fossa) decompression with duraplasty for Chiari-associated disease, or release of tethering/tumor removal; shunting is reserved for selected cases, and asymptomatic stable syrinxes may be observed.

name: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
epi: Most common systemic vasculitis of childhood, mainly ages 3-15, often after an upper respiratory infection; it also occurs in adults, who more often develop significant kidney disease.
eti: Deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in small vessels of skin, gut, joints and kidneys, causing leukocytoclastic vasculitis; triggers include infections, drugs and vaccines.
cli: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthralgia/arthritis, colicky abdominal pain or GI bleeding (risk of intussusception) and glomerulonephritis with hematuria or proteinuria; episodes usually remit within about 4 weeks but may recur.
inv: Clinical diagnosis in typical children; skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on immunofluorescence; urinalysis, blood pressure and renal function are monitored, with renal biopsy for significant nephritis.
tre: Supportive care with hydration and analgesia in most children; corticosteroids for severe abdominal or joint symptoms, and immunosuppression (e.g. steroids with mycophenolate or other agents) for severe nephritis; monitor urine and blood pressure for several months.

name: Psoriatic arthritis
epi: Develops in about 20% of people with psoriasis (roughly 0.05-0.25% of the population); arthritis can precede skin disease in a minority.
eti: Immune-mediated inflammatory spondyloarthritis driven by IL-23/IL-17 and TNF pathways with HLA (e.g. HLA-B27 in axial disease) and environmental contributions.
cli: Asymmetric oligoarthritis or polyarthritis, DIP joint involvement, dactylitis, enthesitis, nail pitting/onycholysis and axial disease; arthritis mutilans is a rare destructive form.
inv: Usually RF and anti-CCP negative; CRP/ESR may be raised; radiographs show erosions with new bone formation and 'pencil-in-cup' deformity; CASPAR criteria aid classification.
tre: NSAIDs and local steroid injections for mild disease; conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate) and biologic/targeted agents (TNF, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, apremilast) using a treat-to-target approach.

name: Primary Hypothyroidism
epi: Common, especially in women and older adults; overt disease affects a small percentage of adults and subclinical disease is more frequent.
eti: Hashimoto (autoimmune) thyroiditis is the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient regions and iodine deficiency worldwide; others include thyroidectomy, radioiodine and drugs such as amiodarone and lithium.
cli: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, depression, menstrual disturbance and delayed reflex relaxation; severe untreated disease can cause myxedema coma.
inv: Elevated TSH with low free T4 (normal free T4 in subclinical disease); TPO antibodies identify autoimmune thyroiditis; lipids and sodium may be abnormal.
tre: Levothyroxine replacement titrated to TSH, starting at a low dose in older or cardiac patients; myxedema coma is treated in intensive care with IV levothyroxine and hydrocortisone.

name: Acute bacterial prostatitis
epi: Accounts for a small minority (about 5-10%) of prostatitis; occurs in adult men, with risk from urinary tract infection, catheterization, prostate biopsy and outflow obstruction.
eti: Usually ascending infection or reflux of infected urine, mainly by E. coli (50-90%) and other gram-negative Enterobacterales or Pseudomonas; sexually transmitted organisms in younger men.
cli: Acute fever, chills, malaise, dysuria, frequency, perineal or pelvic pain and obstructive voiding or retention; the prostate is enlarged, boggy and exquisitely tender.
inv: Urinalysis and midstream urine culture; blood cultures and CBC in systemically unwell patients; avoid prostatic massage, and image (transrectal ultrasound or CT) for suspected abscess or treatment failure.
tre: Culture-directed antibiotics with good prostatic penetration (e.g. fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) for about 2-4 weeks, IV therapy for sepsis; suprapubic catheter for retention and drainage of any abscess.

name: Acute cholangitis
epi: Usually affects people over 50 with gallstone disease, biliary strictures, malignancy or prior biliary procedures and stents.
eti: Bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree, most commonly from choledocholithiasis, typically by gram-negative enteric organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) and sometimes enterococci or anaerobes.
cli: Charcot triad of fever, right-upper-quadrant pain and jaundice (specific but insensitive); Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion in severe suppurative cholangitis.
inv: Tokyo Guidelines combine systemic inflammation (fever, WBC, CRP), cholestatic liver tests and imaging of biliary dilation/cause; ultrasound first, MRCP or EUS for stones, blood cultures, and ERCP for therapy.
tre: Prompt IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, with biliary drainage, usually ERCP, whose urgency depends on severity; percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails, then definitive treatment of the cause (e.g. cholecystectomy).

name: Hyperkalemia
epi: Common electrolyte disorder, especially with chronic or acute kidney disease, diabetes and use of RAAS inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics; severe hyperkalemia can cause fatal arrhythmias.
eti: Impaired renal excretion (kidney failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs), transcellular shift (acidosis, insulin deficiency/DKA, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis) or excess intake; pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis or thrombocytosis must be excluded.
cli: Often asymptomatic; muscle weakness, paresthesias and flaccid paralysis, with bradyarrhythmias, ventricular arrhythmias or cardiac arrest in severe or rapidly rising cases.
inv: Urgent repeat serum potassium and ECG (peaked T waves, flattened P waves, wide QRS, sine-wave pattern); renal function, glucose, blood gas and CK/drug review identify the cause; do not delay treatment if ECG changes are present.
tre: IV calcium to stabilize the myocardium when ECG changes or severe hyperkalemia; shift potassium with IV insulin plus glucose and nebulized beta-agonist (bicarbonate if acidotic); remove potassium with binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), loop diuretics or dialysis, and stop causative drugs.

name: Deep vein thrombosis
epi: Common venous thromboembolic disease; risk rises with age over 60, surgery, immobility, hospitalization, cancer, pregnancy/estrogen, obesity, thrombophilia and previous VTE.
eti: Virchow triad of venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability; thrombi usually start in calf veins and can propagate proximally and embolize to the lungs.
cli: Unilateral leg swelling, pain, tenderness, warmth and erythema, though up to half of patients lack specific signs; pulmonary embolism may be the first presentation.
inv: Pretest probability with the Wells score; D-dimer to exclude DVT when probability is low, and compression duplex ultrasound for likely DVT or positive D-dimer.
tre: Anticoagulation, with DOACs first-line for most patients; at least 3 months for provoked DVT and extended therapy for unprovoked or persistent risk such as cancer; catheter-directed thrombolysis for selected severe iliofemoral DVT.

name: Acute limb ischemia
epi: Vascular emergency defined as sudden loss of limb perfusion (symptoms under 2 weeks); risk is higher with atrial fibrillation, peripheral arterial disease, aneurysms, bypass grafts/stents and trauma.
eti: In-situ thrombosis of a diseased artery or graft (most common) or embolism from the heart or proximal aneurysm, and less often trauma or dissection, abruptly reducing perfusion.
cli: The 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia (cold limb), paresthesia and paralysis; sensory loss and weakness indicate a threatened limb, and the Rutherford classification grades viability (I viable, IIa marginally threatened, IIb immediately threatened, III irreversible).
inv: Urgent clinical assessment of pulses, sensation and motor function with handheld Doppler; CT angiography when it will not delay revascularization, plus ECG and labs including CK.
tre: Immediate IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia and urgent vascular surgery review; revascularization by catheter-directed thrombolysis, endovascular thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy/bypass depending on severity, with monitoring for reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome (fasciotomy) and amputation for nonviable limbs.

name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
epi: Leading cause of healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea and increasingly community-acquired; risk is highest after broad-spectrum antibiotics, with older age, hospitalization, PPI use and immunosuppression.
eti: Disruption of colonic microbiota allows toxin A/B-producing Clostridioides difficile spores to germinate and cause mucosal inflammation and pseudomembranes.
cli: Watery diarrhea (3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours), lower abdominal pain, fever and leukocytosis; severe disease can cause ileus, toxic megacolon, perforation and shock, and recurrence is common.
inv: Test only unformed stool from patients with new diarrhea: GDH antigen or NAAT followed by toxin immunoassay; WBC, creatinine and lactate assess severity, with CT for suspected complications.
tre: Stop inciting antibiotics if possible; oral fidaxomicin (preferred) or oral vancomycin for initial episodes; fulminant disease needs high-dose oral/rectal vancomycin with IV metronidazole and surgical review; recurrences may use fidaxomicin, tapered vancomycin, bezlotoxumab or fecal microbiota therapy.

name: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
epi: Advanced stage of diabetic retinopathy, more likely with long diabetes duration, poor glycemic control, hypertension, dyslipidemia and nephropathy.
eti: Chronic hyperglycemia causes microvascular occlusion and retinal ischemia, driving VEGF release and fragile neovascularization of the disc, retina or iris.
cli: May be asymptomatic until complications: vitreous hemorrhage (sudden floaters or painless visual loss), tractional retinal detachment and neovascular glaucoma; diabetic macular edema may coexist.
inv: Dilated fundus examination and photography; fluorescein angiography or OCT angiography to define neovascularization, OCT for macular edema, and B-scan ultrasound when hemorrhage obscures the view.
tre: Panretinal photocoagulation and/or intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment, plus optimization of glucose, blood pressure and lipids.

name: Viral encephalitis (non-HSV)
epi: Caused by many viruses with regional and seasonal variation; arboviruses such as West Nile, La Crosse, Eastern equine, Japanese and tick-borne encephalitis viruses are major causes, alongside enteroviruses, VZV, CMV, rabies and measles/mumps.
eti: Direct viral invasion of brain parenchyma with inflammatory injury; mosquito/tick-borne arboviruses, person-to-person enteroviruses, reactivated herpesviruses in immunocompromised hosts and animal bites (rabies).
cli: Fever, headache, altered mental status, behavioral change, seizures and focal neurologic deficits; some agents cause flaccid paralysis (West Nile) or movement disorders.
inv: MRI brain and lumbar puncture with CSF showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose; CSF PCR (enteroviruses, VZV, CMV) and CSF/serum IgM serology for arboviruses, with exposure history guiding testing.
tre: Empiric IV acyclovir until HSV/VZV are excluded; mainly supportive care with seizure, airway and intracranial pressure management, and specific antivirals where available (e.g. ganciclovir for CMV); vaccination and vector avoidance prevent some types.

name: Lemierre syndrome
epi: Rare (about 1 per million) but serious, mainly affecting previously healthy adolescents and young adults (median age about 20), more often males.
eti: Usually Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic gram-negative bacillus, spreading from pharyngitis or peritonsillar infection to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic septic emboli, most often to the lungs.
cli: Sore throat followed days later by persistent fever, rigors, unilateral neck pain/swelling along the sternocleidomastoid, sepsis and pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea or hemoptysis from septic pulmonary emboli; joints and other sites may be seeded.
inv: Blood cultures including anaerobic cultures; contrast CT (or ultrasound/MR venography) of the neck shows internal jugular thrombosis, and chest imaging shows multiple peripheral nodules, often cavitating.
tre: Prolonged IV beta-lactamase-resistant antibiotics with anaerobic cover (often 4-6 weeks), drainage of abscesses or empyema; anticoagulation is controversial and reserved for selected cases such as thrombus propagation or cerebral sinus extension.

name: Esophageal variceal bleeding
epi: Major complication of portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, and may be the first presentation of liver disease; carries high mortality and rebleeding risk.
eti: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals, producing dilated submucosal distal esophageal veins that rupture as pressure and wall tension rise.
cli: Painless hematemesis, melena or hematochezia with tachycardia, hypotension and features of chronic liver disease; may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
inv: Urgent upper endoscopy (ideally within 12 hours after resuscitation) confirms and treats the source; CBC, coagulation, liver and renal tests and Child-Pugh/MELD scoring guide management.
tre: Resuscitation with restrictive transfusion, IV vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin), prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) and endoscopic band ligation; balloon tamponade or stent as a bridge and early or rescue TIPS for high-risk or refractory bleeding, then nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat ligation for secondary prevention.

name: Vascular dementia
epi: Second most common cause of dementia in older adults, more common in men, people over 70 and those with vascular risk factors; often coexists with Alzheimer pathology (mixed dementia).
eti: Cognitive decline from cerebrovascular disease: multiple cortical infarcts, strategic infarcts, subcortical small-vessel disease (lacunes, white-matter lesions) or hemorrhages.
cli: Early executive dysfunction, slowed processing and attention problems with relatively later memory loss; stepwise decline after strokes or gradual progression in small-vessel disease, with focal signs, gait disturbance, urinary symptoms and mood change.
inv: Cognitive testing plus brain MRI (or CT) showing infarcts, lacunes or white-matter disease consistent with the deficits; bloods exclude reversible causes.
tre: Control vascular risk factors (blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, smoking), secondary stroke prevention and exercise; cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine give modest benefit mainly in mixed disease, with support for behavioral symptoms and caregivers.

name: Scarlet fever
epi: Most common in children aged about 5-15 years, with seasonal peaks in late winter and spring; spread by respiratory droplets and contact.
eti: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), usually pharyngitis and occasionally skin infection, producing streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins that cause the rash.
cli: Fever, sore throat and tender cervical nodes, followed within 12-48 hours by a fine sandpaper-like rash starting on the chest and abdomen with flushed cheeks, circumoral pallor, Pastia lines and strawberry tongue, then desquamation.
inv: Rapid antigen detection test or throat culture confirms group A streptococcus; diagnosis is often clinical in typical cases.
tre: Oral penicillin V or amoxicillin (alternatives in penicillin allergy) to speed recovery, prevent rheumatic fever and reduce spread; supportive care, and exclusion from school or work until 24 hours after starting antibiotics.

name: Vasovagal syncope
epi: The most common cause of syncope at all ages, often first presenting in adolescence or young adulthood.
eti: Reflex autonomic response to triggers such as prolonged standing, pain, emotion or heat causes vasodilation and/or bradycardia with transient global cerebral hypoperfusion.
cli: Brief loss of consciousness with prodrome of nausea, warmth, sweating, pallor, lightheadedness or visual dimming, and rapid full recovery; brief myoclonic jerks may occur.
inv: History, examination, orthostatic blood pressure and 12-lead ECG usually suffice; tilt-table testing or monitoring is reserved for atypical or recurrent cases.
tre: Reassurance, education, trigger avoidance, adequate fluid and salt intake and physical counter-pressure maneuvers; specialist options for recurrent severe cases.

name: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
epi: Occurs mainly in hospitalized, postoperative, elderly or critically ill patients.
eti: Acute autonomic imbalance causes massive colonic dilation without mechanical obstruction; associated with surgery, trauma, sepsis, electrolyte disturbance and opioid or anticholinergic drugs.
cli: Progressive marked abdominal distension, often with pain, nausea and reduced stool; cecal dilation risks ischemia and perforation.
inv: Abdominal radiograph shows colonic dilation, typically maximal in the cecum and right colon; CT excludes mechanical obstruction and complications.
tre: Bowel rest, nasogastric and rectal tube decompression, electrolyte correction and stopping offending drugs; neostigmine with cardiac monitoring or colonoscopic decompression if conservative care fails; surgery for perforation.

name: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss
epi: Usually affects adults, peaking in middle age, and is typically unilateral; it is an otologic emergency.
eti: Acute cochlear or auditory-nerve dysfunction; most cases are idiopathic, with viral, vascular or immune mechanisms proposed; retrocochlear lesions must be excluded.
cli: Rapid sensorineural hearing loss developing within 72 hours, with tinnitus or aural fullness; vertigo may occur.
inv: Tuning-fork tests and urgent audiometry confirm sensorineural loss; MRI of internal auditory canals excludes vestibular schwannoma; targeted tests for identifiable causes.
tre: Early systemic corticosteroids are standard initial therapy; intratympanic steroids for salvage or when systemic therapy is unsuitable; hearing rehabilitation if recovery is incomplete.

name: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
epi: Paroxysmal SVT is common and can occur in otherwise healthy people of any age, more often women; exercise, caffeine or stress may trigger episodes.
eti: Tachycardia originating at or above the AV node, most commonly AV nodal reentrant tachycardia, then AV reentrant tachycardia via an accessory pathway and focal atrial tachycardia.
cli: Sudden-onset and sudden-offset regular rapid palpitations with chest discomfort, dyspnea or lightheadedness; syncope is uncommon.
inv: 12-lead ECG during tachycardia shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm and helps define mechanism; ambulatory monitoring and echocardiography for recurrent episodes; electrophysiology study before ablation.
tre: Vagal maneuvers then adenosine for stable regular narrow-complex SVT; synchronized cardioversion if unstable; beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers for prevention; catheter ablation for recurrent disease.

name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
epi: Common in working-age adults, peaking in middle age; lumbar disc herniation is the leading cause of sciatica, mostly at the L4-L5 and L5-S1 levels.
eti: Disc degeneration and annular tear allow nucleus pulposus to herniate, usually posterolaterally, compressing the traversing nerve root (L5 at L4-L5, S1 at L5-S1).
cli: Low-back pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal pattern with paresthesia, possible myotomal weakness and reduced reflexes; straight-leg raise is often positive.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; MRI for red flags, severe or progressive deficit, suspected cauda equina, or persistent symptoms when intervention is considered.
tre: Most improve with analgesia, staying active and physiotherapy; epidural steroid injection for selected patients; discectomy for persistent disabling symptoms; emergency surgery for cauda equina syndrome.

name: Choledocholithiasis
epi: Common complication of gallstone disease, found in a meaningful minority of patients undergoing cholecystectomy.
eti: Gallstones migrate from the gallbladder into the common bile duct (secondary) or less often form within the ducts (primary), causing obstruction.
cli: Biliary colic, obstructive jaundice, dark urine and pale stools; complications include ascending cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis; may be asymptomatic.
inv: Cholestatic liver tests and abdominal ultrasound first (dilated duct); MRCP or EUS confirms duct stones when probability is intermediate; ERCP is mainly therapeutic.
tre: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or surgical bile-duct exploration; cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence; antibiotics and urgent drainage for cholangitis.

name: Costochondritis
epi: Common cause of chest pain in adolescents and adults, more often women.
eti: Inflammation or irritation of costochondral or costosternal junctions, often idiopathic or after coughing, strain or minor trauma.
cli: Localized sharp anterior chest wall pain, usually multiple upper ribs, reproduced by palpation and worsened by movement or deep breathing; no swelling, unlike Tietze syndrome.
inv: Clinical diagnosis after excluding cardiac, pulmonary and other serious causes, with ECG and further tests when risk factors or atypical features are present.
tre: Reassurance, rest from aggravating activity, heat and NSAIDs or paracetamol; stretching or physiotherapy for persistent symptoms; usually self-limiting.

name: Parvovirus B19 infection
epi: Common worldwide infection, mostly in school-aged children in late winter and spring; adults, especially women, often develop arthropathy.
eti: Parvovirus B19, a single-stranded DNA virus, infects erythroid progenitors via the P antigen; spread by respiratory droplets, blood products and transplacentally.
cli: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): slapped-cheek rash then lacy reticular body rash in children; symmetric polyarthropathy in adults; transient aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemias; hydrops fetalis.
inv: Usually clinical; IgM serology or PCR in pregnancy, aplastic crisis or immunocompromised patients; reticulocyte count is low in aplastic crisis.
tre: Supportive care for most; transfusion for aplastic crisis; IVIG for chronic infection in immunocompromised patients; fetal surveillance and intrauterine transfusion for fetal anemia.

name: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)
epi: Opportunistic infection in significant cellular immunosuppression, classically HIV with CD4 count below 200 cells/microliter, and also transplant, chemotherapy or high-dose steroid recipients.
eti: Pneumocystis jirovecii, a fungus, causes alveolar infection in immunocompromised hosts.
cli: Subacute fever, dry cough, progressive exertional dyspnea and hypoxemia with exertional desaturation; chest examination may be near normal; pneumothorax can occur.
inv: Chest imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities; induced sputum or BAL with immunofluorescence or PCR confirms; raised LDH and beta-D-glucan support.
tre: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is first line; adjunctive corticosteroids for significant hypoxemia; alternatives for intolerance; prophylaxis for at-risk patients and antiretroviral therapy in HIV.

name: Renal artery dissection
epi: Rare; occurs spontaneously or with fibromuscular dysplasia, trauma, catheter procedures or connective-tissue disorders, more often in middle-aged men when spontaneous.
eti: Intimal tear of the renal artery creates a false lumen that can narrow or thrombose the true lumen, causing renal ischemia or infarction.
cli: Sudden flank or abdominal pain, new or worsening hypertension, hematuria or acute kidney injury; may be asymptomatic.
inv: CT angiography (or MR angiography) shows the dissection flap and perfusion defects; raised LDH, renal function and urinalysis assess injury.
tre: Blood-pressure control and antithrombotic therapy for most; endovascular stenting or surgical repair for persistent ischemia, refractory hypertension or threatened kidney function.

name: Mpox (monkeypox)
epi: Endemic in Central and West Africa with global outbreaks since 2022 (clade II, largely sexual networks among men who have sex with men) and spreading clade I outbreaks.
eti: Monkeypox virus, an orthopoxvirus (clades I and II), spread by close skin-to-skin or sexual contact, respiratory secretions, contaminated materials or animal exposure.
cli: Fever, lymphadenopathy and painful deep-seated lesions progressing through macule, papule, vesicle, pustule and crust; anogenital or oral lesions and proctitis may occur without widespread rash.
inv: PCR of lesion swab confirms diagnosis; test for HIV and other STIs and assess for complications and immunosuppression.
tre: Supportive care, pain control and isolation for most; tecovirimat failed to show benefit in uncomplicated disease in trials and is reserved for severe or high-risk cases under protocols; MVA-BN vaccine for prevention.

name: Pott disease (spinal tuberculosis)
epi: Most common form of skeletal tuberculosis, seen mainly where TB is prevalent and in immunocompromised people, including HIV.
eti: Hematogenous Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of vertebral bodies, usually lower thoracic or upper lumbar, spreading under the anterior longitudinal ligament; the disc is relatively spared until later.
cli: Insidious back pain, fever, night sweats and weight loss; vertebral collapse causes kyphotic gibbus deformity; paraspinal or psoas abscess and cord compression may occur.
inv: MRI spine is preferred; CT assesses bone destruction; CT-guided biopsy for culture, histology and molecular testing; chest imaging and HIV testing.
tre: Prolonged multidrug antituberculous therapy with specialist guidance; surgery for neurologic deficit, instability, deformity or abscess not responding to treatment.

name: Cat-scratch disease
epi: Usually affects children and young adults after contact with cats, especially kittens; more common in autumn and winter.
eti: Bartonella henselae infection transmitted by cat scratch or bite, with cat fleas spreading infection between cats.
cli: Papule at inoculation site followed by tender regional lymphadenopathy, fever and malaise; atypical forms include Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis and hepatosplenic disease.
inv: Usually clinical; Bartonella serology or PCR of node tissue supports uncertain cases; node biopsy may show necrotizing granulomas.
tre: Usually self-limiting; azithromycin may speed node resolution; needle aspiration for suppurative nodes; disseminated or ocular disease requires specialist-directed therapy.

name: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease)
epi: Rare inherited bleeding disorder, predominantly affecting males and less common than hemophilia A.
eti: X-linked recessive deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation factor IX due to F9 variants.
cli: Hemarthroses, deep muscle hematomas and prolonged bleeding after injury or procedures; clinically indistinguishable from hemophilia A and severity correlates with factor IX level.
inv: Prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing with normal PT and platelets, followed by low factor IX activity; inhibitor testing when replacement becomes ineffective.
tre: Factor IX replacement for bleeding and prophylaxis, including extended half-life products; gene therapy for selected adults; avoid NSAIDs and IM injections.

name: Frostbite
epi: Occurs with prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures, worsened by wind, wet conditions, alcohol, homelessness and altitude; hands, feet, nose and ears are most affected.
eti: Tissue freezing causes ice-crystal cellular injury, then reperfusion injury, microvascular thrombosis and ischemia.
cli: Numbness and pale, waxy, hard skin during exposure; after rewarming, pain, swelling, clear or hemorrhagic blisters and later dry gangrene in deep injury.
inv: Clinical diagnosis and grading after rewarming; angiography or technetium bone scan in severe injury assesses perfusion and guides thrombolysis and amputation level.
tre: Treat hypothermia first; rapid rewarming in warm water only if refreezing can be avoided; analgesia, wound care and tetanus prophylaxis; iloprost or thrombolysis in specialized centers; delay amputation until demarcation.

name: Baker cyst
epi: Common, especially in adults with knee osteoarthritis, meniscal tears or inflammatory arthritis; also occurs in children, usually without joint disease.
eti: Synovial fluid distends the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa through a valve-like communication with the knee joint.
cli: Posterior knee swelling or tightness, worse with activity or full flexion; rupture causes calf pain and swelling mimicking DVT (pseudothrombophlebitis).
inv: Ultrasound confirms a fluid-filled popliteal cyst and excludes DVT; MRI evaluates internal knee pathology.
tre: Treat the underlying knee disorder with analgesia and physiotherapy; aspiration or corticosteroid injection for selected patients; surgery is rarely required.

name: Hookworm infection
epi: Common in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation and barefoot soil contact; a leading cause of iron-deficiency anemia in endemic areas.
eti: Necator americanus or Ancylostoma duodenale larvae penetrate skin, migrate via the lungs to the small intestine, and adult worms attach and feed on blood.
cli: Itchy rash at entry site, transient cough during lung migration, then abdominal discomfort and chronic iron-deficiency anemia with fatigue; often asymptomatic.
inv: Stool microscopy for eggs; CBC shows microcytic anemia and often eosinophilia.
tre: Albendazole or mebendazole; iron replacement for anemia; sanitation, footwear and mass deworming to prevent reinfection.

name: Horner syndrome
epi: Uncommon; can occur at any age, with causes ranging from benign to life-threatening such as carotid dissection, Pancoast tumor or neuroblastoma in children.
eti: Interruption of the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway from hypothalamus via the brainstem, spinal cord, sympathetic chain and carotid plexus to the eye.
cli: Ipsilateral miosis with dilation lag, mild ptosis, apparent enophthalmos and variable facial anhidrosis; acute painful Horner syndrome suggests carotid dissection.
inv: Apraclonidine or cocaine eye-drop testing confirms; targeted MRI/MRA or CT of brain, neck and chest guided by onset and associated signs.
tre: Treat the underlying cause; acute painful onset or neurologic symptoms require urgent imaging for carotid dissection or stroke.

name: Horseshoe kidney
epi: The most common renal fusion anomaly, more frequent in males and in Turner syndrome and trisomy 18; most are found incidentally.
eti: Fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys during fetal development; the isthmus is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery, preventing normal ascent.
cli: Often asymptomatic; urinary stasis predisposes to infection, stones and pelviureteric junction obstruction; increased risk of Wilms tumor.
inv: Ultrasound or CT shows midline fusion and anatomy; urinalysis and renal function assess complications; screen for associated anomalies.
tre: No treatment if asymptomatic; manage stones, infection or obstruction conventionally, planning procedures around the anomalous vascular anatomy.

name: Kallmann syndrome
epi: Rare form of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, more often diagnosed in males and usually recognized at expected puberty.
eti: Failed embryonic migration of GnRH neurons with olfactory neurons causes GnRH deficiency and anosmia; genes include ANOS1 (X-linked), FGFR1 and others.
cli: Delayed or absent puberty, infertility and eunuchoid habitus, micropenis or cryptorchidism in males, and anosmia or hyposmia; sometimes renal agenesis or cleft lip/palate.
inv: Low testosterone or estradiol with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH; smell testing, MRI of olfactory bulbs and pituitary, and genetic testing.
tre: Sex-steroid replacement to induce and maintain puberty; pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropin therapy when fertility is desired.

name: Krabbe disease
epi: Rare autosomal-recessive leukodystrophy, most often infantile onset but with later-onset forms; included in some newborn screening programs.
eti: GALC variants cause galactocerebrosidase deficiency, accumulation of toxic psychosine and destruction of myelin-forming cells, with globoid cells in white matter.
cli: Infantile disease: irritability, feeding difficulty, spasticity, developmental regression, seizures, optic atrophy and peripheral neuropathy, with rapid progression.
inv: Low GALC enzyme activity and genetic testing confirm; raised psychosine, MRI white-matter changes, elevated CSF protein and slowed nerve conduction support diagnosis.
tre: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in presymptomatic or very early disease can slow progression; otherwise supportive multidisciplinary care.

name: Leukemia (overview)
epi: Group of blood cancers; ALL peaks in childhood, AML and CLL are mainly diseases of older adults, and CML occurs mostly in middle age.
eti: Clonal malignant proliferation of hematopoietic cells with acquired genetic abnormalities; risks include radiation, chemotherapy, benzene, and conditions such as Down syndrome.
cli: Fatigue and pallor, infections, bruising or bleeding from marrow failure; fever, bone pain, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly from infiltration; chronic forms are often found incidentally.
inv: CBC with differential and blood film, then bone-marrow examination with flow cytometry, cytogenetic and molecular testing to classify subtype.
tre: Subtype-specific chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and/or stem-cell transplantation, with transfusion, infection prophylaxis and tumor lysis prevention as supportive care.

name: Turner syndrome
epi: One of the most common sex-chromosome abnormalities in phenotypic females; many affected pregnancies miscarry.
eti: Complete or partial loss of one X chromosome: 45,X monosomy, mosaicism or structural X abnormalities; usually not related to maternal age.
cli: Short stature, primary ovarian insufficiency, webbed neck, lymphedema in infancy, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, hypothyroidism and hearing loss; intelligence usually normal.
inv: Karyotype confirms (with evaluation for Y material); echocardiography or cardiac MRI, renal ultrasound, thyroid, hearing and metabolic screening.
tre: Growth hormone in childhood, estrogen replacement for puberty and bone health, fertility counseling, and lifelong surveillance especially for aortic dilation and dissection.

name: Bankart lesion
epi: Common in young active people after traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, with high recurrence risk in this group.
eti: Avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum with the inferior glenohumeral ligament during anterior dislocation; a bony Bankart includes a glenoid rim fracture.
cli: Shoulder pain, apprehension in abduction and external rotation, and recurrent anterior dislocation or subluxation; often accompanied by a Hill-Sachs lesion.
inv: Radiographs assess dislocation and bony lesions; MR arthrography demonstrates the labral tear; CT quantifies glenoid bone loss.
tre: Reduction, brief immobilization and rehabilitation initially; arthroscopic Bankart repair for recurrent instability or high-risk young athletes; bone-block procedures for significant glenoid bone loss.

name: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
epi: Most common in postmenopausal women and often triggered by emotional or physical stress; accounts for a small proportion of suspected acute coronary syndromes.
eti: Catecholamine surge causes transient myocardial stunning, typically apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, without culprit obstructive coronary disease.
cli: Acute chest pain and dyspnea mimicking myocardial infarction; complications include heart failure, LV outflow obstruction, arrhythmias, LV thrombus and cardiogenic shock.
inv: ECG changes and raised troponin; echocardiography shows regional wall-motion abnormality beyond one coronary territory; coronary angiography excludes obstructive disease.
tre: Supportive heart-failure therapy and management of complications; avoid inotropes in LV outflow obstruction; function usually recovers over weeks, with recurrence possible.

name: Raynaud phenomenon
epi: Common, especially in young women; primary Raynaud is usually benign, while secondary Raynaud occurs with connective-tissue disease, particularly systemic sclerosis.
eti: Exaggerated digital arterial vasospasm triggered by cold or emotional stress; secondary forms result from connective-tissue disease, vibration injury, drugs or vascular disease.
cli: Episodic, sharply demarcated white then blue then red color changes of fingers or toes with numbness or pain; digital ulcers suggest secondary disease.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; nailfold capillaroscopy, ANA and disease-specific autoantibodies, and inflammatory markers identify secondary causes.
tre: Cold avoidance, warm clothing and smoking cessation; dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine for frequent attacks; specialist vasodilator therapy and treatment of underlying disease for severe secondary Raynaud.

name: Refsum disease
epi: Very rare autosomal-recessive peroxisomal disorder, usually presenting in late childhood to early adulthood.
eti: PHYH or PEX7 variants impair alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid, which accumulates from dietary sources such as dairy, ruminant fat and fish.
cli: Retinitis pigmentosa with night blindness, anosmia, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia, hearing loss, ichthyosis, short metacarpals and cardiac arrhythmia.
inv: Markedly elevated plasma phytanic acid; molecular testing confirms; ECG and echocardiography assess cardiac involvement.
tre: Lifelong dietary phytanic-acid restriction and avoidance of fasting or rapid weight loss; plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis for acute severe decompensation.

name: Sheehan syndrome
epi: Rare in high-income countries but more common where obstetric care is limited; follows severe postpartum hemorrhage and may present years later.
eti: Ischemic necrosis of the physiologically enlarged pituitary after postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension causes partial or complete hypopituitarism.
cli: Failure of lactation and amenorrhea, fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, loss of axillary and pubic hair, and secondary adrenal and thyroid deficiency.
inv: Low target-gland hormones (cortisol, free T4, estradiol) with low or inappropriately normal ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH, low prolactin; pituitary MRI may show an empty sella.
tre: Lifelong hormone replacement, starting glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone to avoid adrenal crisis; estrogen and growth hormone as indicated; stress-dose education.

name: Tapeworm infection
epi: Taeniasis occurs worldwide where undercooked beef or pork is eaten; T. solium cysticercosis is endemic in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
eti: Taenia saginata (beef) and T. solium (pork) are acquired by eating cysticerci in undercooked meat; ingesting T. solium eggs via fecal-oral spread causes cysticercosis.
cli: Intestinal infection is often asymptomatic or causes mild abdominal discomfort, nausea or passage of proglottids; neurocysticercosis causes seizures and raised intracranial pressure.
inv: Stool microscopy for eggs or proglottids, with antigen or PCR testing for species; brain CT/MRI and serology for suspected neurocysticercosis.
tre: Praziquantel or niclosamide for intestinal taeniasis; neurocysticercosis needs specialist care with antiparasitics, corticosteroids and antiseizure medication as indicated.

name: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
epi: The most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability; risk rises with maternal age, though most affected babies are born to younger mothers.
eti: Usually free trisomy 21 from maternal meiotic nondisjunction; Robertsonian translocation (which can be inherited) or mosaicism accounts for a minority.
cli: Characteristic facies, hypotonia, single palmar crease, intellectual disability, congenital heart defects (AVSD), duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism, leukemia, atlantoaxial instability and early Alzheimer disease.
inv: Prenatal screening (combined test, cell-free DNA) and diagnostic CVS or amniocentesis; postnatal karyotype; echocardiography and ongoing hearing, vision, thyroid and blood-count surveillance.
tre: Early intervention, education and multidisciplinary care, with treatment of associated conditions such as cardiac surgery; parental karyotyping when a translocation is found.

name: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
epi: Ventricular pre-excitation is uncommon; WPW syndrome usually presents in children and young adults, with a small risk of sudden death.
eti: Congenital accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node, enabling AV reentrant tachycardia and rapid conduction of atrial fibrillation to the ventricles.
cli: Palpitations from regular orthodromic AVRT, dizziness or syncope; pre-excited atrial fibrillation causes an irregular broad-complex tachycardia that can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation.
inv: Resting ECG shows short PR interval, delta wave and broad QRS; ambulatory monitoring and electrophysiology study assess pathway risk.
tre: Vagal maneuvers or adenosine for stable orthodromic AVRT; avoid AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF, using cardioversion or procainamide; catheter ablation is definitive.

name: Yellow fever
epi: Mosquito-borne viral disease endemic in tropical sub-Saharan Africa and South America, with sylvatic and urban transmission cycles.
eti: Yellow fever virus, a flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes (especially Aedes aegypti) and Haemagogus mosquitoes.
cli: Most infections are mild with fever, headache, myalgia and nausea; after brief remission a minority enter a toxic phase with jaundice, hemorrhage, renal failure and shock.
inv: RT-PCR early and IgM serology later confirm; liver tests, coagulation and renal function assess severity; consider cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses.
tre: No specific antiviral; supportive intensive care for severe disease; live attenuated vaccination gives long-lasting protection and is required for travel to some countries.

name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
epi: Tick-borne rickettsial disease of the Americas, most common in warm months; untreated disease has high mortality.
eti: Rickettsia rickettsii transmitted by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus ticks infects vascular endothelium, causing widespread vasculitis.
cli: Fever, severe headache and myalgia, followed by a rash starting on wrists and ankles and spreading centrally, often involving palms and soles; may progress to organ failure.
inv: Clinical diagnosis early; thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia support; paired serology or skin-biopsy PCR confirm, but treatment must not await results.
tre: Immediate doxycycline for suspected disease in adults and children of all ages, plus supportive care for severe illness.

name: Atrial Fibrillation
epi: Most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age and is higher in males and white populations.
eti: Disorganized atrial electrical activity linked to age, hypertension, structural, valvular or ischemic heart disease, alcohol, hyperthyroidism, diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea.
cli: Ranges from asymptomatic to palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness and fatigue; irregularly irregular pulse on examination; risk of thromboembolic stroke.
inv: ECG shows irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm without distinct P waves; thyroid function, electrolytes, CBC and echocardiography assess causes and structure.
tre: Immediate cardioversion if unstable; rate control with beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers; anticoagulation guided by CHA2DS2-VASc, preferring DOACs over warfarin; rhythm control or ablation in selected patients.

name: Alcoholic Cirrhosis
epi: Alcohol-related liver disease is a leading cause of liver disease in the United States; cirrhosis typically presents in middle-aged heavy drinkers.
eti: Prolonged heavy alcohol use causes progressive hepatic fibrosis; risk is increased by female sex, obesity, hepatitis C co-infection and genetic factors such as PNPLA3 variants.
cli: Jaundice, hepatomegaly or shrunken liver, spider angiomas, ascites, splenomegaly, varices and hepatic encephalopathy from portal hypertension and liver failure.
inv: LFTs with AST elevated relative to ALT, raised INR, low albumin and thrombocytopenia; ultrasound assesses liver and ascites; endoscopy screens for varices; biopsy only if diagnosis uncertain.
tre: Complete alcohol abstinence with addiction support and nutritional supplementation, management of portal hypertension complications, and liver transplantation for eligible patients with end-stage disease.

name: Common Cold (Acute Nasopharyngitis)
epi: Extremely common; adults have several colds per year and children considerably more, with peaks in fall and spring.
eti: Viral infection of the upper respiratory tract, most often rhinovirus, also coronaviruses, adenovirus, parainfluenza and RSV, spread by droplets and contact.
cli: Self-limited sore throat followed by rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, sneezing, cough and malaise, sometimes low-grade fever; usually resolves in 7-10 days, cough may linger.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; laboratory or viral testing is generally unnecessary unless results would change management.
tre: Supportive care with rest, fluids, analgesics, decongestants and saline irrigation; no effective antiviral exists and antibiotics provide no benefit.

name: Rosacea
epi: Common chronic facial skin disorder, most frequent in fair-skinned adults aged 30-50 and more often diagnosed in women.
eti: Multifactorial: genetic predisposition, innate immune activation, neurovascular dysregulation and Demodex mites; triggers include heat, sunlight, spicy food and alcohol.
cli: Centrofacial flushing and persistent erythema, telangiectasias, papules and pustules without comedones, phymatous changes such as rhinophyma, and frequent ocular involvement.
inv: Clinical diagnosis based on persistent centrofacial erythema or phymatous changes, or major features such as flushing, papulopustules, telangiectasia and ocular signs; biopsy rarely needed.
tre: Trigger avoidance, gentle skin care and sunscreen; topical brimonidine for erythema and ivermectin, azelaic acid or metronidazole for papulopustular disease, with oral tetracyclines for more severe cases.

name: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (Prerenal AKI)
epi: Common form of AKI in hospitalized and critically ill patients, especially with sepsis, volume loss or heart failure.
eti: Reduced renal perfusion lowers GFR without intrinsic damage: volume depletion, hypotension, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis, and drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
cli: Rising creatinine and oliguria with signs of hypovolemia or poor perfusion, such as history of vomiting, diarrhea or bleeding, tachycardia and orthostatic hypotension.
inv: Bland urinalysis, FENa below 1%, low FEUrea, BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 and concentrated urine; improvement in creatinine after fluid resuscitation supports diagnosis.
tre: Isotonic fluid resuscitation when hypovolemic, correction of the underlying cause, stopping nephrotoxic or antihypertensive drugs, and management of hyperkalemia or other complications.

name: Minimal Change Disease
epi: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, with male predominance in childhood; accounts for a smaller share of adult nephrotic syndrome.
eti: Usually idiopathic podocytopathy, likely immune-mediated; secondary causes include drugs such as NSAIDs, malignancy such as Hodgkin lymphoma, infections and allergens.
cli: Abrupt nephrotic syndrome with periorbital and dependent edema, possibly anasarca, ascites and effusions; risk of infection and thrombosis; adults may have hypertension or AKI.
inv: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia; light microscopy is normal while electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement; biopsy is routine in adults.
tre: Oral corticosteroids are first line with a gradual taper; frequent relapses or steroid dependence may require calcineurin inhibitors, cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

name: Major Depressive Disorder
epi: Common psychiatric disorder with lifetime prevalence around 12%, roughly twice as frequent in women as in men.
eti: Multifactorial interplay of genetic predisposition, monoamine and other neurotransmitter dysfunction, adverse childhood experiences, trauma and stressful life events.
cli: At least two weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia with symptoms such as sleep and appetite change, fatigue, guilt, poor concentration, psychomotor change and suicidal ideation.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by DSM-5 criteria and mental status examination; PHQ-9 screening; TSH, CBC, metabolic panel and toxicology exclude medical causes; always assess suicide risk.
tre: Psychotherapy such as CBT and antidepressants, with SSRIs first line and combination treatment more effective; ECT for severe or treatment-resistant cases.

name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
epi: Common anxiety disorder, about twice as frequent in women, often beginning in adolescence or early adulthood.
eti: Combination of genetic predisposition, chronic stress, adverse childhood experiences, medical illness and substance use.
cli: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday matters for at least six months with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension and sleep disturbance.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; GAD-7 screening questionnaire; thyroid function, glucose and toxicology screening to exclude organic or substance-induced causes.
tre: Cognitive behavioral therapy and SSRIs or SNRIs as first line, often combined; benzodiazepines only for short-term relief.

name: Panic Disorder
epi: Affects a few percent of people each year, usually beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood and about twice as common in women.
eti: Multifactorial, with genetic predisposition, heightened sensitivity to bodily sensations and psychosocial stressors contributing.
cli: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking within minutes with palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, chest pain and fear of dying or losing control, plus anticipatory anxiety and avoidance.
inv: Clinical diagnosis requiring at least one month of persistent worry or behavior change after attacks; exclude hyperthyroidism, arrhythmias and substance use with targeted tests such as TSH and ECG.
tre: Cognitive behavioral therapy including interoceptive exposure and SSRIs or SNRIs as first line, often combined; benzodiazepines only short term.

name: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
epi: Most common endocrine disorder of reproductive-aged women; prevalence varies widely with the diagnostic criteria used.
eti: Strongly heritable disorder of insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia driving ovarian androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction.
cli: Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia, infertility, and metabolic risks including obesity, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia.
inv: Rotterdam criteria require two of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction and polycystic ovarian morphology on transvaginal ultrasound; exclude thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
tre: Lifestyle modification and weight loss first; combined hormonal contraceptives for menstrual and androgenic symptoms, metformin for metabolic features, and letrozole for ovulation induction.
