name: Uterine Leiomyomas (Fibroids)
epi: Most common benign pelvic tumor in women, present in most women by age 50 and more prevalent and symptomatic in Black women.
eti: Benign monoclonal smooth-muscle tumors of the myometrium whose growth is hormone-dependent; risk rises with early menarche, obesity and hypertension and falls with higher parity.
cli: Often asymptomatic; may cause heavy menstrual bleeding with anemia, pelvic pressure or pain, urinary frequency, constipation, infertility and pregnancy complications.
inv: Pelvic examination with an enlarged irregular uterus; transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging, saline infusion sonography for submucosal fibroids and MRI for surgical planning or atypical growth.
tre: No treatment if asymptomatic; bleeding managed with hormonal contraceptives, progestins, tranexamic acid or NSAIDs; GnRH-based therapy, uterine artery embolization, myomectomy or hysterectomy for bulk or refractory symptoms.

name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
epi: Common infection of the upper female genital tract in sexually active young women; a major cause of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
eti: Ascending polymicrobial infection, often Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, with vaginal flora including anaerobes and possibly Mycoplasma genitalium.
cli: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal discharge or bleeding, dyspareunia and fever, though symptoms are often subtle; complications include tubo-ovarian abscess and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness; NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia, pregnancy test, wet prep, inflammatory markers and pelvic ultrasound for abscess.
tre: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline plus metronidazole; hospitalize for abscess, pregnancy, severe illness or failed outpatient therapy; treat partners.

name: Emphysematous Cystitis
epi: Uncommon complicated UTI, mainly in older women and people with diabetes, urinary obstruction or multiple comorbidities.
eti: Gas-forming bacteria, most often Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae, ferment glucose in the bladder wall producing intramural and intraluminal gas.
cli: Highly variable, from incidental finding to abdominal pain, dysuria, hematuria, pneumaturia and sepsis.
inv: Urinalysis and urine and blood cultures; CT is most sensitive for gas in the bladder wall, though ultrasound or plain radiography may show it.
tre: Culture-directed antibiotics, bladder drainage with catheter, glycemic control and supportive care; surgery is rarely needed for refractory or necrotizing disease.

name: Opioid Overdose
epi: Leading cause of drug overdose death in the United States, driven increasingly by illicit synthetic opioids such as fentanyl.
eti: Excess mu-opioid receptor agonism from misuse, accidental ingestion or therapeutic error; risk rises with loss of tolerance and co-use of sedatives such as benzodiazepines or alcohol.
cli: Classic triad of depressed consciousness, respiratory depression and miosis; may progress to apnea, hypoxic injury and death.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; glucose, blood gas, metabolic panel, ECG, acetaminophen level and co-ingestant screening; routine drug screens may miss synthetic opioids.
tre: Airway support and bag-mask ventilation with oxygen, plus naloxone titrated to restore breathing; observe for recurrent sedation and offer addiction treatment and take-home naloxone.

name: Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts)
epi: Common sexually transmitted infection, peaking in young adults in their early twenties.
eti: Low-risk human papillomavirus types, mainly HPV 6 and 11, transmitted by skin-to-skin sexual contact.
cli: Soft skin-colored or darker papillomatous papules or cauliflower-like growths on the genitals, perianal area or anus; usually painless but may itch or bleed and may regress spontaneously.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; biopsy for atypical, pigmented, ulcerated or treatment-resistant lesions or immunocompromised patients; screen for other STIs.
tre: Patient-applied imiquimod, podofilox or sinecatechins, or clinician-applied cryotherapy, trichloroacetic acid or surgical removal; HPV vaccination prevents infection.

name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear
epi: Most commonly injured knee ligament, typically in young athletes in pivoting sports, with markedly higher rates in female athletes.
eti: Usually a non-contact pivoting or deceleration injury with valgus stress and anterior tibial translation on a slightly flexed knee; also direct contact trauma.
cli: Audible or felt pop, immediate pain and rapid swelling from hemarthrosis, followed by instability or giving way and reduced range of motion.
inv: Lachman test is the most sensitive examination, with anterior drawer and pivot shift tests; radiographs exclude fracture and MRI confirms the tear and associated injuries.
tre: Acute rest, ice, compression and elevation with physiotherapy; nonoperative rehabilitation for low-demand patients and surgical reconstruction with autograft or allograft for active patients with instability.

name: Meniscal Tear
epi: Common knee injury, occurring acutely in young athletes and as degenerative tears in older adults.
eti: Acute tears result from twisting or rotation on a weight-bearing, flexed knee; degenerative tears arise from age-related meniscal weakening with minimal trauma.
cli: Joint-line pain and tenderness, effusion, catching, and mechanical locking or restricted motion, with pain on deep flexion or twisting.
inv: Joint-line tenderness and provocative McMurray and Apley tests; MRI confirms the tear, and arthroscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
tre: Most tears, especially degenerative, are managed conservatively with activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy; arthroscopic repair or partial meniscectomy for large, complex or mechanically symptomatic tears.

name: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
epi: Most common form of glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness; Black individuals develop earlier, more severe disease.
eti: Chronic progressive optic neuropathy linked to impaired aqueous outflow through an open trabecular meshwork; risks include age, family history, Black race, thin corneas, myopia and diabetes.
cli: Asymptomatic early, with gradual painless peripheral visual field loss; optic disc cupping with increased cup-to-disc ratio and rim thinning; intraocular pressure often elevated but may be normal.
inv: Tonometry, ophthalmoscopy or optic disc imaging such as OCT, automated visual field testing, central corneal thickness and gonioscopy to confirm an open angle.
tre: Lower intraocular pressure with topical prostaglandin analogues or beta-blockers, or laser trabeculoplasty as first line; surgical filtration procedures for progression despite therapy.

name: Herpetic Whitlow
epi: Uncommon; occurs mainly in children who suck their thumbs or fingers and in healthcare workers exposed to oral secretions without gloves.
eti: Herpes simplex virus type 1 or 2 inoculated into broken skin of the finger, from another person or by self-inoculation.
cli: Prodromal tingling and disproportionate pain, then erythema, swelling and grouped vesicles on the distal finger that may coalesce; possible fever and lymphadenopathy; may recur.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; HSV PCR of vesicle fluid is most sensitive, with viral culture or Tzanck smear as alternatives.
tre: Self-limiting; supportive care with analgesia and covering the lesion, oral antivirals if started early; incision and drainage should be avoided.

name: Ankle Sprain
epi: Very common musculoskeletal injury, especially in young, physically active people; many develop persistent symptoms or recurrent sprains.
eti: Most are inversion injuries of the lateral ligament complex, particularly the anterior talofibular ligament; eversion injures the deltoid ligament and external rotation causes high (syndesmotic) sprains.
cli: Pain, swelling and bruising over the injured ligaments with reduced weight-bearing; graded I-III from stretching to complete rupture with instability.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; Ottawa ankle rules determine need for radiographs to exclude fracture; MRI for suspected syndesmotic injury or persistent symptoms.
tre: Protection, ice, compression and elevation with early functional rehabilitation and progressive loading, strengthening and proprioceptive training; surgery for chronic instability.

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
epi: Common chronic dermatitis with peaks in infancy and in adults over 40; more frequent and severe in HIV and Parkinson disease.
eti: Inflammatory reaction involving Malassezia yeast, skin lipids and individual susceptibility in sebaceous-rich areas.
cli: Relapsing greasy yellowish scale on erythematous patches of the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears and chest; cradle cap in infants; dandruff in mild cases.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; KOH, biopsy or HIV testing if atypical, severe or of sudden onset.
tre: Topical antifungals such as ketoconazole, ciclopirox or zinc pyrithione shampoos and creams first line; short courses of low-potency topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors for flares.

name: Actinic Keratosis
epi: Very common premalignant lesion in older, fair-skinned people with chronic sun exposure, and in immunosuppressed patients.
eti: Cumulative ultraviolet damage causes dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation in the epidermis.
cli: Rough, scaly, adherent pink, red or brown macules or papules on sun-exposed skin such as face, scalp, ears and forearms; a small fraction progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by inspection and palpation; biopsy for thick, tender, rapidly growing or treatment-resistant lesions to exclude squamous cell carcinoma.
tre: Cryotherapy for isolated lesions; field therapy with topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod or photodynamic therapy for multiple lesions; sun protection.

name: Aortic Stenosis
epi: Most common valvular heart disease requiring intervention in older adults in developed countries; prevalence rises with age.
eti: Age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve, congenital bicuspid valve in younger patients, and rheumatic heart disease in developing countries.
cli: Exertional angina, syncope and dyspnea or heart failure; crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids with slow-rising pulse.
inv: Transthoracic echocardiography confirms and grades severity by valve area, velocity and gradient; ECG may show LVH; exercise testing in selected asymptomatic patients.
tre: No effective medical therapy; aortic valve replacement by surgical or transcatheter approach for symptomatic severe disease or reduced ejection fraction, chosen by a heart valve team.

name: Coarctation of the Aorta
epi: Accounts for a few percent of congenital heart disease, more common in males and strongly associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve.
eti: Congenital narrowing of the aorta, usually near the ductus arteriosus insertion, possibly from ductal tissue extending into the aortic wall.
cli: Neonates develop heart failure or shock when the duct closes; older patients have upper-limb hypertension, headaches, leg claudication, weak delayed femoral pulses and arm-leg blood pressure gradient.
inv: Four-limb blood pressures, echocardiography first line, ECG for LVH, chest X-ray with rib notching and figure-3 sign, and CT or MRI angiography.
tre: Prostaglandin E1 to keep the duct open in critical neonates, followed by surgical repair or balloon angioplasty with stenting; lifelong follow-up for recoarctation, hypertension and aneurysm.

name: Cystic Fibrosis
epi: Autosomal recessive disorder most common in people of Northern European descent; deltaF508 (F508del) is the most frequent variant.
eti: Pathogenic CFTR gene variants on chromosome 7 impair a cAMP-regulated chloride channel, producing thick secretions in lungs, pancreas, intestine and other exocrine organs.
cli: Recurrent lung infections with bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and nasal polyps, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and failure to thrive, meconium ileus, CF-related diabetes, liver disease and male infertility.
inv: Newborn screening with immunoreactive trypsinogen, confirmed by elevated sweat chloride and CFTR genetic testing; spirometry and sputum cultures monitor disease.
tre: Multidisciplinary care with CFTR modulators for eligible genotypes, airway clearance and inhaled mucolytics, antibiotics for infections including Pseudomonas, pancreatic enzymes, fat-soluble vitamins and nutrition; lung transplantation for end-stage disease.

name: Cluster Headache
epi: Uncommon primary headache, about three times more frequent in men, usually beginning around age 30 and strongly associated with smoking.
eti: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia involving the trigeminovascular system, cranial parasympathetic activation and hypothalamic dysfunction, explaining its circadian and seasonal periodicity.
cli: Excruciating strictly unilateral orbital or temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, often nightly in clusters, with ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis or miosis, and restlessness.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by ICHD criteria; brain MRI to exclude structural or pituitary lesions, especially with atypical features.
tre: Acute attacks: high-flow 100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan or intranasal zolmitriptan; prevention with verapamil, short-term corticosteroids or greater occipital nerve block as bridging therapy.

name: Secondary Syphilis
epi: Stage of a common sexually transmitted infection, with rising incidence notably among men who have sex with men; typically weeks to months after the primary chancre.
eti: Hematogenous dissemination of the spirochete Treponema pallidum after untreated primary infection.
cli: Diffuse non-pruritic maculopapular rash often involving palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, patchy alopecia; possible neurologic or ocular involvement.
inv: Nontreponemal tests (RPR or VDRL) with titers, confirmed by treponemal tests (TP-PA, EIA or CIA); test for HIV and other STIs; CSF exam if neurologic or ocular signs.
tre: Parenteral benzathine penicillin G as first line; monitor nontreponemal titers for response, warn of Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction and treat partners.

name: Dengue Fever
epi: Most prevalent mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide, endemic across tropical and subtropical regions.
eti: Dengue virus (four serotypes, flavivirus) transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes; secondary infection with a different serotype raises risk of severe disease.
cli: Abrupt high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia and rash; around defervescence plasma leakage may cause shock and bleeding, heralded by warning signs such as abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and mucosal bleeding.
inv: RT-PCR or NS1 antigen in the first days of illness, IgM serology later; CBC shows leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and rising hematocrit; transaminases often elevated.
tre: Supportive care with acetaminophen, avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs, oral hydration, and careful isotonic crystalloid therapy with close monitoring in the critical phase.

name: Necrotizing Fasciitis
epi: Rare but rapidly fatal soft-tissue infection; risk higher with diabetes, alcohol misuse, cirrhosis, immunosuppression and injection drug use.
eti: Polymicrobial (type I) mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection or monomicrobial (type II) group A Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus, usually entering via skin breaks and spreading along fascial planes.
cli: Pain out of proportion to examination, tenderness beyond erythema, swelling, bullae, skin necrosis or crepitus, with rapid progression to sepsis and shock.
inv: Clinical diagnosis that should not delay surgery; LRINEC score and CT may support, and surgical exploration with tissue cultures is definitive.
tre: Emergency surgical debridement with repeated explorations, plus empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics including anti-MRSA, gram-negative and anaerobic coverage with clindamycin, and ICU resuscitation.

name: Alopecia Areata
epi: Common autoimmune hair loss disorder with about 2% lifetime risk, affecting all ages and both sexes, often beginning in young adulthood.
eti: T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack on anagen hair follicles in genetically predisposed people, sometimes triggered by stress or infection; associated with atopy and autoimmune thyroid disease.
cli: Sudden, well-demarcated, smooth nonscarring patches of hair loss with exclamation-mark hairs at the margins; may progress to alopecia totalis or universalis; nail pitting in some patients.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by dermoscopy and hair pull test; biopsy if uncertain; consider thyroid testing.
tre: Intralesional or topical corticosteroids for limited patches; oral JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib or ritlecitinib for extensive disease; spontaneous regrowth is common.

name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
epi: Inflammatory disorder of adults over 50, about twice as common in women, frequently coexisting with giant cell arteritis.
eti: Unknown cause; imaging shows low-grade synovitis and bursitis of the shoulders, hips and axial structures.
cli: Bilateral proximal pain and prolonged morning stiffness of the shoulders, neck and hip girdle, with systemic symptoms but no true muscle weakness.
inv: Markedly raised ESR and CRP with normal creatine kinase; exclude mimics such as rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, hypothyroidism and myeloma, and screen for giant cell arteritis symptoms.
tre: Low-dose oral glucocorticoids with rapid response, tapered slowly to the lowest effective dose; methotrexate or sarilumab as steroid-sparing options; bone protection during long-term steroids.

name: Intrinsic (Intrarenal) Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
epi: Common in hospitalized patients, with acute tubular necrosis the most frequent intrinsic cause.
eti: Direct kidney parenchymal injury: acute tubular necrosis from ischemia or nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides, contrast or myoglobin; glomerulonephritis; acute interstitial nephritis; and vascular causes such as vasculitis or thrombotic microangiopathy.
cli: Rising creatinine with oliguria or normal urine output, fluid overload, and uremic symptoms such as nausea, confusion and pericarditis, plus features of the underlying cause.
inv: Urine microscopy with muddy brown granular casts in ATN, RBC casts in glomerulonephritis and white cells or casts in interstitial nephritis; FENa above 2% typical of ATN; renal ultrasound; biopsy when unclear.
tre: Treat the underlying cause and stop nephrotoxins, careful fluid and electrolyte management and drug dose adjustment; dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uremic complications.

name: Polycystic Kidney Disease
epi: Most common inherited kidney disease and a leading genetic cause of kidney failure, with many patients reaching kidney failure by late adulthood.
eti: Autosomal dominant variants in PKD1 (most cases, more severe) or PKD2 cause progressive bilateral renal cyst formation.
cli: Hypertension, flank pain, hematuria, UTIs, nephrolithiasis and progressive CKD; extrarenal liver cysts, intracranial aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse and diverticulosis.
inv: Renal ultrasound showing multiple bilateral cysts with age-specific criteria and family history; CT or MRI for kidney volume; genetic testing when imaging is equivocal.
tre: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, salt restriction and fluids; tolvaptan for patients at risk of rapid progression; dialysis or transplant for kidney failure.

name: Lactose Intolerance
epi: Lactase non-persistence is the usual state for most adults worldwide, least common in people of Northwest European descent.
eti: Primary age-related decline in intestinal lactase, secondary to small-bowel mucosal injury such as celiac disease or gastroenteritis, or rare congenital deficiency; undigested lactose is fermented in the colon.
cli: Bloating, abdominal cramps, flatulence, borborygmi, nausea and osmotic diarrhea after ingesting dairy, often dose-dependent.
inv: Clinical history and response to dairy withdrawal; lactose hydrogen breath test confirms; consider testing for secondary causes such as celiac disease.
tre: Reduce dietary lactose to tolerance, use yogurt, hard cheeses, lactose-free products or lactase enzyme supplements, and ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D.

name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
epi: Most common primary kidney cancer in adults, peaking at 50-70 years with male predominance.
eti: Arises from renal tubular epithelium, most often clear-cell type linked to VHL loss; risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, CKD/dialysis and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
cli: Often incidental on imaging; classic triad of hematuria, flank pain and palpable mass is uncommon; may cause weight loss, fever, varicocele and paraneoplastic hypercalcemia, polycythemia or hypertension.
inv: Contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis is key for diagnosis and staging, with chest imaging for metastases; urinalysis, CBC, calcium and renal function.
tre: Partial or radical nephrectomy for localized disease, active surveillance or ablation for small masses in selected patients; immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations and VEGF-targeted therapy for advanced disease.

name: Testicular Torsion
epi: Urologic emergency most common in adolescent boys, with a smaller peak in neonates.
eti: Twisting of the spermatic cord, often due to bell clapper deformity, causing venous obstruction then arterial ischemia of the testis.
cli: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain with nausea and vomiting, a high-riding horizontally lying tender testis and usually absent cremasteric reflex.
inv: Clinical diagnosis aided by TWIST score; color Doppler ultrasound shows absent or reduced flow but must not delay surgery when suspicion is high.
tre: Emergency surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy, or orchiectomy if nonviable; manual detorsion only as a temporizing measure; salvage is time-dependent, best within six hours.

name: Sickle Cell Disease
epi: Common inherited hemoglobinopathy, most prevalent in people of African, Middle Eastern, Indian and Mediterranean ancestry.
eti: Autosomal recessive beta-globin point mutation (glutamic acid to valine) producing HbS, which polymerizes when deoxygenated, causing rigid sickled red cells, hemolysis and vaso-occlusion.
cli: Painful vaso-occlusive crises, chronic hemolytic anemia, functional asplenia with infection risk, acute chest syndrome, stroke, avascular necrosis, priapism, splenic sequestration, aplastic crises and kidney damage.
inv: Newborn screening; hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC confirms; CBC shows anemia with reticulocytosis and sickle cells on smear; transcranial Doppler screens children for stroke risk.
tre: Hydroxyurea, analgesia and hydration for crises, transfusion for specific complications, penicillin prophylaxis and vaccinations in childhood, folic acid; hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy for selected patients.

name: Schizophrenia
epi: Lifetime prevalence below 1%, equal in men and women, with onset typically in late adolescence or early adulthood and earlier in men.
eti: Highly heritable neurodevelopmental disorder involving dopamine and glutamate dysregulation, with environmental risks such as cannabis use, obstetric complications and social adversity.
cli: Positive symptoms such as delusions and auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech and behavior, negative symptoms such as blunted affect, alogia and avolition, and cognitive deficits.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by DSM-5-TR criteria with continuous signs for at least six months; exclude substance-induced and medical causes with toxicology, basic labs and neuroimaging when indicated.
tre: Antipsychotic medication combined with psychosocial interventions such as CBT, family support and supported employment; clozapine for treatment-resistant illness or persistent suicidality.

name: Bipolar I Disorder
epi: Affects about 2% of people over a lifetime, equally in men and women, usually beginning from the teens to the thirties.
eti: Highly heritable mood disorder involving monoamine dysregulation, with psychosocial stressors, sleep disruption and substances triggering episodes.
cli: At least one manic episode of elevated or irritable mood for one week or more with grandiosity, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility and risky behavior; depressive episodes are common.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by DSM-5 criteria; thyroid function and toxicology screen to exclude secondary causes, plus baseline renal, thyroid and metabolic tests before mood stabilizers.
tre: Acute mania treated with lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic; maintenance mood stabilizer, often lithium, with psychoeducation; avoid antidepressant monotherapy.

name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
epi: Affects about 1-3% of people, slightly more women in adulthood, with onset often in childhood, adolescence or early adulthood.
eti: Multifactorial, with genetic predisposition and dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits; rarely follows streptococcal infection in children.
cli: Intrusive distressing obsessions and repetitive compulsions such as washing, checking, counting or ordering, which are time-consuming or impairing; frequent comorbid anxiety, depression and tics.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by psychiatric assessment and DSM-5 criteria; scales such as Y-BOCS gauge severity; exclude substance or medical causes.
tre: Cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention and SSRIs as first line, often combined; clomipramine as an alternative.

name: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
epi: Common, with lifetime prevalence of several percent; higher in women and in those exposed to combat, assault or disasters.
eti: Develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, with risk shaped by trauma severity, prior trauma and limited social support.
cli: Intrusive memories, nightmares and flashbacks, avoidance of reminders, negative mood and cognitions, and hyperarousal with hypervigilance, irritability and sleep disturbance.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by DSM-5-TR criteria with symptoms lasting over one month causing impairment; screening tools such as PC-PTSD-5 or PCL-5; assess comorbid depression, substance use and suicide risk.
tre: Trauma-focused psychotherapies such as trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure or EMDR are first line; SSRIs or venlafaxine for medication management.

name: Anorexia Nervosa
epi: Most common in adolescent girls and young women, with the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder.
eti: Multifactorial, combining genetic vulnerability, perfectionistic or anxious traits, and sociocultural pressures toward thinness.
cli: Restriction of intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image; bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo, amenorrhea and osteopenia.
inv: Clinical diagnosis by DSM-5 criteria; BMI, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver tests, ECG and bone density to assess medical complications.
tre: Multidisciplinary nutritional rehabilitation with gradual refeeding and monitoring for refeeding syndrome, plus psychotherapy, with family-based treatment for adolescents; hospitalize if medically unstable.

name: Preeclampsia
epi: Pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder affecting a few percent of pregnancies and a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity.
eti: Abnormal placentation with impaired spiral artery remodeling leads to placental ischemia and systemic endothelial dysfunction; risks include first pregnancy, prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, obesity and multiple gestation.
cli: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; severe features include headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, pulmonary edema, HELLP syndrome and eclamptic seizures.
inv: Serial blood pressures, urine protein-creatinine ratio, CBC with platelets, creatinine and liver enzymes, plus fetal assessment with ultrasound and monitoring.
tre: Delivery is definitive, timed by gestational age and severity; antihypertensives for severe hypertension, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and low-dose aspirin for prevention in high-risk women.

name: Ectopic Pregnancy
epi: Occurs in about 2% of diagnosed pregnancies and is a leading cause of first-trimester maternal death.
eti: Implantation outside the uterine cavity, usually in the fallopian tube; risks include prior ectopic, tubal surgery or damage, pelvic inflammatory disease, assisted reproduction, smoking and pregnancy with an IUD.
cli: Amenorrhea with lower abdominal or pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding; rupture causes sudden severe pain, peritonism, syncope and hemorrhagic shock.
inv: Pregnancy test, quantitative serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound showing no intrauterine pregnancy or an adnexal mass; serial hCG when location is uncertain.
tre: Methotrexate for stable, unruptured cases meeting criteria; laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy for rupture, instability or medical failure; anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh-negative patients.

name: Endometriosis
epi: Common chronic gynecologic condition affecting about 10% of reproductive-aged females, and far more of those with chronic pelvic pain or infertility; usually diagnosed between ages 25 and 45.
eti: Endometrial-type glands and stroma grow outside the uterus, most likely from retrograde menstruation, with coelomic metaplasia, vascular/lymphatic spread and immune dysregulation also implicated.
cli: Chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and infertility; symptom severity does not correlate with disease extent, and exam may show uterine tenderness, reduced mobility or adnexal masses.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by transvaginal ultrasound or MRI; histopathology of excised lesions showing ectopic endometrial glands and stroma is the gold standard.
tre: NSAIDs for pain plus hormonal suppression with combined hormonal contraceptives or progestins first-line; surgical excision for refractory disease, endometriomas or infertility.

name: Placental Abruption
epi: Complicates roughly 0.4-1% of pregnancies and is a leading cause of bleeding in the second half of gestation, with most cases occurring preterm.
eti: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall due to tearing of uteroplacental vessels; risk factors include hypertension/preeclampsia, smoking, cocaine use, prior abruption and abdominal trauma.
cli: Sudden abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding (which may be concealed), uterine tenderness and frequent contractions, decreased fetal movement, and in severe cases maternal shock, DIC and fetal death.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; ultrasound has low sensitivity, so fetal heart rate monitoring, CBC, type and screen, coagulation studies and fibrinogen guide management, with Kleihauer-Betke testing for fetomaternal hemorrhage.
tre: IV access, fluid and blood resuscitation, and continuous maternal-fetal monitoring; mild cases remote from term may be observed, while severe abruption or fetal compromise requires urgent delivery.

name: Small Bowel Obstruction
epi: Accounts for a large share of admissions for acute abdominal pain and about 80% of bowel obstructions; more common in older adults with prior abdominal surgery.
eti: Postoperative adhesions are the leading cause, followed by hernias; malignancy, Crohn disease, gallstone ileus and volvulus are other causes, with proximal distension risking ischemia and necrosis.
cli: Crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and obstipation, with dehydration; bowel sounds are hyperactive early, and fever, peritonism or constant pain suggest strangulation.
inv: CT abdomen is the imaging of choice, identifying the transition point and signs of ischemia; plain radiographs are less sensitive, and labs assess electrolytes, renal function and lactate.
tre: IV fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, bowel rest and nasogastric decompression; nonoperative management for uncomplicated cases, with surgery for strangulation, ischemia or failed conservative treatment.

name: Inguinal hernia
epi: Inguinal hernias are far more common in males, with peaks in early childhood and older age; indirect hernias are the most common type and incarceration is an acute complication.
eti: Abdominal contents become trapped in the hernia sac (incarceration); compromised blood supply to the trapped contents causes strangulation, with risk raised by increased intra-abdominal pressure and connective tissue weakness.
cli: Painful, tender, irreducible groin bulge, sometimes with bowel obstruction symptoms; strangulation adds severe pain, overlying erythema, fever and systemic toxicity.
inv: Mainly clinical examination; ultrasound or CT can confirm the diagnosis and look for bowel obstruction or ischemia, with labs such as lactate and white cell count.
tre: Emergency surgical repair for strangulation, with resection of nonviable bowel; gentle reduction may be attempted for incarceration without signs of strangulation, followed by timely repair.

name: Splenic Laceration (Trauma)
epi: The spleen is one of the most commonly injured abdominal organs in trauma, with blunt mechanisms such as motor vehicle collisions causing the vast majority.
eti: Blunt or penetrating injury to the left upper quadrant or lower left ribs; preexisting splenomegaly increases vulnerability to rupture.
cli: Left upper quadrant pain and tenderness, peritoneal signs, left shoulder pain worsened by inspiration (Kehr sign), and hemorrhagic shock; some patients have few initial signs.
inv: FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid in unstable patients; contrast CT is the gold standard in stable patients for grading injury and detecting active extravasation.
tre: Nonoperative management with monitoring for stable patients, splenic artery embolization for selected stable patients with vascular injury, and splenectomy for instability; vaccinate against encapsulated organisms after splenectomy.

name: Perforated Peptic Ulcer
epi: Uncommon but serious complication of peptic ulcer disease, more frequent with advanced age and carrying high mortality if surgery is delayed.
eti: Full-thickness ulceration of the stomach or duodenum, mainly due to Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAIDs including aspirin; smoking and alcohol contribute.
cli: Sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalized, with diffuse tenderness, guarding and board-like rigidity, tachycardia and features of sepsis or shock.
inv: Erect chest or abdominal X-ray may show free air under the diaphragm; CT abdomen is more sensitive for pneumoperitoneum and identifying the site.
tre: Resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, IV proton pump inhibitors and broad-spectrum antibiotics, with early surgical repair (omental patch and peritoneal lavage) and H. pylori eradication.

name: Acetaminophen Toxicity
epi: The most common pharmaceutical overdose and a leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States.
eti: In overdose, CYP450 metabolism produces excess toxic NAPQI, which depletes hepatic glutathione and causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis.
cli: Often minimal early symptoms (nausea, vomiting), followed by rising transaminases and right upper quadrant pain, then peak hepatotoxicity with encephalopathy, coagulopathy and renal failure before recovery or death.
inv: Serum acetaminophen level at 4 hours or later plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for single acute ingestions, plus LFTs, PT/INR, renal function and other co-ingestant screening.
tre: N-acetylcysteine, most effective when started early; activated charcoal for early presentation, supportive care, and liver transplant referral using King's College criteria.

name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
epi: Common cause of poisoning-related emergency visits and deaths, peaking in winter with use of heating appliances.
eti: Inhalation of CO from faulty furnaces, vehicle exhaust, generators, fires or methylene chloride; CO binds hemoglobin far more avidly than oxygen and impairs tissue oxygen delivery.
cli: Headache, dizziness, nausea and fatigue, often in several household members; severe exposure causes confusion, syncope, seizures, coma, arrhythmias and delayed neurologic sequelae.
inv: Carboxyhemoglobin level by co-oximetry on blood gas; standard pulse oximetry is falsely normal, and ECG, troponin and lactate assess end-organ injury.
tre: Remove from exposure and give high-flow 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask; consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe cases such as loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits or pregnancy.

name: Heat Stroke
epi: Classic heatstroke affects older, sedentary or chronically ill people and infants during heat waves; exertional heatstroke affects healthy athletes, military recruits and laborers and is a common cause of death in young athletes.
eti: Failure of thermoregulation from environmental heat exposure (classic) or a massive heat load from intense exertion in hot conditions (exertional), triggering cytokine-mediated multiorgan injury.
cli: Core temperature above 40 C with CNS dysfunction (confusion, delirium, seizures, coma); sweating may be present or absent, with complications such as rhabdomyolysis, AKI, liver injury and DIC.
inv: Core (rectal or esophageal) temperature; CBC, coagulation studies, electrolytes, renal and liver function, creatine kinase, glucose and urinalysis for myoglobin, plus drug screen when indicated.
tre: Immediate rapid cooling, preferably cold-water immersion or evaporative cooling, stopping around 39 C to avoid overshoot, plus IV fluids and organ support; antipyretics and dantrolene are not recommended.

name: Retinal Detachment
epi: Uncommon but sight-threatening condition, slightly more common in males and in highly myopic populations.
eti: Separation of neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium: rhegmatogenous (retinal break; myopia, lattice degeneration, trauma, prior surgery), tractional (e.g. proliferative diabetic retinopathy) or exudative (tumor, inflammation).
cli: Painless new floaters and photopsia followed by a progressive peripheral visual field defect described as a curtain; central vision is lost once the macula detaches.
inv: Dilated fundoscopy with scleral depression; B-scan ultrasound when the view is obscured, and OCT to assess macular involvement.
tre: Urgent ophthalmology referral; rhegmatogenous and tractional detachments are repaired surgically (pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle or vitrectomy), while exudative detachment is managed by treating the cause.

name: Age-Related Macular Degeneration
epi: Leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults in developed countries, most common after 60 and in people of European ancestry.
eti: Degeneration of the macula linked to age, smoking and complement gene variants such as CFH; drusen beneath the RPE mark early disease and choroidal neovascularization defines wet AMD.
cli: Dry AMD causes gradual central vision loss with drusen and geographic atrophy; wet AMD causes more rapid central vision loss, metamorphopsia and scotoma from leaking neovascular membranes.
inv: Dilated fundoscopy and Amsler grid testing, with OCT to assess retinal fluid and structure and fluorescein angiography to characterize choroidal neovascularization.
tre: Smoking cessation and AREDS-type antioxidant supplements for intermediate dry disease; wet AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

name: Chemical Ocular Burn
epi: Chemical burns make up a significant minority of eye injuries, mostly in young working-age adults, with alkali injuries somewhat more common than acid injuries.
eti: Alkalis (e.g. ammonia, lime, lye) saponify cell membranes and penetrate deeply, causing the most severe injury; acids coagulate surface proteins, which usually limits penetration.
cli: Severe pain, reduced vision, redness, tearing, photophobia and blepharospasm, with corneal epithelial defects, chemosis and limbal blanching, which predicts poor outcome.
inv: Check ocular surface pH with litmus paper, but do not delay irrigation; after neutralization, slit-lamp exam with fluorescein staining grades the injury and intraocular pressure is measured.
tre: Immediate, copious irrigation started at the scene and continued until pH is neutral, removal of retained particles from the fornices, then urgent ophthalmology care with anti-inflammatory and supportive therapy.

name: Acute Epiglottitis
epi: Once mainly a disease of young children, it became rare in children after Hib vaccination and is now seen mostly in adults.
eti: Usually bacterial infection of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures, historically Haemophilus influenzae type b, now also Streptococcus pneumoniae, group A streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus; thermal or caustic injury can also cause it.
cli: Rapid onset of fever, severe sore throat, odynophagia, drooling, muffled voice, stridor and respiratory distress; children often sit leaning forward in a tripod position.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with the airway secured first; lateral neck X-ray may show the thumb sign, and flexible laryngoscopy is used in stable adults, while upsetting the child or using a tongue depressor is avoided.
tre: Secure the airway in a controlled setting, ideally with anesthesia and ENT present, then give IV empiric antibiotics such as a third-generation cephalosporin.

name: Rotator Cuff Tear
epi: The most common tendon injury treated in adults, with prevalence rising steeply with age; many tears in older adults are asymptomatic.
eti: Degenerative tears from age-related microtrauma, most often of the supraspinatus, in older adults; acute traumatic tears in younger patients; smoking and overhead activity raise risk.
cli: Shoulder pain worse with overhead activity and at night, with weakness of abduction or rotation; positive empty can, drop arm or external rotation lag tests suggest a tear.
inv: Clinical exam supported by ultrasound or MRI, which show tear size, retraction and muscle atrophy; plain radiographs exclude other causes.
tre: Initial physical therapy, analgesia and activity modification for most tears; surgical repair for acute traumatic tears in younger active patients or symptomatic tears not responding to conservative care.

name: Achilles Tendon Rupture
epi: Most common in men aged 30-50 during recreational sports; a notable proportion are initially misdiagnosed as ankle sprains.
eti: Sudden forceful plantarflexion or push-off loading on a degenerated tendon; risk factors include fluoroquinolones, corticosteroids, prior tendinopathy and intermittent sport participation.
cli: Sudden pain at the back of the heel with an audible pop or a feeling of being kicked, weak plantarflexion, a palpable tendon gap and difficulty walking.
inv: Clinical diagnosis using the Thompson test (no plantarflexion on calf squeeze) and palpable gap; ultrasound or MRI for unclear or chronic cases.
tre: Either nonoperative functional bracing with early rehabilitation or surgical repair; surgery lowers re-rupture risk but has wound complications and is often chosen for athletes.

name: Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow)
epi: Common overuse condition affecting men and women equally, mostly over age 40; only a minority of patients play tennis, and most recover within 1-2 years.
eti: Repetitive gripping and wrist extension cause tendinosis of the common extensor origin, mainly the extensor carpi radialis brevis, at the lateral epicondyle.
cli: Lateral elbow pain radiating to the forearm, worse with gripping and lifting, with tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and pain on resisted wrist extension.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; imaging such as X-ray, ultrasound or MRI is reserved for refractory cases or suspected alternative diagnoses.
tre: Activity modification, ice, NSAIDs, counterforce bracing and physical therapy with eccentric strengthening; injections are options, and surgery is for failure of prolonged nonoperative care.

name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN 1)
epi: Rare autosomal dominant tumor syndrome; most patients have an affected parent, while a minority have de novo variants.
eti: Pathogenic variants in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene encoding menin predispose to multiple endocrine tumors.
cli: Primary hyperparathyroidism from multigland disease (most common, often first), pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors such as gastrinoma or insulinoma, and pituitary adenomas such as prolactinoma, plus angiofibromas, collagenomas and lipomas.
inv: Clinical diagnosis with two or more MEN1 tumors or one plus an affected first-degree relative; MEN1 genetic testing confirms it, with biochemical screening (calcium, PTH, prolactin, gastrin) and imaging for tumors.
tre: Subtotal or total parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism, surgery or medical therapy for pancreatic and pituitary tumors (e.g. PPIs for gastrinoma, dopamine agonists for prolactinoma), and lifelong surveillance with family testing.

name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
epi: Rare disease (WHO group 1 pulmonary hypertension) that mostly affects young and middle-aged women; idiopathic PAH is very rare.
eti: Idiopathic, heritable (e.g. BMPR2 variants), drug- or toxin-induced, or associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension or congenital heart disease; vasoconstriction and remodeling of small pulmonary arteries raise resistance.
cli: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain and syncope, often with delayed diagnosis; signs include a loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur and right heart failure.
inv: Echocardiography for screening; right heart catheterization confirms precapillary pulmonary hypertension with raised mean pulmonary artery pressure, normal wedge pressure and raised PVR, with vasoreactivity testing.
tre: Calcium channel blockers only for vasoreactive patients; otherwise endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors and prostacyclin-pathway agents, often combined, with lung transplantation for advanced disease.

name: Nasal Polyposis
epi: Affects a small percentage of the population, with slight male predominance; strongly associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma and aspirin sensitivity, and in children should prompt evaluation for cystic fibrosis.
eti: Benign inflammatory outgrowths of the sinonasal mucosa due to chronic inflammation, often type 2/eosinophilic, linked to allergic rhinitis, cystic fibrosis, fungal sinusitis and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
cli: Nasal obstruction and congestion, rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, hyposmia or anosmia and snoring; polyps appear as pale, translucent grape-like masses.
inv: Anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy confirms the diagnosis; CT of the sinuses defines extent, particularly when surgery is planned.
tre: Intranasal corticosteroids first-line, short oral corticosteroid courses for severe symptoms, endoscopic sinus surgery for refractory disease, and biologics such as dupilumab for severe recurrent disease.

name: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)
epi: Rare opportunistic brain infection in immunocompromised patients, mainly advanced HIV, hematologic malignancy and immunomodulatory therapies such as natalizumab or rituximab.
eti: Reactivation of latent JC polyomavirus, which infects and destroys oligodendrocytes, causing multifocal demyelination.
cli: Subacute progressive focal deficits such as hemiparesis, clumsiness, aphasia, dysarthria and visual field loss, with cognitive impairment; often fatal within months without immune recovery.
inv: MRI shows multifocal white matter lesions with little mass effect or enhancement; CSF PCR for JC virus DNA with compatible imaging is nearly diagnostic, with brain biopsy if needed.
tre: No specific antiviral; restore immunity by starting antiretroviral therapy in HIV or stopping immunosuppressants (plasma exchange to clear natalizumab), and monitor for IRIS.

name: Neurosyphilis
epi: CNS infection that can occur at any stage of syphilis, with higher risk in people with HIV; early forms occur within months to years and late forms 10-30 years after infection.
eti: Invasion of the central nervous system by Treponema pallidum, which may also involve the eye (ocular syphilis) and inner ear (otosyphilis).
cli: Early: meningitis, cranial nerve palsies, meningovascular stroke and altered mental status; late: general paresis (dementia, personality change) and tabes dorsalis (sensory ataxia, lightning pains, Argyll Robertson pupils).
inv: Serum treponemal and nontreponemal tests plus CSF examination in patients with neurologic signs; CSF pleocytosis, raised protein and reactive CSF VDRL (specific but insensitive) support the diagnosis.
tre: IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10-14 days, with procaine penicillin plus probenecid as an alternative, and follow-up serology to confirm response.

name: C3 Glomerulopathy (Dense Deposit Disease)
epi: Rare kidney disease affecting all ages, often diagnosed in adolescents and young adults, with equal sex distribution; subtypes are dense deposit disease (DDD) and C3 glomerulonephritis.
eti: Uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway due to complement gene variants (e.g. CFH, C3, CFI) or autoantibodies such as C3 nephritic factor, causing glomerular C3 deposition.
cli: Hematuria and proteinuria presenting as nephritic or nephrotic syndrome, hypertension and progressive CKD; associations include acquired partial lipodystrophy and retinal drusen.
inv: Low serum C3; kidney biopsy shows dominant C3 staining on immunofluorescence, with electron microscopy distinguishing dense intramembranous deposits (DDD) from C3GN; complement studies and genetic testing aid evaluation.
tre: Supportive care with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, blood pressure and lipid control, immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with mycophenolate for active disease, complement inhibitors in selected cases, and dialysis or transplant, where recurrence is common.

name: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
epi: Mainly affects young children, especially under 5, and is a leading cause of acute kidney injury in childhood; most cases follow Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection.
eti: Thrombotic microangiopathy most often from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (e.g. O157:H7); atypical HUS results from complement dysregulation, and some cases follow Streptococcus pneumoniae infection.
cli: Bloody diarrhea followed days later by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, with pallor, oliguria, edema and hypertension.
inv: Schistocytes on smear, thrombocytopenia, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, negative Coombs test (except pneumococcal HUS), raised creatinine, stool testing for STEC/Shiga toxin and ADAMTS13 to exclude TTP.
tre: Supportive care with fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion as needed and dialysis for severe AKI; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents in STEC-HUS, and use complement inhibitors such as eculizumab for atypical HUS.

name: Delirium Tremens
epi: Severe form of alcohol withdrawal occurring in a small minority of patients with alcohol withdrawal syndrome; mortality is low with prompt treatment.
eti: Abrupt cessation of heavy chronic alcohol use leaves reduced GABA activity and excess glutamate (NMDA) activity, producing CNS and autonomic hyperexcitability.
cli: Typically begins about 2-4 days or more after the last drink, with fluctuating delirium, disorientation, hallucinations, agitation, tremor, fever, tachycardia, hypertension and diaphoresis, sometimes with seizures.
inv: Clinical diagnosis using withdrawal scales such as CIWA-Ar; check electrolytes, magnesium, phosphate, glucose and liver function and exclude infection, head injury and other causes of delirium.
tre: Benzodiazepines are first-line, with phenobarbital as an adjunct for refractory cases; give IV thiamine before glucose, fluids and electrolyte replacement, and manage in a monitored or ICU setting.

name: Amniotic Fluid Embolism
epi: Rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency during labor, delivery or immediately postpartum, with high maternal mortality.
eti: Entry of fetal material into the maternal circulation triggers an anaphylactoid-like inflammatory cascade with vasoactive mediator release, rather than simple mechanical obstruction.
cli: Sudden hypoxia and respiratory distress, hypotension or cardiac arrest, and coagulopathy (DIC) with hemorrhage, often with seizures, altered mental status and fetal distress.
inv: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion based on the triad during labor or soon after delivery, ruling out PE, MI, anaphylaxis, sepsis and hemorrhage; coagulation studies and fibrinogen guide management.
tre: Immediate resuscitation with airway, oxygenation and CPR, vasopressors and fluid support, aggressive transfusion for DIC, and prompt delivery, including perimortem cesarean delivery if arrest persists.

name: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (Molar Pregnancy – hydatidiform mole)
epi: More common in Southeast Asia and at the extremes of maternal age, especially over 40 and in adolescents.
eti: Abnormal fertilization: complete mole is usually diploid with only paternal DNA (46,XX) from an empty ovum; partial mole is triploid (e.g. 69,XXY) from a normal ovum fertilized by two sperm.
cli: First-trimester vaginal bleeding, uterus larger than dates, hyperemesis, and less commonly hyperthyroidism, early-onset preeclampsia and theca lutein cysts.
inv: Markedly elevated serum beta-hCG and pelvic ultrasound showing a heterogeneous snowstorm or cystic pattern; histology of evacuated tissue confirms the diagnosis.
tre: Suction dilation and curettage, then serial hCG monitoring until undetectable with reliable contraception; persistent or rising hCG indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia requiring further treatment.

name: Congenital Toxoplasmosis
epi: Uncommon congenital infection; most infected newborns appear asymptomatic at birth but can develop late sequelae.
eti: Transplacental transmission of Toxoplasma gondii after primary maternal infection from undercooked meat or oocyst-contaminated food, water or cat feces; transmission is more likely later in pregnancy, but disease is more severe when earlier.
cli: Classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications, with seizures, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice and thrombocytopenia; late vision loss, hearing loss and developmental delay.
inv: Maternal serology (IgG, IgM, avidity), amniotic fluid PCR, infant IgM/IgA serology, cranial imaging for calcifications or hydrocephalus, ophthalmologic exam and CSF analysis.
tre: Spiramycin in pregnancy to reduce transmission; infected infants receive pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid for about a year.

name: Esophageal Perforation (Boerhaave Syndrome)
epi: Rare, life-threatening condition most common in middle-aged and older men, often associated with alcohol use or overeating.
eti: Spontaneous full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, typically the distal left posterolateral wall, from a sudden rise in intraesophageal pressure during forceful vomiting or retching.
cli: Severe retrosternal or upper abdominal pain after vomiting, with subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler triad, rarely complete), dyspnea, fever, sepsis and sometimes a mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign).
inv: Chest X-ray may show pneumomediastinum or pleural effusion; CT chest and water-soluble contrast esophagram confirm the leak, while barium is avoided initially.
tre: NPO, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, drainage of collections and nutritional support, with early surgical repair as the standard; endoscopic stenting is an option in selected patients.

name: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig Syndrome)
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive disorder of lipoprotein metabolism presenting in infancy.
eti: MTTP gene variants cause loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, preventing formation of apoB-containing lipoproteins and causing malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins.
cli: Steatorrhea and failure to thrive in infancy, acanthocytosis, and later vitamin E deficiency-related ataxia, peripheral neuropathy and retinitis pigmentosa, with bleeding tendency.
inv: Very low plasma cholesterol and triglycerides with absent apoB-containing lipoproteins, acanthocytes on blood smear, low fat-soluble vitamin levels, and MTTP genetic testing for confirmation.
tre: Low-fat diet with high-dose supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin E, plus monitoring for neurologic, ophthalmologic and liver complications.

name: Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose
epi: Less common than in the past but still a major cause of serious overdose, with higher hospitalization rates than SSRI overdose because of a narrow therapeutic margin.
eti: Fast sodium channel blockade, muscarinic anticholinergic effects, alpha-adrenergic blockade and potassium channel blockade cause cardiotoxicity, CNS toxicity and hypotension.
cli: Anticholinergic toxidrome (tachycardia, hyperthermia, dry skin, urinary retention, delirium), hypotension, seizures, coma and ventricular dysrhythmias, which may deteriorate rapidly.
inv: ECG is key: QRS widening and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR predict seizures and arrhythmias; check glucose, electrolytes, blood gas and acetaminophen/salicylate levels for co-ingestants.
tre: Airway and supportive care, IV sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, arrhythmias or hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, and avoidance of physostigmine and flumazenil.

name: Salicylate Toxicity
epi: Common poisoning from aspirin and other salicylates; overall mortality is low, but severe and chronic toxicity carry substantial risk, especially in older adults.
eti: Salicylates stimulate the respiratory center (respiratory alkalosis) and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, causing anion gap metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia and cellular energy failure.
cli: Tinnitus, nausea, vomiting and tachypnea early, progressing to confusion, hyperthermia, seizures, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, cerebral edema and cardiovascular collapse.
inv: Serial salicylate levels with arterial blood gas showing mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, plus electrolytes, glucose, lactate, renal function and ECG; the Done nomogram is unreliable.
tre: Activated charcoal when appropriate, IV fluids with glucose, sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize serum and urine, and hemodialysis for severe toxicity; intubation is hazardous and needs careful ventilatory management.

name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
epi: Uncommon ocular emergency whose incidence rises sharply with age, slightly more common in men, and regarded as a stroke equivalent.
eti: Most cases are nonarteritic, caused by emboli (often cholesterol from carotid atherosclerosis) or thrombosis; a minority are arteritic due to giant cell arteritis.
cli: Sudden, painless, severe monocular vision loss with relative afferent pupillary defect; fundoscopy shows retinal whitening, a cherry-red spot at the macula and sometimes visible emboli.
inv: Dilated fundoscopy, urgent ESR and CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis, and stroke workup including carotid imaging, ECG/cardiac monitoring and echocardiography.
tre: Urgent referral via a stroke pathway; no proven therapy restores vision, though thrombolysis may be considered in selected early cases; focus on secondary prevention of stroke and treat GCA with immediate steroids if suspected.

name: Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis)
epi: The most common systemic vasculitis in older adults, occurring almost exclusively over age 50, more often in women and people of Northern European descent.
eti: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches, especially cranial branches of the carotid artery, causing intimal thickening and luminal narrowing.
cli: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual disturbance or sudden vision loss, and constitutional symptoms; often overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica.
inv: Raised ESR and CRP; temporal artery biopsy remains the gold standard, with temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or other vascular imaging as alternatives.
tre: Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately on suspicion, without waiting for biopsy; tocilizumab is used as a steroid-sparing agent.

name: Ludwig Angina
epi: Uncommon but dangerous deep neck infection, often in adults with poor dental hygiene or recent dental procedures, that can obstruct the airway within hours.
eti: Rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually from infected second or third mandibular molars, caused by mixed aerobic and anaerobic oral flora.
cli: Fever, tooth pain, bilateral submandibular swelling with board-like floor of mouth, elevated tongue, drooling, dysphagia, trismus, muffled voice and stridor.
inv: Mainly clinical diagnosis; contrast CT of the neck confirms extent and abscess formation once the airway is secure.
tre: Airway protection first (fiberoptic intubation or tracheostomy), IV antibiotics covering oral flora such as ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin, and surgical drainage when needed.

name: Acute Compartment Syndrome
epi: Most often affects the lower leg and forearm, typically after fractures (especially tibial) or crush injuries, mainly in young men.
eti: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment from bleeding or edema due to fracture, crush injury, reperfusion, burns or constrictive casts compromises tissue perfusion.
cli: Pain out of proportion to the injury and worse with passive stretch, with a tense compartment; paresthesia, paralysis, pallor and pulselessness are late signs.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by compartment pressure measurement, comparing compartment pressure with diastolic pressure when the picture is unclear.
tre: Remove constrictive casts and dressings, keep the limb at heart level, correct hypotension, and perform urgent fasciotomy of all affected compartments.

name: Central Diabetes Insipidus
epi: Uncommon disorder that can occur at any age, often after pituitary surgery, head trauma or with sellar tumors.
eti: Deficient vasopressin (ADH) secretion from hypothalamic or posterior pituitary damage due to tumors, surgery, trauma, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, rare genetic causes, or idiopathic disease.
cli: Polyuria with large volumes of dilute urine, nocturia and polydipsia; hypernatremia and dehydration develop when water intake is limited.
inv: Low urine osmolality with high-normal or raised serum osmolality and sodium; water deprivation test with response to desmopressin, copeptin where available, and pituitary MRI to find the cause.
tre: Desmopressin is first-line, with free access to water and treatment of the underlying cause; monitor sodium to avoid hyponatremia.

name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
epi: Common, serious infection in patients with cirrhosis and ascites, with frequent recurrence without prophylaxis.
eti: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, usually from bacterial translocation from the gut, most often E. coli or Klebsiella, sometimes streptococci or enterococci.
cli: Often subtle: fever, abdominal pain or tenderness, encephalopathy, worsening liver or kidney function or unexplained deterioration; some patients are asymptomatic.
inv: Diagnostic paracentesis showing an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells/mcL or more, with culture by inoculating blood culture bottles at the bedside.
tre: Empiric third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime plus IV albumin to reduce hepatorenal syndrome, followed by long-term antibiotic prophylaxis after an episode.

name: Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis
epi: Life-threatening opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients, especially those with prolonged neutropenia, hematopoietic stem cell or organ transplants, or prolonged high-dose corticosteroids.
eti: Inhaled Aspergillus spores, most often A. fumigatus, evade impaired host defenses and invade lung tissue and blood vessels, with possible dissemination.
cli: Fever despite antibiotics, cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea and hemoptysis, which can progress to respiratory failure or spread to the brain and other organs.
inv: Chest CT showing nodules with halo sign or cavitation; serum and BAL galactomannan, Aspergillus PCR, culture and histopathology support the diagnosis.
tre: Prompt antifungal therapy with voriconazole or isavuconazole (posaconazole as another option), liposomal amphotericin B as an alternative, and reduction of immunosuppression where possible.

name: Botulism
epi: Rare but life-threatening; forms include foodborne (home-canned foods), infant (often linked to honey), wound (injection drug use) and iatrogenic botulism.
eti: Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin irreversibly blocks acetylcholine release at peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, causing neuromuscular paralysis.
cli: Symmetric cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia) followed by descending flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure, without sensory loss in an alert, usually afebrile patient; infants show constipation, poor feeding and floppiness.
inv: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by toxin assays of serum, stool, gastric contents or food; EMG shows an incremental response to rapid repetitive stimulation.
tre: Give botulinum antitoxin as early as possible (human botulism immune globulin for infants), provide ventilatory support and monitoring, and notify public health authorities urgently.

name: Takayasu Arteritis
epi: Rare large-vessel vasculitis that mainly affects young women, usually under 40, and is most common in Asia.
eti: Granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and its major branches (subclavian, carotid, renal) causes stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm.
cli: Early constitutional symptoms followed by limb claudication, weak or absent pulses, unequal arm blood pressures, bruits, hypertension from renal artery stenosis and neurologic or visual symptoms.
inv: Raised ESR and CRP (nonspecific); MR or CT angiography of the aorta and branches confirms the diagnosis, with PET helping assess activity.
tre: Glucocorticoids first-line, with steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, TNF inhibitors or tocilizumab, and revascularization for critical stenoses ideally when disease is quiescent.

name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)
epi: Uncommon overlap syndrome that predominantly affects women and occurs worldwide.
eti: Autoimmune disease of unknown cause with overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis and polymyositis, defined by high-titer anti-U1 RNP antibodies; some cases evolve into a classic connective tissue disease.
cli: Raynaud phenomenon, puffy swollen hands, polyarthritis, myositis, esophageal dysmotility, serositis and interstitial lung disease, with pulmonary hypertension the major cause of death.
inv: High-titer speckled ANA with very high anti-U1 RNP antibodies, usually without anti-Sm or anti-dsDNA; screen with echocardiography and pulmonary function tests for pulmonary hypertension and lung disease.
tre: Tailored to organ involvement: NSAIDs, hydroxychloroquine or low-dose glucocorticoids for mild disease, glucocorticoids with immunosuppressants for severe disease, and calcium channel blockers for Raynaud.

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
epi: Common cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in ICU patients, with high mortality that rises with severity.
eti: Diffuse inflammatory lung injury with increased capillary permeability from direct (pneumonia, aspiration, contusion) or indirect (sepsis, trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, burns) insults; sepsis and pneumonia cause most cases.
cli: Acute dyspnea, tachypnea and refractory hypoxemia within a week of the insult, with diffuse crackles, progressing to respiratory failure.
inv: Berlin criteria: onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities on imaging not explained by effusion or collapse, respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure, and PaO2/FiO2 ratio to grade severity.
tre: Treat the underlying cause; lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volumes, limited plateau pressure and appropriate PEEP, prone positioning for severe disease, conservative fluids, and ECMO as rescue.

name: Legionnaires Disease
epi: Pneumonia most common in older adults, smokers and immunocompromised people, often in outbreaks linked to contaminated water systems; it does not spread person to person.
eti: Inhalation of aerosolized water containing Legionella, mainly L. pneumophila serogroup 1, from cooling towers, plumbing, hot tubs and similar sources.
cli: Pneumonia with high fever, chills, myalgia, headache and cough, often with diarrhea, confusion, relative bradycardia and hyponatremia.
inv: Chest X-ray showing pneumonia; Legionella urinary antigen (detects serogroup 1), respiratory culture on special media and PCR.
tre: A respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin or azithromycin, with supportive care and public health notification for outbreak investigation.

name: Psittacosis
epi: Uncommon, reportable zoonosis occurring in people exposed to birds, such as pet bird owners, pet shop workers and poultry workers.
eti: Chlamydia psittaci, acquired mainly by inhaling dust from dried droppings or respiratory secretions of infected birds; human-to-human spread is very rare.
cli: After an incubation of about 1-2 weeks, abrupt fever, chills, severe headache, myalgia and dry cough, sometimes with pulse-temperature dissociation, splenomegaly or rash, and pneumonia.
inv: Chest X-ray may show lobar or interstitial infiltrates; diagnosis by nucleic acid amplification (PCR), serology or culture, with a history of bird exposure.
tre: Doxycycline first-line; macrolides for those in whom tetracyclines are contraindicated, such as young children and pregnant women.

name: Brucellosis
epi: Common zoonosis worldwide, mostly in people with occupational livestock exposure or who consume unpasteurized dairy; young adult men are most often affected.
eti: Brucella species (B. melitensis, B. abortus, B. suis, B. canis) acquired from unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat or direct contact with infected animals.
cli: Undulant or cyclical fever, sweats, fatigue, headache, arthralgia and myalgia; complications include sacroiliitis/spondylitis, orchitis, hepatic abscess, meningitis and endocarditis, the main cause of death.
inv: Blood or bone marrow culture (slow-growing) confirms diagnosis; serum agglutination serology and PCR support it; CBC may show anemia and neutropenia.
tre: Combination antibiotics to prevent relapse: doxycycline plus rifampin or an aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative partner, with longer regimens for spondylitis or endocarditis.

name: Q Fever
epi: Worldwide zoonosis; farmers, veterinarians and others with livestock exposure are at highest risk, and about half of infections are asymptomatic.
eti: Coxiella burnetii, usually acquired by inhaling contaminated dust or aerosols from infected animals, especially birth products of cattle, sheep and goats.
cli: Acute illness 2-3 weeks after exposure with fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia, cough, pneumonia or hepatitis; persistent (chronic) infection in a minority, most often culture-negative endocarditis.
inv: Serology (phase I and II antibodies) plus PCR of whole blood or serum early in illness, as early serology is often negative; treatment should not wait for confirmation.
tre: Doxycycline is first-line for acute Q fever; persistent infection such as endocarditis needs prolonged doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine with specialist input.

name: Tularemia
epi: Rare zoonosis of the Northern Hemisphere; in the US it is linked to tick and deer fly bites and to handling infected rabbits or rodents.
eti: Francisella tularensis, transmitted by tick or deer fly bites, contact with infected animals, contaminated food or water, or inhaled aerosols; a potential bioterrorism agent.
cli: Abrupt fever, chills, headache and malaise; forms include ulceroglandular (skin ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy), glandular, oculoglandular, oropharyngeal, pneumonic and typhoidal.
inv: Diagnosis by culture, PCR and serology; the laboratory must be warned when tularemia is suspected because the organism is a laboratory biohazard.
tre: Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or doxycycline for mild to moderate disease; gentamicin (or streptomycin), often with a fluoroquinolone, for severe disease.

name: Anthrax (Inhalational)
epi: Rarest but deadliest form of anthrax; occurs after occupational exposure to contaminated animal products or bioterrorism, with no person-to-person spread.
eti: Inhaled Bacillus anthracis spores are carried to mediastinal lymph nodes, where they germinate and release toxins causing hemorrhagic mediastinitis and sepsis.
cli: Biphasic illness: nonspecific flu-like prodrome with fever, cough and chest discomfort, then rapid dyspnea, stridor, shock and respiratory failure; meningitis is common.
inv: Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum and pleural effusions; CT shows enlarged hilar/mediastinal nodes; blood, pleural fluid and CSF culture or PCR confirm diagnosis.
tre: Urgent combination IV antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin plus a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or linezolid), with antitoxin (monoclonal antibodies or anthrax immune globulin), pleural drainage and ICU support.

name: Plague (Bubonic/Pneumonic)
epi: Most cases occur in Africa, especially Madagascar and Central/East Africa; rare in the US, where cases cluster in southwestern states.
eti: Yersinia pestis, a gram-negative bacillus spread from rodent reservoirs by flea bites, by handling infected animals, or person to person by respiratory droplets in pneumonic plague.
cli: Bubonic: sudden fever, chills and a painful swollen regional lymph node (bubo); pneumonic: high fever, cough, chest pain and hemoptysis with rapid progression and high mortality.
inv: Gram stain and culture of bubo aspirate, blood or sputum, F1 antigen rapid testing and PCR; CBC often shows leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia.
tre: Prompt empiric aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin); doxycycline or fluoroquinolones as alternatives; droplet precautions for pneumonic plague and doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts.

name: Melioidosis
epi: Endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia and emerging elsewhere; cases rise after heavy rain and flooding. Diabetes is the main risk factor.
eti: Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from soil or freshwater by skin inoculation, inhalation or ingestion; other risks include alcohol use, renal or liver disease and immunosuppression.
cli: Wide range from pneumonia (most common) with fever and cough to localized abscesses or ulcers and fulminant septicemia; chronic or latent infection can reactivate.
inv: Culture of blood, sputum, urine, pus or other fluids is the diagnostic standard; serology is supportive; imaging looks for liver, spleen and prostate abscesses.
tre: Intensive phase IV ceftazidime or meropenem, then a prolonged eradication phase of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline as alternatives) to prevent relapse.

name: Chagas Disease
epi: Endemic in rural Central and South America, affecting millions of people; cases occur elsewhere in Latin American migrants.
eti: Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted mainly by feces of triatomine (kissing) bugs entering wounds or mucosa, and also congenitally, by blood transfusion, organ transplant or contaminated food.
cli: Acute phase often mild with fever, lymphadenopathy and Romana sign (unilateral eyelid swelling); chronic disease in a minority causes cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, megaesophagus and megacolon.
inv: Acute: parasites on blood smear or PCR; chronic: IgG serology using two different tests; ECG, chest X-ray and echocardiography for cardiac involvement.
tre: Antiparasitic benznidazole or nifurtimox, most effective in acute and early infection; manage heart failure, arrhythmias and GI complications supportively.

name: Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar)
epi: Most cases occur in East Africa (Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia), South Asia (India) and Brazil; it is fatal if untreated.
eti: Leishmania donovani or L. infantum, spread by female sand fly bites; parasites infect macrophages of the spleen, liver and bone marrow.
cli: Prolonged fever, weight loss, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and pancytopenia with hypergammaglobulinemia; skin may darken, and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis can follow.
inv: Amastigotes on bone marrow or splenic aspirate (splenic aspirate risks bleeding), culture, PCR, and rK39 rapid serology in endemic areas.
tre: Liposomal amphotericin B, or regional regimens such as sodium stibogluconate plus paromomycin in East Africa; miltefosine is an oral alternative.

name: Cholangiocarcinoma
epi: Uncommon cancer that peaks in ages 50-70 and is slightly more common in men; much more frequent in Southeast Asia because of liver flukes.
eti: Malignancy of the bile duct epithelium (intrahepatic, perihilar or distal); risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver flukes, choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis and chronic liver disease.
cli: Extrahepatic tumors cause painless obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine and pale stools; intrahepatic tumors present late with abdominal pain, weight loss and fatigue.
inv: CA 19-9 is supportive but nonspecific; MRI/MRCP and CT for staging and resectability; tissue by ERCP brushings or EUS-guided biopsy when feasible.
tre: Surgical resection with negative margins is the only cure; advanced disease gets gemcitabine plus cisplatin with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (durvalumab or pembrolizumab), plus biliary stenting for palliation.

name: Acute Liver Failure (Fulminant Hepatic Failure)
epi: Rare; acetaminophen and other drugs predominate in high-income countries, whereas viral hepatitis predominates where sanitation is poor.
eti: Massive hepatocyte injury without prior liver disease, from acetaminophen, idiosyncratic drug reactions, hepatitis A, B or E, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, Budd-Chiari or ischemia; often idiopathic.
cli: Jaundice, coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without prior liver disease, with risk of cerebral edema, infection, hypoglycemia, renal failure and hypotension.
inv: Prolonged INR (at least 1.5) with raised transaminases and bilirubin; ammonia, acetaminophen level, viral and autoimmune serology and toxicology; head CT if mental status worsens.
tre: ICU supportive care at a transplant center, N-acetylcysteine (for acetaminophen and also other causes), management of cerebral edema and organ failure, and urgent liver transplantation evaluation.

name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
epi: Most common inherited (monogenic) heart disease; symptoms usually begin between the 30s and 50s, and it is a recognized cause of sudden death in young athletes.
eti: Mostly autosomal dominant sarcomere gene variants (MYH7, MYBPC3) causing unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric septal, with or without outflow obstruction.
cli: Exertional dyspnea, angina-like chest pain, palpitations and syncope; systolic murmur that gets louder with Valsalva or standing and softer with squatting; risk of arrhythmia and sudden death.
