inv: Echocardiography shows LV wall thickening and any outflow obstruction; ECG shows LVH and repolarization changes; cardiac MRI assesses fibrosis; genetic testing helps cascade family screening.
tre: Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers first line; cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten) or disopyramide for obstruction; septal myectomy or alcohol ablation if refractory; ICD for high-risk patients; avoid dehydration and vasodilators.

name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
epi: Least common type of cardiomyopathy; cardiac amyloidosis is the most frequent cause in developed countries, whereas endomyocardial fibrosis occurs mainly in the tropics.
eti: Stiff, poorly filling ventricles from infiltrative disease (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), storage disease (hemochromatosis, Fabry), endomyocardial disease (endomyocardial fibrosis, hypereosinophilic syndrome, carcinoid) or idiopathic causes.
cli: Heart failure with fatigue, exertional dyspnea, raised JVP with rapid y-descent, peripheral edema, ascites and hepatomegaly; atrial fibrillation is common.
inv: Echocardiography shows non-dilated ventricles with preserved EF, biatrial enlargement and diastolic dysfunction; cardiac MRI characterizes tissue; catheterization and endomyocardial biopsy distinguish it from constrictive pericarditis and define the cause.
tre: Treat the underlying cause (e.g. amyloid- or sarcoid-specific therapy, iron chelation, enzyme replacement); careful diuretics, management of atrial fibrillation with anticoagulation, and heart transplant for advanced disease.

name: Myocarditis
epi: Inflammatory heart muscle disease that mostly affects people under 40; probably underdiagnosed because presentations vary widely.
eti: Most often viral (coxsackievirus, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, SARS-CoV-2); also bacteria, Trypanosoma cruzi, autoimmune disease, drugs (immune checkpoint inhibitors), hypersensitivity, giant cell myocarditis and sarcoidosis.
cli: Often follows a viral illness, with chest pain, dyspnea, fatigue and palpitations; can progress to heart failure, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock (fulminant form) or sudden death.
inv: Elevated troponin, ECG ST-T changes, echocardiography for function, cardiac MRI using Lake Louise criteria, and endomyocardial biopsy for definitive or etiologic diagnosis in selected cases.
tre: Supportive care with standard heart failure and arrhythmia therapy, mechanical circulatory support if fulminant, avoidance of competitive exercise for several months, and immunosuppression for giant cell, eosinophilic or autoimmune forms.

name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A (MEN 2A)
epi: Rare autosomal dominant syndrome that accounts for most MEN2 cases; a minority arise from new mutations.
eti: Germline gain-of-function RET proto-oncogene mutations, classically in the cysteine-rich domain (codon 634 most common).
cli: Medullary thyroid carcinoma in nearly all patients, pheochromocytoma (often bilateral) in up to half, and primary hyperparathyroidism; some have cutaneous lichen amyloidosis or Hirschsprung disease.
inv: RET genetic testing of patients and relatives; serum calcitonin and CEA; plasma free or fractionated metanephrines; serum calcium and PTH; neck ultrasound.
tre: Prophylactic total thyroidectomy timed by RET codon risk; exclude or remove pheochromocytoma (adrenalectomy after alpha-blockade) before thyroid surgery; parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism.

name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN 2B)
epi: Very rare MEN2 subtype; most cases are de novo mutations.
eti: Germline RET mutation, usually M918T in the tyrosine kinase domain, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
cli: Very early, aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of lips and tongue, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis and marfanoid habitus; hyperparathyroidism is not a feature.
inv: RET genetic testing, serum calcitonin and CEA, plasma metanephrines, and neck ultrasound; the distinctive phenotype helps identify de novo cases.
tre: Total thyroidectomy in the first year of life for carriers, with pheochromocytoma excluded or treated first; RET-targeted kinase inhibitors (selpercatinib, pralsetinib) are used for advanced MTC.

name: Fatal Familial Insomnia
epi: Extremely rare inherited prion disease, usually beginning in middle age and fatal within months to a few years.
eti: Autosomal dominant PRNP D178N mutation with methionine at codon 129 on the same allele, causing prion deposition and neuronal loss mainly in the thalamus.
cli: Progressive, intractable insomnia with loss of normal sleep, autonomic overactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, hyperthermia), dysautonomia, ataxia, myoclonus and cognitive decline.
inv: Polysomnography shows loss of sleep spindles and markedly reduced sleep; PET shows thalamic hypometabolism; PRNP genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: No cure; supportive and palliative care, symptom management and genetic counseling for families.

name: Stiff-Person Syndrome
epi: Rare autoimmune neurologic disorder, about twice as common in women and usually starting in midlife.
eti: Autoantibodies, chiefly anti-GAD65, reduce GABA-mediated inhibition; associated with type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity; paraneoplastic forms (anti-amphiphysin) occur with breast and lung cancer.
cli: Progressive axial and proximal limb muscle rigidity with lumbar hyperlordosis, painful spasms triggered by noise, touch or emotion, exaggerated startle, falls and anxiety.
inv: High-titer anti-GAD65 antibodies; EMG shows continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles; search for malignancy in antibody-positive paraneoplastic cases.
tre: Symptomatic GABAergic drugs (diazepam and other benzodiazepines, baclofen) plus immunotherapy such as IVIG; rituximab or plasma exchange in selected cases; treat any underlying tumor.

name: Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis
epi: Rare post-infectious autoimmune disorder affecting children and adults; it is part of the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome spectrum with Miller Fisher syndrome.
eti: Post-infectious (often respiratory or Campylobacter) immune response with anti-GQ1b antibodies targeting brainstem and cranial nerve structures.
cli: Acute progressive ophthalmoplegia and ataxia with impaired consciousness or hyperreflexia; may overlap with Guillain-Barre syndrome limb weakness.
inv: Serum anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies in most patients; MRI may show brainstem lesions but is often normal; CSF may show protein elevation; EEG may show slowing.
tre: Supportive care with airway monitoring; immunotherapy with IVIG or plasma exchange is commonly used; prognosis is usually good.

name: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)
epi: Rare, fatal late complication of wild-type measles, appearing years after infection, usually in children or adolescents; risk is highest after measles in early childhood.
eti: Persistent defective measles virus infection of the CNS causing progressive inflammation and demyelination; measles vaccine strains do not cause it.
cli: Staged decline: behavioral change and intellectual deterioration, then periodic myoclonus and seizures, then extrapyramidal signs and spasticity, ending in akinetic mutism and death; chorioretinitis may occur.
inv: Raised measles antibody titers in CSF (with high CSF-to-serum ratio); EEG shows periodic high-voltage complexes (Radermecker complexes); MRI shows white matter changes and atrophy.
tre: No cure; inosine pranobex with intrathecal interferon may slow progression in some; antiseizure and supportive care; prevention through measles vaccination.

name: Huntington Disease
epi: Autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, more prevalent in people of European ancestry, with onset usually between ages 30 and 50.
eti: Expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, with anticipation (especially via paternal transmission) and striatal (caudate) neuronal loss.
cli: Chorea that later becomes rigidity and dystonia, with dysarthria and dysphagia; psychiatric symptoms (depression, irritability, apathy) often come first; progressive subcortical dementia.
inv: Genetic testing for HTT CAG repeat length confirms diagnosis; MRI may show caudate atrophy; predictive testing requires genetic counseling.
tre: Symptomatic: VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) for chorea, antipsychotics and SSRIs for psychiatric symptoms, plus multidisciplinary therapy and genetic counseling; no disease-modifying therapy.

name: Dunbars Syndrome (Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome / MALS)
epi: Rare; most common in thin women aged 30-50, although radiographic celiac compression without symptoms is far more frequent.
eti: Compression of the celiac artery (and possibly celiac plexus) by the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm, worse on expiration.
cli: Postprandial epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, food fear and weight loss; an epigastric bruit that varies with respiration may be heard.
inv: Duplex ultrasound shows raised celiac artery velocities on expiration; CT or MR angiography shows focal proximal celiac narrowing with a hooked appearance and post-stenotic dilatation; other causes should be excluded.
tre: Surgical division of the median arcuate ligament (often laparoscopic), often with celiac ganglionectomy, plus celiac artery revascularization if stenosis persists.

name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Type II / Perinatal Lethal)
epi: Most severe form of osteogenesis imperfecta; usually there is no family history because it arises from new mutations.
eti: Usually de novo dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 producing structurally abnormal type I collagen; parental germline mosaicism gives a recurrence risk.
cli: Multiple fractures in utero and at birth, short crumpled long bones, beaded ribs, a soft poorly mineralized skull, dark blue sclerae, and a small chest with underdeveloped lungs causing fatal respiratory failure.
inv: Prenatal ultrasound shows short, fractured, poorly mineralized bones; postnatal skeletal radiographs; COL1A1/COL1A2 molecular testing confirms diagnosis and guides counseling.
tre: Mainly palliative and comfort care, given death in the perinatal period, with genetic counseling about recurrence risk for future pregnancies.

name: Prader-Willi Syndrome
epi: Occurs in roughly 1 in 20,000-30,000 births, equally in males and females; it is the most common genetic cause of life-threatening obesity.
eti: Loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13 from paternal deletion (most), maternal uniparental disomy or an imprinting defect.
cli: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, then hyperphagia and obesity from early childhood, short stature, hypogonadism, almond-shaped eyes, intellectual disability, skin picking and obsessive behaviors.
inv: DNA methylation analysis detects nearly all cases; FISH, chromosomal microarray or UPD studies define the mechanism; endocrine and sleep evaluation.
tre: Multidisciplinary care: growth hormone therapy, strict food security and calorie control, sex hormone replacement, behavioral and psychiatric support; diazoxide choline is approved for hyperphagia.

name: Williams Syndrome
epi: Occurs in roughly 1 in 7,500-20,000 births, affecting both sexes and all ethnicities; most cases are sporadic.
eti: Microdeletion at chromosome 7q11.23 including the elastin (ELN) gene, with autosomal dominant transmission from affected individuals.
cli: Elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis and other arterial stenoses, infantile hypercalcemia, intellectual disability with visuospatial weakness, and an overly friendly 'cocktail party' personality.
inv: FISH or chromosomal microarray confirms the 7q11.23 deletion; echocardiography, serum calcium, thyroid function and developmental assessment.
tre: Multidisciplinary care: cardiac surgery for significant stenosis, avoidance of extra calcium and vitamin D for hypercalcemia, developmental and educational support, and regular surveillance.

name: Xeroderma Pigmentosum
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder, about 1 per million in the US and Europe, more common in Japan, North Africa and the Middle East.
eti: Mutations in nucleotide excision repair genes (XPA, XPC, ERCC2 and others) or POLH prevent repair of UV-induced DNA damage.
cli: Severe sunburn after minimal sun, early freckling, dry pigmented skin, and nonmelanoma skin cancers and melanoma in childhood; photophobia and keratitis; progressive neurodegeneration in some.
inv: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by molecular genetic testing of XP genes; cellular DNA repair assays; regular skin, eye and neurologic examination.
tre: Strict lifelong UV protection (clothing, sunscreen, UV-filtering windows), frequent skin surveillance with early excision of premalignant and malignant lesions, and eye protection.

name: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex
epi: Most common type of inherited epidermolysis bullosa, accounting for about 70% of cases.
eti: Mostly autosomal dominant KRT5 or KRT14 mutations (keratins 5/14) causing a split within the basal epidermis; rarer genes include PLEC.
cli: Friction-induced blisters, often on hands and feet, that usually heal without scarring; palmoplantar keratoderma and nail changes; severe generalized forms present at birth.
inv: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping and/or electron microscopy shows intraepidermal cleavage; genetic testing confirms the subtype.
tre: Supportive: avoid trauma and overheating, lance and dress blisters with non-adhesive dressings, prevent and treat infection, and give pain and podiatric care.

name: Epidermolysis Bullosa Dystrophica (Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa)
epi: Rare, severe subtype of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, which makes up about a quarter of inherited EB cases.
eti: Biallelic COL7A1 mutations cause loss of type VII collagen anchoring fibrils, with blistering below the lamina densa.
cli: Generalized blistering from birth with severe scarring, pseudosyndactyly (mitten hands), nail loss, microstomia, esophageal strictures, anemia, growth failure and a very high risk of aggressive cutaneous SCC.
inv: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence mapping (reduced or absent collagen VII) and/or electron microscopy; COL7A1 genetic testing.
tre: Multidisciplinary wound care, nutrition, pain control and esophageal dilation; topical gene therapy beremagene geperpavec and birch triterpene gel for wounds; regular SCC surveillance with early excision.

name: Netherton Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive ichthyosis, estimated at about 1 in 200,000 newborns.
eti: SPINK5 mutations cause loss of the serine protease inhibitor LEKTI, leading to excessive epidermal protease activity and a defective skin barrier.
cli: Triad of congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma or ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, bamboo hair (trichorrhexis invaginata) and atopy (eczema, food allergy, asthma, high IgE); neonatal hypernatremic dehydration, infections and failure to thrive.
inv: Hair microscopy shows trichorrhexis invaginata; skin biopsy with LEKTI immunostaining; SPINK5 genetic testing; IgE and eosinophils are often raised.
tre: Supportive: emollients and barrier care, neonatal fluid, electrolyte and temperature management, infection treatment, and caution with topical drugs because absorption is increased (e.g. tacrolimus); biologics are being studied.

name: Incontinentia Pigmenti (Bloch-Sulzberger Syndrome)
epi: Rare X-linked dominant genodermatosis seen almost exclusively in females, since it is usually lethal in males in utero.
eti: Mutations in IKBKG (NEMO) impair NF-kB signaling, making cells prone to apoptosis in ectodermal tissues.
cli: Four overlapping skin stages along Blaschko lines (vesicular, verrucous, whorled hyperpigmentation, atrophic hypopigmentation) plus dental anomalies, alopecia, nail dystrophy, retinal vasculopathy and seizures.
inv: Clinical criteria, skin biopsy (eosinophilic spongiosis in vesicular stage) and IKBKG genetic testing; early and repeated retinal exams and neurologic assessment.
tre: Multidisciplinary care: skin wound care, retinal surveillance with laser treatment for neovascularization, dental care, seizure management and genetic counseling.

name: Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis; only a few hundred cases have been described.
eti: Biallelic RECQL4 helicase mutations (type 2) or ANAPC1 mutations (type 1).
cli: Facial rash in infancy that becomes poikiloderma, sparse hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, short stature, radial ray and skeletal defects, juvenile cataracts (type 1), and osteosarcoma (type 2) and skin cancer risk.
inv: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by RECQL4 or ANAPC1 molecular testing; skeletal radiographs; prompt imaging for bone pain or swelling.
tre: Sun protection, pulsed dye laser for telangiectasias, yearly skin and eye exams, cataract surgery, and standard osteosarcoma therapy when it occurs.

name: Kindler Syndrome
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive form of epidermolysis bullosa, with a few hundred cases reported worldwide.
eti: Biallelic FERMT1 mutations cause loss of kindlin-1, impairing keratinocyte adhesion with variable levels of skin cleavage.
cli: Acral blistering from infancy that improves with age, photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma and skin atrophy, gingivitis, esophageal and urethral strictures, colitis, and increased SCC risk.
inv: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence mapping showing reduced kindlin-1, and FERMT1 genetic testing for confirmation.
tre: Supportive: blister and wound care, strict sun protection, dental and periodontal care, esophageal dilation when needed, and regular skin and mucosal surveillance for SCC.

name: Pachyonychia Congenita
epi: Very rare autosomal dominant keratin disorder; about a third of cases arise from new mutations.
eti: Heterozygous mutations in keratin genes KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT6C, KRT16 or KRT17 cause fragile keratinocytes in nails, palms, soles and mucosa.
cli: Thickened, dystrophic nails, painful plantar keratoderma with blistering, oral leukokeratosis, pilosebaceous cysts, follicular keratoses and hyperhidrosis; natal teeth occur with KRT17 variants.
inv: Clinical diagnosis based on toenail thickening, plantar keratoderma and plantar pain, confirmed by molecular testing of the keratin genes.
tre: Symptomatic: regular paring and grooming of calluses and nails, emollients and keratolytics, cushioned footwear, infection prevention and pain management.

name: Olmsted Syndrome
epi: Extremely rare genodermatosis, usually beginning in early childhood, with cases reported worldwide.
eti: Most cases are caused by gain-of-function TRPV3 mutations (usually autosomal dominant or de novo); rarer X-linked cases involve MBTPS2.
cli: Painful, mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma with periorificial keratotic plaques around the mouth, nose and anus; may have digital constriction, nail dystrophy, alopecia and severe itch.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by skin biopsy, confirmed by TRPV3 or MBTPS2 genetic testing.
tre: Symptomatic: emollients, keratolytics, topical or systemic retinoids, and pain and itch control; EGFR inhibitors such as erlotinib have shown benefit in case reports.

name: Darier Disease (Keratosis Follicularis)
epi: Uncommon autosomal dominant skin disorder that usually starts in late childhood or adolescence; reported prevalence ranges from about 1 in 30,000 to 1 in 100,000.
eti: ATP2A2 mutations reduce SERCA2 calcium pump function, impairing keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis with dyskeratosis).
cli: Greasy, warty, yellow-brown papules in seborrheic areas (scalp, chest, back), worse with heat, sweat, UV and friction; red and white longitudinal nail bands with V-shaped notches, palmar pits and oral papules.
inv: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by skin biopsy showing suprabasal acantholysis with dyskeratosis (corps ronds and grains); ATP2A2 genetic testing if needed.
tre: Avoid triggers (heat, sweating, sun); emollients, topical retinoids or corticosteroids, treatment of secondary infection, and oral retinoids (acitretin, isotretinoin) for severe disease.

name: Hailey-Hailey Disease (Familial Benign Pemphigus)
epi: Rare autosomal dominant blistering disorder affecting both sexes equally, usually beginning in adolescence or early adulthood.
eti: ATP2C1 mutations impair the Golgi calcium pump SPCA1, causing loss of keratinocyte adhesion; flares are triggered by friction, heat, sweating and infection.
cli: Recurrent painful vesicles, erosions and macerated fissured plaques in flexures (neck, axillae, groin, perineum); longitudinal white nail bands; chronic relapsing course.
inv: Skin biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis with a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance and negative direct immunofluorescence; swabs for secondary infection.
tre: Reduce friction and sweating; topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors and topical or oral antibiotics; options for refractory disease include botulinum toxin, laser and procedural therapies.

name: Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (Günther Disease)
epi: Ultra-rare porphyria, usually presenting at birth or in infancy.
eti: Autosomal recessive UROS deficiency (rarely X-linked GATA1) causes buildup of type I porphyrins that are phototoxic and cause hemolysis.
cli: Pink-red urine in infancy, severe blistering photosensitivity with scarring and photomutilation, hypertrichosis, erythrodontia, hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly and corneal scarring.
inv: Markedly raised uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I in urine and erythrocytes; teeth fluoresce under UV light; UROS or GATA1 genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: Strict sun and visible-light protection, wound care, transfusions to suppress erythropoiesis with iron chelation, vitamin D supplementation, and hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation as the only cure.

name: Wolfram-like Mitochondrial Encephalopathy
epi: Very rare; it is the nonclassic, usually milder autosomal dominant part of the WFS1 spectrum.
eti: Heterozygous (often de novo) WFS1 mutations affecting wolframin, an endoplasmic reticulum protein; classic Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) is autosomal recessive.
cli: Variable combination of sensorineural hearing loss, optic atrophy and diabetes mellitus (including neonatal diabetes) or cataracts, typically without the progressive neurodegeneration of classic Wolfram syndrome.
inv: Molecular genetic testing for a heterozygous WFS1 pathogenic variant; audiology, ophthalmologic exam and glucose testing to define the phenotype.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care: hearing aids or cochlear implants, diabetes management, visual support, phenotype-based surveillance and genetic counseling.

name: Cockayne Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder; type I appears in early childhood, type II (most severe) at birth, and type III later and milder.
eti: Mutations in ERCC6 (CSB) or ERCC8 (CSA) impair transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair.
cli: Growth failure ('cachectic dwarfism'), microcephaly, progressive neurologic decline with demyelination, photosensitivity, sunken eyes, pigmentary retinopathy, cataracts and sensorineural hearing loss; no increased skin cancer risk.
inv: ERCC6/ERCC8 genetic testing; brain MRI shows white matter changes and calcification; ophthalmologic exam, electroretinography and audiometry.
tre: Supportive: sun protection, nutritional support, physical and occupational therapy, hearing and vision aids; life expectancy is reduced, especially in type II.

name: Trichothiodystrophy
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive disorder, about 1 per million newborns in the US and Europe.
eti: Mutations in at least 10 genes; the photosensitive form involves ERCC2, ERCC3 or GTF2H5 (TFIIH), impairing DNA repair and transcription.
cli: Brittle, sparse, sulfur-deficient hair, ichthyosis, photosensitivity in about half (without increased skin cancer), intellectual disability, short stature, cataracts and recurrent infections.
inv: Polarized light microscopy shows 'tiger tail' alternating light and dark hair banding; low hair sulfur and cysteine content; genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care: sun protection for photosensitive forms, skin care, prompt treatment of infections, developmental support and cataract management.

name: Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive chromosomal instability disorder, most common in Slavic populations because of a founder NBN deletion.
eti: Biallelic NBN mutations (mostly c.657_661del5) cause loss of nibrin, impairing DNA double-strand break repair and causing radiosensitivity.
cli: Progressive microcephaly, sloping forehead and prominent midface, growth deficiency, combined immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, very high lymphoma risk, declining cognition and premature ovarian failure.
inv: NBN genetic testing and/or absent nibrin on immunoblot; chromosome breakage and radiosensitivity studies; immunoglobulin and lymphocyte subset assessment.
tre: Avoid ionizing radiation; immunoglobulin replacement and infection prophylaxis, no live vaccines, modified chemotherapy for malignancy, hormone replacement, and HSCT consideration.

name: Werner Syndrome (Adult Progeria)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive adult-onset progeroid syndrome, more common in Japan than in the US.
eti: Biallelic WRN mutations disable a RecQ helicase involved in DNA replication and repair, causing genomic instability.
cli: Absent pubertal growth spurt, then from the 20s premature graying and hair loss, scleroderma-like skin and leg ulcers, bilateral cataracts, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, hypogonadism, early atherosclerosis and cancers.
inv: Clinical criteria with WRN molecular genetic testing for confirmation; screening for diabetes, dyslipidemia, cataracts and malignancy.
tre: No cure; manage diabetes, lipids and cardiovascular risk, cataract surgery, skin ulcer care and cancer surveillance; death usually comes from atherosclerosis or cancer in the 40s to 50s.

name: Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome
epi: Extremely rare, about 1 in 4 million newborns; nearly always sporadic.
eti: De novo dominant LMNA mutation (usually c.1824C>T) creates progerin, an abnormal lamin A that destabilizes the nuclear envelope.
cli: Normal at birth, then in early childhood failure to thrive, alopecia, aged thin skin, prominent scalp veins, small jaw, joint stiffness and lipodystrophy, with normal intelligence; accelerated atherosclerosis causes stroke and heart attack.
inv: Clinical suspicion confirmed by LMNA genetic testing; cardiovascular monitoring with echocardiography, ECG and carotid imaging.
tre: Farnesyltransferase inhibitor lonafarnib to extend survival, plus supportive cardiovascular care (often low-dose aspirin), nutrition, physical therapy and dental care.

name: Aarskog-Scott Syndrome (Faciodigital Syndrome)
epi: Rare disorder seen mainly in males; true prevalence is unknown because mild cases go undiagnosed.
eti: X-linked recessive FGD1 mutations affecting Cdc42 signaling in some cases; many have no identified FGD1 variant.
cli: Short stature, hypertelorism, small nose with long philtrum and widow's peak, short broad hands with clinodactyly and mild webbing, and shawl scrotum with cryptorchidism; intelligence usually normal.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by FGD1 molecular testing; skeletal survey, cardiac and genitourinary assessment as indicated.
tre: Supportive: orchiopexy and hernia repair, orthodontic and orthopedic care, educational support if needed and genetic counseling.

name: Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1A (Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy)
epi: Rare inherited disorder of end-organ PTH resistance, usually recognized in childhood.
eti: Maternally inherited inactivating GNAS mutations reduce Gs-alpha signaling, causing PTH resistance (and resistance to TSH and other hormones) plus Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
cli: Hypocalcemia symptoms (tetany, seizures), short stature, round face, obesity, short fourth and fifth metacarpals, subcutaneous ossification and developmental delay; may have hypothyroidism and hypogonadism.
inv: Low calcium and high phosphate despite high PTH, with blunted urinary cAMP response to PTH; screen thyroid and other hormones; GNAS genetic or methylation testing.
tre: Oral calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol) to normalize calcium and lower PTH, plus treatment of other hormone deficiencies (e.g. levothyroxine) and monitoring for obesity.

name: McCune-Albright Syndrome
epi: Rare sporadic disorder with estimated prevalence between 1 in 100,000 and 1 in 1,000,000; not inherited.
eti: Postzygotic activating GNAS mutation causes mosaic constitutive Gs-alpha signaling with increased intracellular cAMP in affected tissues.
cli: Classic triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, peripheral precocious puberty and jagged-border café-au-lait macules; may include hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, phosphate wasting or Cushing syndrome.
inv: Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by radiographs or CT of bone lesions and endocrine hormone testing; GNAS testing may be falsely negative because of mosaicism.
tre: Treat each endocrinopathy (aromatase inhibitors or tamoxifen for peripheral precocious puberty, antithyroid therapy, somatostatin analogs); surgery for fracture or deformity and bisphosphonates for bone pain.

name: Bartter Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive salt-wasting tubulopathy, estimated around 1 per million; antenatal forms present prenatally, classic forms in early childhood.
eti: Mutations in SLC12A1, KCNJ1, CLCNKB, BSND or CLCNKA/CLCNKB impair thick ascending limb salt reabsorption, mimicking loop diuretic effect.
cli: Polyhydramnios and prematurity in antenatal forms; polyuria, dehydration, failure to thrive, hypokalemic muscle weakness, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis; BSND forms have sensorineural deafness.
inv: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with normal blood pressure, high renin and aldosterone, and elevated urinary chloride and calcium; genetic testing confirms subtype.
tre: Lifelong potassium and salt replacement with fluids, NSAIDs such as indomethacin to reduce prostaglandin-driven salt wasting, and potassium-sparing agents in selected patients under specialist care.

name: Gitelman Syndrome
epi: Autosomal recessive tubulopathy affecting an estimated 1 in 40,000 people; usually presents in late childhood, adolescence or adulthood.
eti: Mostly SLC12A3 mutations (less often CLCNKB) impair the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, mimicking thiazide effect.
cli: Muscle cramps, weakness, tetany, paresthesias, fatigue, salt craving and low-normal blood pressure; chondrocalcinosis and ventricular arrhythmia risk; often mild.
inv: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria, normal blood pressure and high renin; genetic testing confirms diagnosis.
tre: Liberal salt intake with oral potassium and magnesium supplementation; potassium-sparing diuretics may be added in selected cases.

name: Liddle Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal dominant cause of early-onset hypertension with no racial or sex predilection; likely underdiagnosed among young patients with resistant hypertension.
eti: Gain-of-function mutations in ENaC subunit genes SCNN1A, SCNN1B or SCNN1G prevent channel degradation, increasing distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
cli: Early-onset, often resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; muscle weakness, polyuria and arrhythmia risk when hypokalemia is severe.
inv: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with low or normal plasma renin and aldosterone (pseudohyperaldosteronism); genetic testing of ENaC genes confirms diagnosis.
tre: ENaC blockers such as amiloride or triamterene with dietary sodium restriction; spironolactone is ineffective because aldosterone is low.

name: Dent Disease
epi: Rare X-linked proximal tubulopathy, about 250 families reported and likely underdiagnosed; affects males, while female carriers are usually asymptomatic.
eti: Pathogenic variants in CLCN5 (Dent disease 1) or OCRL (Dent disease 2) impair proximal tubule endocytosis.
cli: Low-molecular-weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, hematuria, hypophosphatemia and rickets; progressive CKD, often reaching ESRD in mid-adulthood.
inv: Urine low-molecular-weight proteins (e.g., beta2-microglobulin) markedly raised, urine calcium measurement and renal ultrasound; CLCN5 or OCRL genetic testing confirms.
tre: Supportive: thiazide diuretics to reduce hypercalciuria with monitoring, high fluid intake, avoid nephrotoxins, treat rickets, monitor renal function and dialysis or transplant for ESRD.

name: Dubin-Johnson Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder, most common in Iranian and Moroccan Jews in Israel (about 1 in 1,300); usually presents in adolescence or early adulthood.
eti: ABCC2 mutations cause deficient MRP2 canalicular transport, impairing excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile.
cli: Chronic or intermittent mild jaundice, sometimes with weakness, mild abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting; benign, with a characteristically black liver.
inv: Predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with otherwise normal liver enzymes; elevated urinary coproporphyrin I fraction, and liver biopsy showing dark pigment when needed.
tre: Benign condition requiring no specific treatment; reassurance and avoiding unnecessary investigations, with caution regarding estrogen-containing contraceptives and pregnancy, which can worsen jaundice.

name: Rotor Syndrome
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder of unknown prevalence, reported worldwide with no sex predisposition; often diagnosed incidentally.
eti: Biallelic loss of both SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 causes OATP1B1/1B3 deficiency, impairing hepatic reuptake of conjugated bilirubin.
cli: Mostly asymptomatic, non-pruritic jaundice or scleral icterus from birth or childhood that may fluctuate; no hepatosplenomegaly.
inv: Mixed, predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes; markedly increased total urinary coproporphyrin and normal liver histology, distinguishing it from Dubin-Johnson.
tre: Benign with normal life expectancy; no treatment is needed beyond reassurance.

name: Crigler-Najjar Syndrome Type 1
epi: Extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder, about 0.6 to 1 per million newborns.
eti: UGT1A1 mutations completely abolish bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity, preventing bilirubin conjugation.
cli: Severe persistent unconjugated jaundice from the first days of life; risk of bilirubin encephalopathy and kernicterus with seizures, choreoathetosis and hearing loss.
inv: Markedly raised serum unconjugated bilirubin without hemolysis; UGT1A1 genetic testing confirms, with no response to phenobarbital distinguishing it from type 2.
tre: Intensive daily phototherapy, with plasmapheresis or exchange transfusion for crises; liver transplantation is the only cure.

name: Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency
epi: Rare autosomal recessive red cell enzymopathy, more frequent in Pennsylvania Amish and Romani communities.
eti: PKLR mutations cause red cell pyruvate kinase deficiency, reducing ATP generation and shortening red cell survival.
cli: Chronic hemolytic anemia ranging from neonatal jaundice or hydrops to mild adult disease; pallor, fatigue, jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones and iron overload.
inv: Normocytic anemia with reticulocytosis, raised LDH and low haptoglobin, negative Coombs test; reduced PK enzyme activity and PKLR genetic testing confirm.
tre: Folic acid, transfusions for symptomatic anemia, iron overload monitoring and chelation, and splenectomy for severe disease with appropriate vaccination.

name: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
epi: One of the most common enzymopathies, about 400 million people worldwide; X-linked, mainly affecting males in historically malaria-endemic regions.
eti: G6PD gene variants reduce NADPH production, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative damage and hemolysis.
cli: Neonatal jaundice with kernicterus risk; acute hemolysis triggered by infection, oxidant drugs or fava beans causing pallor, jaundice, dark urine and fatigue.
inv: Hemolysis labs with bite and blister cells and Heinz bodies; G6PD enzyme assay confirms, repeated after recovery as levels may be falsely normal during acute hemolysis.
tre: Avoid oxidant triggers, treat infection and support hydration, transfuse for severe anemia, phototherapy or exchange transfusion for neonates; avoid methylene blue.

name: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive disorder, fewer than 500 cases reported; usually presents in early childhood, more often with consanguinity.
eti: Biallelic LYST mutations disrupt lysosomal trafficking, producing giant fused granules and defective immune cell, platelet and melanocyte function.
cli: Partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair, recurrent pyogenic infections, mild bleeding, progressive neuropathy and an accelerated HLH-like phase.
inv: Peripheral smear shows giant azurophilic granules in neutrophils; hair microscopy shows clumped melanin; LYST genetic testing confirms.
tre: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only cure for immune defects; HLH-directed immunosuppression for accelerated phase and supportive infection and bleeding care.

name: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)
epi: Rare primary immunodeficiency, about 1 in 200,000 US live births; around 80% of patients are male because the commonest form is X-linked.
eti: Mutations in NADPH oxidase subunits (most often X-linked CYBB/gp91phox, or autosomal recessive NCF1/p47phox) abolish phagocyte respiratory burst and microbial killing.
cli: Recurrent bacterial and fungal infections from early childhood, especially Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus, causing pneumonia, abscesses (skin, liver, lymph nodes) and obstructive granulomas.
inv: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium test shows absent oxidative burst; genetic testing identifies the defective subunit.
tre: Lifelong antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole), aggressive treatment of infections, interferon-gamma in some centers and hematopoietic cell transplantation as cure.

name: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD-1)
epi: Very rare autosomal recessive immunodeficiency, about 1 per million; severe forms historically have high mortality in early childhood.
eti: ITGB2 mutations cause deficient CD18 (beta-2 integrin), preventing leukocyte adhesion to endothelium and migration to infection sites.
cli: Delayed umbilical cord separation, omphalitis, recurrent necrotizing bacterial skin and mucosal infections without pus, poor wound healing and severe periodontitis.
inv: Marked persistent neutrophilia; flow cytometry shows absent or reduced CD18/CD11 on leukocytes; ITGB2 sequencing confirms.
tre: Prompt aggressive antimicrobial therapy and prophylaxis, good dental care, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe disease.

name: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)
epi: About 1 in 58,000 US live births; most infants present within the first six months, and newborn screening now detects most US cases.
eti: Genetic defects in T-cell development (e.g., X-linked IL2RG, JAK3, RAG1/2, ADA deficiency), with variable B and NK cell involvement.
cli: Recurrent severe and opportunistic infections, persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive in infancy; absent lymph nodes and tonsils.
inv: Newborn TREC screening, lymphopenia with very low or absent T cells on flow cytometry, low immunoglobulins and absent lymphocyte proliferation; genetic testing defines subtype.
tre: Infection protection, immunoglobulin replacement, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and irradiated blood products, followed by early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; enzyme replacement or gene therapy for ADA-SCID.

name: Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)
epi: Uncommon primary immunodeficiency of undetermined incidence affecting all ethnic groups without sex predilection; usually begins in infancy.
eti: Heterozygous dominant-negative STAT3 mutations impair IL-6/IL-21/IL-23 signaling and Th17 differentiation, weakening defense against staphylococci and Candida.
cli: Newborn rash and eczema, cold staphylococcal skin abscesses, recurrent pneumonias with pneumatoceles, mucocutaneous candidiasis, coarse facies, retained primary teeth, scoliosis and minimal-trauma fractures.
inv: Markedly elevated serum IgE with eosinophilia and normal other immunoglobulins; chest imaging for pneumatoceles; STAT3 genetic testing confirms.
tre: Prophylactic antistaphylococcal antibiotics and antifungals, abscess drainage, skin care with antiseptic baths, immunoglobulin replacement in selected patients; HSCT for refractory disease.

name: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED)
epi: Rare autosomal recessive disorder, more common in Finns, Sardinians and Iranian Jews; manifestations begin in childhood or adolescence.
eti: AIRE mutations impair thymic negative selection of self-reactive T cells, causing multiorgan autoimmunity.
cli: Classic triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison disease, plus enamel dysplasia, alopecia, vitiligo, keratitis, hypogonadism and autoimmune hepatitis.
inv: Diagnosis by two triad components or one plus affected sibling; anti-interferon-omega/alpha antibodies, calcium, cortisol/ACTH testing and AIRE genetic testing.
tre: Organ-specific management: antifungals for candidiasis, calcium and active vitamin D for hypoparathyroidism, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for adrenal insufficiency, with lifelong surveillance.

name: Homocystinuria
epi: Autosomal recessive disorder affecting at least 1 in 200,000 to 335,000 people worldwide, more frequent in some populations such as Qatar and Norway.
eti: Most cases are due to CBS mutations impairing conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine; rarer forms involve MTHFR, MTR, MTRR or MMADHC.
cli: Downward lens dislocation, myopia, tall marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, intellectual disability and thromboembolism.
inv: Newborn screening by elevated methionine; markedly raised plasma total homocysteine and methionine, confirmed by CBS genetic or enzyme testing.
tre: Pyridoxine trial for responders, methionine-restricted diet with methionine-free formula, betaine, plus folate and vitamin B12 supplementation.

name: Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome
epi: Rare genetic disorder of unknown frequency found in all ethnic groups; most present in infancy as early-onset encephalopathy.
eti: Type I interferonopathy caused by variants in TREX1, RNASEH2A/B/C, SAMHD1, ADAR or IFIH1, mostly autosomal recessive, driving inappropriate interferon activation.
cli: Irritability, sterile fevers, developmental regression, acquired microcephaly, spasticity and dystonia; chilblains, seizures and glaucoma may occur.
inv: Brain CT shows basal ganglia and white matter calcification; MRI leukodystrophy; CSF lymphocytosis with raised interferon-alpha and neopterin; interferon signature and genetic testing.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care including seizure control, nutritional and respiratory support, and surveillance for glaucoma and endocrine complications; immunomodulatory therapies such as JAK inhibitors are under investigation.

name: Rett Syndrome
epi: Affects about 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 live-born females; second most common genetic cause of intellectual disability in girls.
eti: Mostly de novo X-linked MECP2 mutations (about 95% of classic cases); CDKL5 and FOXG1 cause atypical phenotypes.
cli: Normal early development then regression from 6-18 months with loss of purposeful hand use and speech, hand stereotypies, gait abnormality, decelerating head growth, seizures and breathing irregularities.
inv: Clinical diagnosis based on developmental regression and consensus criteria, supported by MECP2 genetic testing.
tre: Multidisciplinary supportive care with physical, occupational and speech therapy, antiseizure medication and scoliosis and nutrition management; trofinetide is FDA-approved for patients aged 2 years and older.

name: Glycogen Storage Disease Type V (McArdle Disease)
epi: Autosomal recessive myopathy, clinically diagnosed in about 1 in 50,000 to 200,000; symptoms begin in childhood but diagnosis is often delayed to adulthood.
eti: PYGM mutations cause muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, blocking glycogen breakdown for energy during exercise.
cli: Exercise intolerance with myalgia, cramps and fatigue in early exercise, second-wind phenomenon, and exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of acute kidney injury.
inv: Persistently raised CK; forearm exercise test shows flat lactate with normal or exaggerated ammonia rise; PYGM genetic testing confirms, with biopsy showing absent myophosphorylase.
tre: No cure; regular moderate aerobic exercise, avoid intense or isometric exertion, pre-exercise sucrose intake, and prompt treatment of rhabdomyolysis.

name: Blau Syndrome
epi: Extremely rare autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disease, affecting fewer than 1 in 1 million children; onset usually before age 4.
eti: Gain-of-function NOD2 mutations cause abnormal innate immune activation and noncaseating granulomatous inflammation.
cli: Triad of granulomatous dermatitis, symmetric polyarthritis with boggy tenosynovitis, and uveitis that can threaten vision; may involve kidneys, vessels and other organs.
inv: Biopsy of skin or synovium shows noncaseating granulomas; NOD2 genetic testing confirms; ophthalmologic screening for uveitis.
tre: Corticosteroids and methotrexate, with TNF inhibitors or other biologics for refractory disease; regular eye monitoring under rheumatology and ophthalmology.

name: Smith-Magenis Syndrome
epi: Estimated birth incidence of about 1 in 25,000; usually sporadic.
eti: De novo 17p11.2 deletion including RAI1 in most cases, or a pathogenic RAI1 variant.
cli: Mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, coarse broad face, short stature, severe sleep disturbance with inverted melatonin rhythm, self-hugging, self-injury and hearing loss.
inv: Chromosomal microarray is first-line, followed by RAI1 sequencing if negative.
tre: Supportive multidisciplinary care: sleep management (melatonin, beta-1 blockers such as acebutolol), early intervention, behavioral and educational support, and comorbidity surveillance.

name: Cogan Syndrome
epi: Rare disorder, about 250 cases reported; mainly affects young adults (mean age about 25) without clear sex predominance.
eti: Presumed autoimmune vasculitis targeting cornea and inner ear, often preceded by an upper respiratory infection.
cli: Non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis with red painful eyes and photophobia plus Meniere-like audiovestibular dysfunction (vertigo, tinnitus, rapidly progressive sensorineural hearing loss); may include aortitis and systemic vasculitis.
inv: Diagnosis of exclusion: slit-lamp examination, audiometry, raised inflammatory markers, syphilis and autoimmune serology to exclude mimics, and vascular imaging or echocardiography for aortitis.
tre: High-dose corticosteroids first-line, with methotrexate, other immunosuppressants or TNF inhibitors for refractory disease; topical steroids for keratitis and cochlear implantation for profound deafness.

name: Acute Superior Mesenteric Vein Thrombosis
epi: Causes about 5-15% of mesenteric ischemia; the superior mesenteric vein is involved in over 90% of cases, mostly in middle-aged adults.
eti: Hypercoagulable states in most patients (inherited thrombophilia, malignancy, myeloproliferative neoplasm, oral contraceptives), plus local abdominal inflammation, cirrhosis or surgery.
cli: Acute form presents with days of diffuse abdominal pain out of proportion to examination, nausea and vomiting; bowel infarction causes peritonitis, GI bleeding and shock.
inv: Contrast-enhanced CT in the portal venous phase shows SMV filling defect and bowel wall thickening; lactate rises with ischemia; thrombophilia and JAK2 screening.
tre: Prompt anticoagulation with heparin then oral anticoagulation, bowel rest and supportive care; thrombolysis or thrombectomy selectively, and surgery for peritonitis or infarcted bowel.

name: Acute Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
epi: Highly contagious respiratory infection resurging despite vaccination; adolescents and adults are common sources, while infants under 1 year bear most deaths.
eti: Bordetella pertussis, a gram-negative coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium and releases toxins; humans are the only reservoir.
cli: Catarrhal phase, then paroxysmal coughing with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting, then convalescence; infants may present with apnea or cyanosis.
inv: Nasopharyngeal PCR (best in first weeks) or culture; lymphocytosis on CBC; serology for late presentation.
tre: Macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin preferred; TMP-SMX alternative), supportive care with infant monitoring, prophylaxis for close contacts, and prevention by DTaP/Tdap including vaccination in pregnancy.

name: Giardiasis
epi: One of the most common treatable causes of gastroenteritis worldwide and the most commonly identified intestinal parasite in the US; peaks in young children.
eti: Protozoan Giardia duodenalis spread fecal-orally by cysts in contaminated water, person-to-person (e.g., childcare) or sexual contact.
cli: Foul-smelling fatty diarrhea, bloating, flatulence and abdominal cramps without blood; chronic infection causes malabsorption, weight loss and lactose intolerance.
inv: Stool antigen tests or PCR; microscopy for cysts or trophozoites, ideally on multiple samples.
tre: Tinidazole, metronidazole or nitazoxanide with rehydration; paromomycin is an option in pregnancy.

name: Pseudogout (Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Deposition)
epi: Disease of older adults, increasing sharply with age, affecting men and women similarly.
eti: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in cartilage; associated with aging, osteoarthritis, hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatasia.
cli: Acute pseudogout causes sudden painful hot swollen joint, most often the knee or wrist; other forms are asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis, OA-like and chronic RA-like arthritis.
inv: Synovial fluid shows rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals on polarized microscopy; radiographs or ultrasound show chondrocalcinosis; exclude septic arthritis.
tre: Acute flares: joint aspiration and intra-articular steroid, NSAIDs, colchicine or oral steroids; colchicine prophylaxis for recurrent attacks and treat underlying metabolic causes.

name: Polycythemia Vera
epi: Myeloproliferative neoplasm with median age at diagnosis around 60, slightly more common in men.
eti: Acquired JAK2 mutation (V617F in about 90%, or exon 12) causes constitutive signaling and erythropoietin-independent myeloproliferation.
cli: Headache, dizziness, aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, facial plethora and splenomegaly; arterial and venous thrombosis and progression to myelofibrosis or leukemia.
inv: Raised hemoglobin or hematocrit, JAK2 mutation, low serum erythropoietin and hypercellular marrow with panmyelosis per WHO criteria.
tre: Phlebotomy to keep hematocrit below 45% plus low-dose aspirin for all; hydroxyurea (or interferon or ruxolitinib) for high-risk patients aged 60 or older or with prior thrombosis.

name: Insulinoma
epi: Rare, but the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor; mostly sporadic and benign, with a minority linked to MEN1.
eti: Pancreatic beta-cell tumor secreting insulin autonomously, despite hypoglycemia.
cli: Whipple triad with fasting hypoglycemia causing adrenergic symptoms (tremor, sweating, palpitations) and neuroglycopenia (confusion, behavior change, seizures); weight gain.
inv: Supervised 72-hour fast showing hypoglycemia with inappropriately raised insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin, low beta-hydroxybutyrate and negative sulfonylurea screen; localize with CT, MRI or endoscopic ultrasound.
tre: Surgical resection (enucleation or partial pancreatectomy) is curative; diazoxide and somatostatin analogs for unresectable disease or bridging.

name: Anti-LGI1 Encephalitis
epi: One of the two most common autoimmune encephalitides, typically affecting older adults with male predominance; rarely paraneoplastic.
eti: Autoantibodies (mainly IgG4) against LGI1, a protein of the VGKC complex, disrupt synaptic function in the hippocampus and cortex.
cli: Subacute limbic encephalitis with memory loss, confusion, psychiatric change and seizures; faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatremia are characteristic.
inv: Serum LGI1 antibodies (more sensitive than CSF); MRI may show medial temporal T2 hyperintensity; EEG; serum sodium; CSF often bland.
tre: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, with antiseizure medication; most respond to first-line therapy, and tumor screening is advised.

name: PAPA Syndrome (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, and Acne)
epi: Very rare autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder that usually begins in childhood with arthritis, while skin features often appear around puberty.
eti: PSTPIP1 mutations increase pyrin inflammasome activity and IL-1 beta production, causing neutrophilic inflammation.
cli: Recurrent sterile pyogenic arthritis causing joint damage, pyoderma gangrenosum and severe cystic acne, often triggered by minor trauma.
inv: Sterile neutrophil-rich synovial fluid with negative cultures, raised inflammatory markers and PSTPIP1 genetic testing confirming diagnosis.
tre: Corticosteroids for flares, with IL-1 blockers (e.g., anakinra) or TNF inhibitors for persistent disease; dermatologic care for acne and pyoderma.

name: Erythrasma
epi: Common superficial skin infection of healthy adults, more frequent in hot humid climates, with diabetes, obesity and older age.
eti: Corynebacterium minutissimum, a gram-positive bacterium, overgrows in moist skin folds.
cli: Well-demarcated reddish-brown, finely scaling, wrinkled patches in the toe webs, groin or axillae; often asymptomatic or mildly itchy.
inv: Wood lamp shows coral-red fluorescence due to porphyrins; skin scraping or Gram stain helps exclude fungal infection.
tre: Topical fusidic acid, clindamycin or erythromycin; oral erythromycin or single-dose clarithromycin for extensive disease, with management of moisture and risk factors.

name: Cyclosporiasis
epi: Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, causing travel-related illness and seasonal US outbreaks linked to imported fresh produce.
eti: Coccidian parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis acquired from contaminated food or water; oocysts must sporulate in the environment, so direct person-to-person spread is unlikely.
cli: Watery diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, cramps, bloating, nausea and prolonged fatigue; relapsing illness lasting weeks to months if untreated.
inv: Stool examination specifically requested: modified acid-fast staining, UV autofluorescence microscopy or molecular PCR panels.
tre: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is first-line with hydration; immunocompromised patients may need longer courses.

name: Calcific Tendonitis
epi: Common cause of shoulder pain in middle-aged adults, more often women; the rotator cuff, especially supraspinatus, is most often affected.
eti: Deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within a tendon by a poorly understood cell-mediated process, with pain peaking during the resorptive phase.
cli: Chronic activity-related shoulder pain or sudden severe pain with restricted movement during resorption, often with night pain and impingement signs.
inv: Plain radiographs show calcific deposits in the tendon; ultrasound localizes deposits and guides intervention.
tre: Most resolve with NSAIDs, physiotherapy and subacromial corticosteroid injection; ultrasound-guided barbotage or shockwave therapy for persistent cases, with arthroscopic removal rarely needed.

name: Subclavian Steal Syndrome
epi: Subclavian stenosis is uncommon and often asymptomatic, affecting men about twice as often as women; the left side is more often involved.
eti: Proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion, usually atherosclerotic, causes reversed flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery to supply the arm.
cli: Arm claudication, numbness or fatigue with exercise and vertebrobasilar symptoms (dizziness, vertigo, syncope, visual disturbance); diminished delayed radial pulse and inter-arm systolic BP difference of at least 15 mmHg.
inv: Duplex ultrasound showing reversed vertebral flow is first-line; CT or MR angiography confirms, with catheter angiography for intervention planning.
tre: Atherosclerotic risk factor control and antiplatelet therapy for asymptomatic patients; angioplasty with stenting or surgical bypass for symptomatic disease.

name: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison Syndrome)
epi: Very rare neuroendocrine tumor, about 1 per million per year, usually in adults aged 30-50; most are pancreatic and over half are metastatic at diagnosis.
eti: Neuroendocrine tumor, usually of the pancreatic tail, secreting excess vasoactive intestinal peptide, which drives intestinal secretion; a small minority is linked to MEN1.
cli: WDHA syndrome: large-volume watery secretory diarrhea persisting with fasting, hypokalemia and achlorhydria, with dehydration, weakness and flushing.
inv: Raised fasting plasma VIP, secretory diarrhea with low stool osmotic gap, hypokalemia; localization with multiphasic CT and somatostatin receptor imaging.
tre: Aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement and somatostatin analogs (octreotide) for symptom control; surgical resection is the only cure.

name: Essential Thrombocythemia
epi: Myeloproliferative neoplasm with incidence of about 1-2.5 per 100,000 per year, more common in women and typically diagnosed at 50-60 years.
eti: Clonal stem cell disorder driven by JAK2 V617F (about half), CALR or MPL mutations, causing megakaryocyte proliferation.
cli: Often incidental thrombocytosis; headache, dizziness, erythromelalgia, arterial or venous thrombosis, bleeding and mild splenomegaly.
inv: Persistent platelet count above 450,000/microL, JAK2/CALR/MPL testing, bone marrow biopsy with enlarged mature megakaryocytes, and exclusion of reactive thrombocytosis and other myeloid neoplasms.
tre: Risk-adapted therapy: low-dose aspirin for most patients, plus hydroxyurea cytoreduction for high-risk patients (age over 60 or prior thrombosis); anagrelide or interferon as alternatives.

name: Isovaleric Acidemia
epi: Autosomal recessive organic acidemia affecting at least 1 in 250,000 people in the US; detected by newborn screening.
eti: IVD mutations cause isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, blocking leucine catabolism and causing toxic isovaleric acid accumulation.
cli: Neonatal poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and coma with a sweaty-feet odor, or later intermittent crises triggered by infection, fasting or protein load, with developmental delay.
inv: Newborn screening showing elevated C5-acylcarnitine; metabolic acidosis with ketosis and hyperammonemia in crises; urine isovalerylglycine on organic acids and IVD genetic testing confirm.
tre: Leucine-restricted, protein-limited diet with glycine and carnitine supplementation; acute crises need high-calorie glucose, stopping protein and metabolic specialist care.

name: Relapsing Polychondritis
epi: Rare immune-mediated disease affecting men and women equally, typically starting in middle age.
eti: Autoimmune inflammation of cartilage and proteoglycan-rich tissue, sometimes with other autoimmune diseases or VEXAS syndrome (UBA1 mutation).
cli: Recurrent painful auricular chondritis sparing the lobule, nasal chondritis with saddle nose, arthritis, eye inflammation, hearing loss and laryngotracheal involvement causing airway collapse; aortic regurgitation may occur.
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by raised inflammatory markers; pulmonary function tests and airway CT for tracheobronchial disease, echocardiography, and cartilage biopsy rarely needed.
tre: NSAIDs, colchicine or dapsone for mild disease; corticosteroids with methotrexate for moderate disease, and immunosuppressants or biologics (e.g., TNF inhibitors) for severe organ involvement.

name: Ovarian Torsion
epi: Gynecologic emergency mostly in women of reproductive age, also seen in girls and in pregnancy; risk is highest with an enlarged ovary or ovarian mass over about 5 cm.
eti: Twisting of the ovary (often with the fallopian tube) on its supporting ligaments, usually around a cyst, dermoid or stimulated ovary, causing venous then arterial obstruction and ischemia.
cli: Sudden severe unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain, often intermittent, with nausea and vomiting; a tender adnexal mass may be felt and fever suggests necrosis.
inv: Pregnancy test to exclude ectopic; pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged edematous ovary, often with a mass and a whirlpool sign; normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion.
tre: Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian preservation whenever possible, cystectomy for an underlying cyst; oophorectomy only if clearly nonviable or malignant.

name: Ruptured Corpus Luteum Cyst
epi: Common cause of acute pelvic pain in women of reproductive age, typically in the second half of the menstrual cycle; more frequent with anticoagulation or bleeding disorders.
eti: The corpus luteum, a vascular cyst formed after ovulation, ruptures and bleeds into the peritoneal cavity, often after intercourse or exercise.
cli: Sudden unilateral lower abdominal pain in the luteal phase, sometimes with peritonism; heavy bleeding causes dizziness, tachycardia and hypotension.
inv: Pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy; pelvic ultrasound shows a complex adnexal cyst with free fluid; full blood count to judge blood loss.
tre: Most settle with analgesia and observation; hemodynamic instability or ongoing bleeding needs resuscitation and laparoscopy to stop the bleeding while preserving the ovary.

name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
epi: Mainly older men over 65, especially smokers, with hypertension or a family history; screening of older men finds most aneurysms before rupture.
eti: Permanent dilatation of the abdominal aorta to 3 cm or more, usually below the renal arteries, from degeneration of the aortic wall linked to atherosclerosis and smoking.
cli: Usually silent; may cause a pulsatile abdominal mass. Rupture presents with sudden abdominal, back or flank pain, hypotension and collapse.
inv: Ultrasound for screening and surveillance; CT angiography for sizing and planning; an unstable patient with suspected rupture goes straight to theatre.
tre: Stop smoking and control blood pressure; repair (endovascular or open) at about 5.5 cm, fast growth or symptoms; rupture needs permissive hypotension and emergency repair.

name: Herpes Zoster (shingles)
epi: Affects up to one in three people over a lifetime, rising sharply after 50 and in immunosuppression; only people who had chickenpox can develop it.
eti: Reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a sensory ganglion, which travels along the nerve to the skin of one dermatome.
cli: Burning pain in one dermatome followed by grouped vesicles on a red base that do not cross the midline; ophthalmic zoster involves the forehead and eye, and a nose-tip rash (Hutchinson sign) warns of eye involvement.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; PCR of vesicle fluid when atypical; urgent eye review with slit lamp for ophthalmic zoster.
tre: Oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir within 72 hours, plus pain control; ophthalmic zoster needs ophthalmology; recombinant zoster vaccine prevents it and postherpetic neuralgia.

name: Breast Abscess
epi: Mostly in breastfeeding women in the first weeks after birth as a complication of mastitis; non-lactational abscesses occur in smokers and around the areola.
eti: Localized collection of pus, usually Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), following milk stasis and mastitis or blocked periareolar ducts.
cli: Painful, red, hot breast lump that is fluctuant, often with fever and malaise, and failure of mastitis to improve on antibiotics.
inv: Breast ultrasound confirms the collection and guides drainage; culture of the aspirated pus; imaging after recovery in older women to exclude cancer.
tre: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated if needed) or incision and drainage, with antibiotics covering S. aureus; breastfeeding or expressing should continue.

name: Acute Mastoiditis
epi: Mostly young children, as a complication of acute otitis media; less common since antibiotics but still the commonest serious complication of ear infection.
eti: Spread of middle ear infection into the mastoid air cells, usually Streptococcus pneumoniae, Group A streptococcus or S. aureus, with possible bone destruction.
cli: Fever, ear pain and recent otitis media with tender red swelling behind the ear that pushes the pinna forward and down; discharge may be present.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; blood tests and cultures; contrast CT of the temporal bone if complications such as abscess, sinus thrombosis or meningitis are suspected.
tre: Admission and IV antibiotics; myringotomy or grommet, and mastoidectomy or abscess drainage if there is no improvement or a complication.

name: Malignant Otitis Externa (necrotizing otitis externa)
epi: Mainly elderly people with diabetes or immunosuppression; rare but dangerous.
eti: Invasive infection of the ear canal, usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa, that spreads to the skull base causing osteomyelitis.
cli: Severe ear pain worse at night, discharge and granulation tissue on the canal floor; cranial nerve palsies, facial nerve first, signal skull base spread.
inv: Raised ESR and CRP, culture of the discharge; CT or MRI to show skull base involvement, with nuclear scans for extent and response.
tre: Prolonged anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin or IV agents) for weeks, tight glucose control, and debridement; surgery is rarely needed.

name: Toxic Shock Syndrome
epi: Rare; staphylococcal cases linked to tampons, nasal packing and wounds, and streptococcal cases to skin and soft tissue infection.
eti: Superantigen toxins from Staphylococcus aureus (TSST-1) or Group A streptococcus activate T cells massively, causing a cytokine storm.
cli: Sudden high fever, diffuse sunburn-like rash, hypotension and multi-organ failure, with desquamation of palms and soles one to two weeks later.
inv: Clinical criteria; blood and site cultures; tests for organ failure (renal, liver, platelets, creatine kinase).
tre: Remove the source (tampon, packing, debride tissue), fluids and vasopressors, and antibiotics including clindamycin to stop toxin production; IV immunoglobulin in severe cases.

name: Foreign Body Aspiration
epi: Most common in toddlers aged 1-3 years (nuts, small toys) and in older adults with poor swallowing or reduced consciousness.
eti: An inhaled object lodges in the larynx or bronchial tree, more often the right main bronchus in adults, causing obstruction and later infection.
cli: Sudden choking then cough, stridor or wheeze; unilateral reduced breath sounds or wheeze; delayed cases present with recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe.
inv: Chest X-ray may show the object or air trapping on expiration; normal films do not exclude it; bronchoscopy confirms.
tre: Complete obstruction needs back blows, chest or abdominal thrusts per age; otherwise rigid bronchoscopy to remove the object.

name: Herpes Simplex Encephalitis
epi: The most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis, occurring at any age with peaks in children and older adults.
eti: Herpes simplex virus type 1 infects the brain, favouring the temporal and frontal lobes and causing hemorrhagic necrosis.
cli: Fever, headache, confusion, behaviour change, seizures and focal signs such as aphasia; reduced consciousness as it progresses.
inv: MRI shows temporal lobe changes; CSF has lymphocytes, red cells and raised protein; HSV PCR of CSF confirms; EEG shows temporal abnormalities.
tre: Start IV acyclovir immediately on suspicion, without waiting for results, for about 14-21 days; manage seizures and raised pressure.

name: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
epi: Heart failure in late pregnancy or the months after birth; more common with older maternal age, multiple pregnancy, preeclampsia and African ancestry.
eti: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction thought to arise from vascular and hormonal injury (including a cleaved prolactin fragment) in susceptible women.
cli: Breathlessness, orthopnea, leg swelling and fatigue around delivery that are easily mistaken for normal pregnancy; arrhythmia and clots can occur.
inv: Echocardiogram showing ejection fraction under 45% with no other cause; raised natriuretic peptide; ECG and chest X-ray.
tre: Standard heart failure therapy adjusted for pregnancy and breastfeeding, anticoagulation when the heart is very weak, bromocriptine in selected cases; many recover, and later pregnancies carry risk.

name: Intracerebral Hemorrhage
epi: About 10-15% of strokes, more common in older people and those with hypertension, anticoagulation or amyloid angiopathy.
eti: Bleeding into the brain tissue, most often from rupture of small vessels damaged by hypertension (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) or amyloid angiopathy in lobar bleeds.
cli: Sudden focal deficit with headache, vomiting and falling consciousness; cerebellar bleeds cause vertigo, ataxia and vomiting and can quickly compress the brainstem.
inv: Urgent non-contrast CT head; clotting tests; CT angiography to look for an underlying vessel lesion.
tre: Reverse anticoagulation, lower blood pressure carefully, supportive stroke care; large cerebellar bleeds or hydrocephalus need neurosurgical evacuation or drainage.

name: Cellulitis
epi: Very common skin infection, especially of the legs in older adults, with risk from leg swelling, obesity, skin breaks, fungal toe infection and diabetes.
eti: Bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat, usually streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, entering through broken skin.
cli: Spreading red, warm, swollen, tender skin, usually on one side, often with fever; erysipelas is the more superficial form with a raised sharp edge.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; marking the edge to follow spread; blood tests and cultures if unwell; ultrasound for abscess or DVT when in doubt.
tre: Oral antibiotics covering streptococci and staphylococci (e.g. flucloxacillin), IV if severe, elevation of the limb, and treatment of the entry point.

name: Influenza
epi: Seasonal winter epidemics worldwide; severe illness mainly in older adults, young children, pregnant women and people with chronic disease.
eti: Influenza A or B virus spread by respiratory droplets; changes in surface proteins (drift and shift) cause yearly outbreaks and pandemics.
cli: Sudden fever, muscle aches, headache, sore throat, dry cough and marked tiredness; complications include viral and secondary bacterial pneumonia.
inv: Usually clinical during outbreaks; rapid antigen or PCR of a nasal swab when it changes care; chest X-ray for suspected pneumonia.
tre: Rest, fluids and fever control; oseltamivir for high-risk or hospitalized patients, best within 48 hours; yearly vaccination prevents it.

name: Hypoglycemia
epi: Most common in people with diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas; also with alcohol, liver or kidney failure, sepsis and rarely insulinoma.
eti: Blood glucose below about 4 mmol/L (70 mg/dL), from too much insulin effect, missed meals, exercise, alcohol or failure of glucose production.
cli: Sweating, shaking, hunger and palpitations, then confusion, odd behaviour, seizures and coma; Whipple triad confirms it.
inv: Bedside and lab glucose; outside diabetes, measure insulin, C-peptide and drug screen during an episode.
tre: If awake, fast-acting oral sugar then a longer carbohydrate; if not, IV glucose or IM glucagon; find the cause and adjust diabetes treatment.

name: Concussion
epi: Common mild traumatic brain injury in contact sports, falls and road accidents, especially in young people.
eti: A blow or jolt to the head causes a temporary disturbance of brain function without structural damage on standard imaging.
cli: Headache, confusion, amnesia around the event, dizziness, nausea, slowed thinking and sometimes brief loss of consciousness.
inv: Clinical assessment with tools such as SCAT; CT head only for red flags (vomiting, falling GCS, seizure, skull fracture signs, anticoagulation).
tre: Brief rest then gradual return to school, work and sport, removed from play the same day; most recover in weeks; repeat injury before recovery is dangerous.

name: Alcoholic Hepatitis
epi: Occurs in heavy long-term drinkers, often after a binge; severe cases carry high short-term mortality.
eti: Alcohol-induced inflammation and liver cell injury, frequently on top of fatty liver or cirrhosis.
cli: Recent onset jaundice, fever, tender enlarged liver, ascites and confusion; often with signs of chronic liver disease.
inv: High bilirubin, AST raised above ALT (usually 2:1, under 400), raised neutrophils and INR; ultrasound to exclude obstruction; Maddrey or MELD to judge severity.
tre: Stop alcohol, nutrition and thiamine, treat infection and withdrawal; prednisolone in severe disease without contraindications; transplant in selected patients.

name: Hypertensive Emergency
epi: Occurs in a small share of people with hypertension, often after stopping treatment, and with drugs such as cocaine or in kidney disease.
eti: Very high blood pressure (often over 180/120) causing acute damage to organs such as the brain, heart, kidneys, eyes or aorta.
cli: Headache, visual change, confusion, chest pain, breathlessness or seizures, with signs such as retinal hemorrhages, papilledema and acute kidney injury.
inv: Repeat blood pressure; fundoscopy, ECG, troponin, kidney function, urinalysis, and CT head or chest imaging guided by symptoms.
tre: ICU-level care with IV agents (e.g. labetalol, nicardipine), lowering pressure by no more than about 25% in the first hour, faster only for aortic dissection or eclampsia.

name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
epi: Mostly people over 50, more often women; in younger people it raises the question of multiple sclerosis.
eti: Usually compression of the trigeminal nerve root by a blood vessel; secondary causes are multiple sclerosis plaques and tumours.
cli: Sudden electric-shock pain in one side of the face along the maxillary or mandibular branches, lasting seconds, triggered by touch, chewing, talking or brushing teeth.
inv: Clinical diagnosis; MRI of the brain to look for vessel compression, MS or tumour, especially in younger or atypical patients.
tre: Carbamazepine first line (oxcarbazepine as an alternative); microvascular decompression or ablative procedures when drugs fail.

name: Forearm Fracture
epi: Very common in children and in older adults after a fall on an outstretched hand; distal radius fractures dominate in osteoporotic women.
eti: A break of the radius, ulna or both, from falls, sports or direct blows; patterns include Colles, Smith, Monteggia and Galeazzi fractures.
cli: Pain, swelling, tenderness and deformity of the forearm or wrist, with reduced movement; check for nerve damage and circulation.
inv: X-rays of the forearm including the elbow and wrist joints, to catch associated dislocations.
tre: Closed reduction and cast for stable fractures; surgical fixation for displaced or unstable fractures and most adult both-bone fractures; watch for compartment syndrome.

name: Supracondylar Humerus Fracture
epi: The most common elbow fracture in children, peaking around ages 5-7, usually after a fall on an outstretched hand.
eti: A break of the distal humerus just above the condyles, mostly extension type with the lower part displaced backwards.
cli: Painful swollen elbow held still, with deformity; check the radial pulse and the anterior interosseous, median, radial and ulnar nerves.
inv: Elbow X-rays; a posterior fat pad sign suggests a hidden fracture; the Gartland classification guides treatment.
tre: Undisplaced fractures go in a cast; displaced fractures need closed reduction and pinning; a pulseless pale hand is an emergency; watch for compartment syndrome.

name: Red Man Syndrome (vancomycin flushing reaction)
epi: A common infusion reaction to vancomycin, more likely with fast infusion and large doses.
eti: Direct release of histamine from mast cells caused by the drug, not a true allergy; it can also occur with some other drugs.
cli: Flushing, itching and red rash of the face, neck and upper body during or soon after the infusion, sometimes with low blood pressure and chest discomfort.
inv: Clinical diagnosis linked to infusion timing; distinguish from anaphylaxis, which has wheeze, swelling or severe hypotension.
tre: Stop or slow the infusion and give an antihistamine; restart more slowly (over at least 1-2 hours); it does not prevent future use of vancomycin.

name: Arrhythmia (dysrhythmia)
epi: Very common at all ages and rising steeply with age; atrial fibrillation is the most frequent sustained arrhythmia, while benign ectopic beats and sinus arrhythmia are common in healthy people.
eti: Disturbed impulse formation (abnormal automaticity, triggered activity) or conduction (re-entry, block), often from ischemic or structural heart disease, electrolyte imbalance, thyroid disease, drugs, stimulants or inherited channelopathies.
cli: Palpitations, dizziness, breathlessness, chest discomfort, presyncope or syncope; may be silent, and dangerous ventricular rhythms can cause cardiac arrest or sudden death.
inv: 12-lead ECG during symptoms, with ambulatory (Holter or event) monitoring for intermittent episodes; electrolytes, thyroid function and echocardiography look for causes, and electrophysiology study maps selected rhythms.
tre: Unstable patients need immediate cardioversion or defibrillation (or pacing for bradycardia); otherwise correct the cause and use rate or rhythm control drugs, catheter ablation, pacemakers or ICDs, with anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation by stroke risk.

name: Monoplegia
epi: Uncommon pattern of weakness seen at any age; in children it is most often a form of cerebral palsy, and in adults it follows stroke, trauma or nerve injury.
eti: A focal lesion of the motor cortex (stroke, tumor, abscess, demyelination) or of the brachial or lumbosacral plexus, nerve roots or peripheral nerves; also cerebral palsy, spinal cord lesions and functional neurological disorder.
cli: Paralysis or marked weakness of one limb; upper motor neuron causes give spasticity and brisk reflexes, while plexus or nerve causes give flaccid weakness, wasting, reduced reflexes and sensory loss in that territory.
inv: Careful neurological examination to localize the lesion; MRI of the brain or spine for central causes, nerve conduction studies and electromyography for plexus or nerve injury, and plexus imaging when needed.
tre: Treat the underlying cause (acute stroke care, decompression, surgery for nerve injury); physiotherapy, occupational therapy, splints and spasticity management support recovery of function.
